IN PARLIAMENT, SESSION 1888. FRODSHAM GAS AND WATER (Dissolution of Frocisham Gas Company, Limited • Incorporation of New Company; vesting in them of undertaking of dissolved Company ; Re- gulation of capital, &c., of new company; additional eapital ; separation of gas and water undertakings; power to supply gas and water; maintenance and extension of gas works; manufacture and storage of gas and residual products ; manufacture of meters, &e. ; patent rights; construction of water works ; prevention of waste of gas and water, &c.;
• • • . acquisition of lands, rates and charges ; price, ke., of gas and water; breaking up of streets; agreements with local

. - - ' authorities, bodies, and persons; incorporation and amend- ment of Acts, and other purposes). NOTICE 'IS HEREBY GIVEN that application is intended to be Ingule to Parliament in the ensuing session for leave to bring in a Bill (hereinafter called the Bill) for all or some of the following, among other purposes, that is to say:— To dissolve the Frodsham Gas Company, Limited (herein- after called "the Limited Company") and to cancel or annul their memorandum and Articles of Association, and certificate of incorporation, and provide for the winding up of the Limited Company, and the discharge of their liabilities. To incotrrate into a company (hereinafter called "the Company ) the shareholders of the Limited Company or some of them, with or without other persons, or corporations, under such name as may be prescribed by the Bill. To apply, for the purposes of the Company and of the Bill, the capital and funds of the Limited Company, and to define, declare, and regulate the undertaking capital and borrowing powers of the Company, and the rights and privileges of the shareholders.

_ To make provision for the vesting and apportionment of the shares and capital of the Limited Company, or of any new shares or stock instead thereof, in and among the shareholders of the Company. To authorize the Company to raise _further capital; to bor. row on mortgage or otherwise, and to create and issue deben- ture stock.

To make provision (if thought fit) for the separation of the Gas and Water Undertakings of the Company, and of the capital employed therein, and the profits and revenue arising therefrom, and for the keeping of separate accounts in relation to such undertakings respectively. To vest in the Company the undertaking lands, buildings, mains, pipes, plant, moneys, rights, powers privileges, liabiliGes, easements, agreements, and licenses of Limited Company, and to authorise the Company to execute the works and exercise all or any of the powers,, and to effect all or any of the objects hereinafter mentioned.

To empower the Company to supply with gas and water for domestic trading, public, sanitary, and other purposes, the whole or any part of all or some of the townships following, that is to say, Frodsham, Frodsham Lordship, Relsby, Alvanley, Newton-by-Frodsham, and Kingsley, in the Parish of Prod- sham, and Sutton, in the Parish of Runcorn, all in the County Palatine of Chester. _ . _ _ _

To authorise the Company to purchase, take on lease, or ac- quire by compulsion or agreement, and to hold and use for thepurposes of their undertaking, all or some of the following lands, that is to say—A piece of land in the said township and parish of Frodsham belonging or reputed to belong to John Higson, and adjoining the present site of the Limited Com- pany's gas works in Gas Works-road, and bounded on the south-east by the said present site of the Limited Company's gas works, on the south-west by land belonging, or reputed to belong to John Ashton ; on the north-east by an occupation road running from the Gas Works-road to the field numbered 116 on sheet xxivls of the Ordnance Ordnance Survey, 1873, for the Parish of Frodsham; and on the north-west by other lands belonging, or reputed to belong to the said John Higson, and to authorise the Company on thosellands, or part or parts thereof, and on the lands hereinafter described as the sites of the Limited Company's existing gas works, to erect, construct, and make, and to maintain, and continue, and from time to time to extend, enlarge, and improve gas works and works for the manufacture, distribution, storage, and supply of gas, and for the manufacture, conversion, utilization, storage, and dis- tribution of materials used in and about the manufacture of gas, and of residual products resulting from such manefacture, and to empower the Company on, and from all such lauds, to manufacture, store, and supply gas, and to manufacture, con- vert, utilise, distribute., and store such materials and residual products as aforesaid. The sites of the Limited Company's existing gas works consists of the pieces, of land hereinafter described, that is to say:— (a) A piece of land belonging, or reputed to belong to the Limited Company, in the said township and parish of Frod- sham, bounded on the north-east by an occupation road running from the Gas Works-road to the field numbered 116 on sheet xxiv 15 of the ni6T, Ordnance Survey (1873), for the said parish of Frodsham ; on thenorth-westby land belonging, or reputed to belong to John Hives' _Lori the south-west,partly by land belonging, or reputed to belong to John Ashton, and partly by an occupation road running from the main street of Frodsham to the field numbered 167 on the said Ordnance Sur- vey; and on the south-east partly by the bowling-green belong- ing to the Bear's Paw Hotel, and partly by gardens belonging, or reputed to belong to Halstead Clough. (b) A piece of land belonging, or reputed to belong to the Limited Company in the said township aud parish of Prod- sham, bounded on the north-west by Ship-street; an the south- west by Plunibton-lane - on the south-east by certain gar- dens belonging, or reputed to belong to William Mayes Picker- ing, Mrs Margaret Ashton, and John Robinson respectively; pus on;the north-east by land belonging, or reputed to belong to William Hayes. To authdise the Company to manufacture, purchase, sell, let on hire, or otherwise deal in meters, tubes, pipes, lamps, burners, fittings, and other apparatus, articles, and things used in the supply of gas and water, and to have, hold, use, enjoy, and exercise all powers, rights, privileges, and authori- ties necessary, proper, or convenient for the purposes aforesaid, and generally to carry on the business usually carried on by gas and water companies. To empower the Company to Manu- facture, purchase, provide, sell, let On hire, and fix stoves, ranges, fittings, engines, machinery, apparatus, and appliances for lighting, for motive power, for heating, cooking, ventilat- ing, manufacturing, or any other purpose whatever, and to supply or work the same by means of gas. To give powers to the Company to acquire, hold, use, and exercise pateut rights and licenses in relation to the manufacture, storage, and dis- tribution, and utilization of gas and residual products, and in relation to the supply of water. To authorise the Company to make and maintain the water- works and other works and conveniences following, or some of them, that is to say:— .(1) A Well and bore hole and Pumping Station with pump- . ing Engines, Engines and Boiler House, chimney and all other necessary works buildings and conveniences, situatenear the town of Frodsham in the township and parish of Prod- sham, in the County Palatine of Chester, in a field belonging to Henry Linaker and in the occupation of Mary Forster, and numbered 206 on sheet No. XXIV, 16, of the -,-Arcs ordnance Survey, dated 1873, for the Parish of Frodsham. (2) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 1) to be situate in the ; townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship in the said I parish of Frodsham commencing at the said well and borehole land Pumping Station, above described, and terminating in the Inteildedlow service or Overton Reservoir hereinafter de- scribed at the north cast angle thereof. (3) A Low service rectangular Reservoir to be called the Overton Reservoir and to be situated in the said townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordshipandparlsh of Frorlsistm at or near the south east end of the Field belonging to and in the occupation of Mrs. Martha Aston and numbered an the said ordnance Survey 334 in the township of Frodsham and 216 in the township of Frodsham Lordship. (4) An approach road to be situate in the said townsh,ips of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship and parish: of Frodsharn commencing by a junction with Townfield Lane, at a point about 319 yards measured in a straight line eastwards of the entrance gate to the Vicarage of Frodsham and terminating at the south-west corner of the said Fieldmumber 334, in the said township of Frodsham and 216 in the said township of Prod- sham Lerdship. (5) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 2) to be situate wholly In the said township of Frodshani Lordship and parish of Frodsham commencing by a junction with the said intended aqueduct, or line of pipes (No. 1 at a point about 44 yards eastwards of the north 'west corner of the said field No. 134 in the township of Frodsham and 216 in the township of Frodsham Lordship and about 129 yards northwards of the south-west corner of that Field and terminating in an intended well or tank to be situate in the south-east corner of the said field. (6) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 3) to be situate in the said townships of FrodsluunandFrodsham Lordship anal parish of Frodsham commencing at a pond in the north-west corner of a field forming part of the Glebe of the vicarage of Frodsham In the occupation of John Pollard, and numbered 333 on the said ordnance survey and terminating in the said intended Overton Reservoir at the north-west angle thereof. (7) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 4) to be situate in the said townships of Frodsliam and Frodsham Lordship and parish of Frodsham, commencing by a junction with the aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 5) hereinafter described at a point in the Main-street of the town of Frodsham, at the junc- tion of Church-street with Main-street, and terminating in the said intended Overton Reservoir at the South East angle thereof. (8) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 6) to be situate in the townships of Helsby, Frodsham Lordship, and Frodsham, in , the parish of Frodsham, and in the township of Sutton, in the , parish of Runcorn, in the County Palatine of Chester, com- mencing at a point on the highway leading from Chester to Warringtomabout 390 yards south westwards of the south west corner of the station master's house at the Helsby and Alvan- ley Station, on the West Cheshire Railway, and terminating at a point on the same road about 200 yards north eastwards of the centre of the bridge carrying that road over the river Weaver, known as Frodsham Bridge, (9) A high -service reservoir, to be called the Beacon Reser- voir, and to be situate wholly in the said township of Prod- sham Lordship, at the southern 'end of the field or en- closure on Beacon Hill, belonging to Edward Abbott Wright, numbered 8 on sheet xxxii. 1. of the rkr„ ordnance survey, dated 1873, for the said parish of Frodsham. (10) An aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 8) to be situate in the townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship, or one of them, in the said parish of Frodsham, commencing in the said Intended Beacon Reservoir, on the north east side thereof, and terminating in the said intended Overton Reservoir at the south east angle thereof. . (11) An aqueduct or line of Pipes: (No. 7) to be situate in the townships of Alvanley, Helsby, and Frodsham Lordship in the said parish of Frodsham commencing at a point in the highway at or near the junction of the roads in the village of Alvanley opposite Green Bank Farm House, and about 83 , yards westwards of the north-west angle of the Church of St. • John the Baptist In Alvanley, and terminating in the said Intended Beacon Reservoir on the south-west side thereof. (12) An aqueduct or line of Pipes (No. 8) 40 be situate in

the said townships of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship and parish oi Frodsham, commencing in the said intended Baacon Reservoir on the south-west side thereof and terminating by a innetion with the said intended aqualuet or line of pipes (No. 3) at a point in Townfield-lane about 44 yards north-east- wards of the north-west corner of the said field No. 334 in the said township of Frodsham, and 216 in the said township of Frodsham Lordship.

(13) An aqueduct or line of Pipes (No. 9) to be situate in the townships of Frodsharn Lordship, Newton-by-Frodsbam, and Kingsley, and the said parish of Frodsham, commeneingby a junction with the said intended aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 7) at a point in the highway in the village of Overton about 9 yards eastwards of the north-east angle of the Ring-o- Bells publichouse, and terminating at a point in the highway at or near the junction of the roads in the village of Kingsley opposite the farm buildings of Kingsley Hall, and about 23 yards eastwards of the north-east angle of the Post Office. (14) An aqueduct or line of Pipes (No. 10) to be situate in the said townships of Newton-by Frodshatri and Kingsley and parish of Frodsham, commencing at a point in the highway in the village of Newton about 113 yards eastwards of the south- east angle of the old Manor House, and terminating by a junction with the said intended aqueduct or line of pipes (No. 9) at a point about 190 yardsaoutli-eastwards of the south, eastern angle of the Lowerhowse Farm House. Together with all necessary and prpper embankments, walls, fences, tanks, wells, dams, drains, iluices, cloughs, valves, hydrants, air-calves, cleansing pipes, culverts, engines, pipes, buildings, machinery, roads, and other works and conveni- ences for the collecting, storing. anddistributing of water. To enable the Company to ,divert into the said intended waterworks, and to collect, take, use, and appropriate for the purpose of their undertaking all such underground streams, springs, and waters as can be collected or obtained by the pro- I posed works, or any of them, or as may be found in or under ' any of the lands belonging to, or to be acquired by, or vested in the Company under the powers of the Bill. To enable the Company to make effectual Provisions and regulations for the protection of tho Waterworks, and other I works and property of the Company, and for preventing the waste, fouling, and misuse of gas and water, and for defining • andregulatingthe supply-of gas and vratPr by them, whether by ' meter or otherwise, and the terms mid conditions of such , supply. To authorise the Company to deviate laterally from the lines of the intended waterworks within the limits shown upon the ' plans hereinafter mentioned, or as may beprovided by the Bill, and whether within or beyond the limits lot deviation allowed by the Waterworks Clauses Act, 1847, and to deviate vertically , to any extent from the levels of those waterworks as shown !upon the sections hereinafter mentioned. To empower the Company by compulsion or agreement to purchase, acquire, and to'take on leaite, lands, houses, springs, streams, wells, waters, waterworks, and other hereditameuts within the parishes, townships, and places mentioned in this notice, or some of them which may be required for the purposes of the intended gasworks and waterworks, or otherwise requisite or desirable for the purposes of the VII, and to take compul- sorily or by agreement easements iu or over any such lands, houses, or other property and hereditaments, and to vary and ex- tinguish all rights of way and other tights and privileges con- nected with any such lands, property, and hereditaments, To exempt the Company from the operation of section 92 of the Lands Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845, so as to enable them to purchase compulsorily parts only of certain properties. To empower the Company to levy and recover rents, rates, and charges, differential and otherwise, for, or in respect of the supply of gas and water, and for the sale or hire of meters, fittings, stoves, ranges, engines, machinery, apparatus, and ap- pliances—to alter existing 'rates, rents, duties, and charges, and to confer, vary, and extinguish exemptions from the pay- ment of rates, rents, duties, and charges. \ To make provision with respect to, and to regulate the price of water and gas to be charged by the Company, and the quality and pressure of gas to be supplied by them, and the amount of profit which may be divided among the Shareholders of the Company in respect of their gas and water under- takings or either of them. , To authorise the Company to lay down, maintain, take up, alter, and repair mains, pipes, culverts, conduits, sluices, drains, and other works in, through, under, over, across, and along, and to cross, break up, opeu; alter, divert, stop up, or otherwise interfere with, either temporarily or permanently, any roads, highways, occupation roads, footpaths, public places, bridges, canals, navigations, 'towing paths, railways tramways, works, pipes, sewers, drains, rivers, atriums, brooks. I and watercourses in any of the parishes, ;townships, and I places before mentioned, so Mr as may be necessary or con- venient for the supply of gas and water; or for all or any of the purposes of the bill. . To empower the Company from time to time, to sell, ex- change, let on lease, or otherwise to, dispose of any lands or pfoperty at the time belonging to thentrwhich they may not require for the purposes of their undertaking', To enable the Company on the one hand, and any Sanitary Authority, Local Board, Public Body, Company, or persons on the other hand, to enter into, and carry into effect, contracts, agreements, and arrangements for, or with respect to, the sup- ply by the Company to any Sanitary Autherity, lecsl Board, Public Body, Company, .or persons, of gas and water, in bulk or otherwise, within and beyond the limits of supply of the Company for any public, sanitary, trading, or other purpose, or for, or with respect to, the transfer to and vesting in any such Public Body of any part of the Company's undertakings; and to authorise any such Sanitary. Authority, Local Board, Public Body, Company, or persons respectively, to apply their • funds, and to raise further moneys for the purpose of any such ' Contract, agreement, or arrangement, and to sanction and confirm any such Contract, agreement, or arrangement already made, or which, prior to the passing of the Bill, may be made with respect to ,he matters aforesaid, or to make other pro- visions in relation to any such matters. • To confer upon the Company all powers, rights, and authori- ties which are or may become necessary for carrying into effect the powers and objects of the Bill, or are usually conferred on Gas and Water Companies. To vary or extinguish all rights and privileges which would in ally manner impede or interfere with the objects and pur- poses of the Bill, and to confer other rights and privileges. To incorporate with the Bill, with or without such variations and modifications as may be deemed expedient, all or some of the provisions of "The Companies Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845," "The Companies Clauses Act, 1863," "The Lands Clauses Consolidation Acts, 1845, 1880, and 1869," "The Waterworks Clauses Acts, 1847 and "The Gas Works Clauses Act, 1647,"" The Gas Works Clauses Act, 1871," and such parts of "The Railways Clauses Consolidation Act, 1845 " as relate to roads and the temporary occupation of lands, and such other parts of such Act as may be provided by the Bill. To alter, amend, extend, enlarge, or repeal, so far as may be necessary for the purposes of the Bill, all tu some of the provi- sions of any Act whicla may relate to or be affected by the Bill. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIMES, that on or before the 30th day of November instant, plans and sections of the works proposed to be authorised by the Bill, and- plans of the lands to be taken compulsorily under the powers of the Bill. together with a book of reference to suCh plans, containing the names the owLiere or reputed owners, lessees or reputed lessees, and occupiers of the lands, and a copy of this notice, as published in the " Loudon Gazette," trill be deposited for public inspection with the Clerk of the Peace for the County Palatina, of Chester, at his "Office at Chester; and that on or before the. mid 30th day of November, a copy of so much of the said plans, sections, and books of reference at relates to each of the parishes from, in, through, or into which the said intended works will be made, or in which any lands or houses intended to be taken are situate, and is copy Of .this notice published as aforesaid, will be depositel for public inspection with the parish clerk of each such parish at his, residence. On or before the 21st day of December next printed copies of the Bill will he deposited in the Private Bill Office of tke • House of Commons. • Dated this 11th day of November, 1887. • LINAKER is LINARICR, Solicitors, Runcorn. div.p: A. • RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. TO TR' "OWD RIB."

lleaw time's rolled on sin fost we met th' days o' " owd tang syne !' Tha's bin ml comfort sin tha sw;.pt Thad name o' thine for mine. Tho trouble's pelted us wi storms, Tin eleawds slipt t' leet between, Aveve allus fun luv glintin eawt I' th' glances o' thi een.

We've hed cawr share o' ups un deawns, Bud getten thro"em o; For lowly foak—siteh like as us— They hevn'd far to fo. God knows life's black ennff fort' poor, As suffer, toil, un dare; Bud mates like thee meks monkind laff th' face o' grim Despair.

We've built up lots o' gowden hopes, As tumbled, one bi one; We'd two sweet blooms as breetened life, Deoth touched 'em,—un ther gone! Ther's four yet—two o' eyther sooart— As cluster at thi knee; Two lasses, pretty as thisel, Two lads as favver me. Tha thinks reet weel o't' childer, lass; Hey, mony a time aw've thowt If they bud knew ther mother's mind, They'd ne'er be cramm'd un nowt. Theis nobry knows, bud thee un me, Wed cares we've lied to face, Thin' t' childer, bless 'em! ther breet smiles, Like sunshine, nh ot' place. Heaw oft o' wintry neets we've set Un camped un tawkt o'er t' past; Un towd eawr thowts o'er t' lad we took To Cemetery t' last. Un then tha's sobbed, un tears he 3 fo'n, I mother's grief to tell, Un awve stown softly eawt to hey A quate cry bi misel.

Tha,'s allus done t' best way tha cud When awve bin eavrt o' wark, To keep mi spirits cheerful, un Tha's sung just like a lark. This tried hard to decave me then, When meyt wur scarce as brass; Bud th' quiver fluttered i' thi voice As towd me t' truth, mi lass. Aw know we're geddin owder, lass, 800 l youth stops ytt th' heart, lin wheer thers comfortable foak, Luv acts a gradely part. Thad same to me as e'er tha wort lin dearer, if its owt ; Fr t' bits o' flys, i' temper heots, 0 reckon up to nowt.

'Ma's moythert oft thad heyd o' thine To try and keep o streyt ; When things wur bad, tba helped me through A rough, un uphill f eight. 1.7 n whether th' eawtlook's breet or dark, Thar t upreet, square un true; to to thi childer, hooam un me, Tha sticks as clooase as glue!
JACK e ANN'S.

. Speaking about alacrity, you should observe a clerk back up an early-closing notice on a store door. Some singers at a concert were somewhat startled the ether evening by finding that the selection "When wearied wretches sink to sleep," had been printed on the ptogramme "When married wretches," &c. "Never marry a widower," was the advice of a young matron to a friend. "But you married one, " Why ?", "It's bad enough to have to hear about your husband's mother's cooking, but to have his first wife's biscuits thrown in your face every morning is simply unbearable.' David Dale, who was a man of short stature, on enter- ing, his counting-house one frosty morning' 'complained of the state of the streets, and mentioned that he had "fallen a his length." "And what of that, sir," remark- ed an old bookkeeper, "I'm sure a gentleman o' your beight couldna fa ony great length.' A young man from the city who had fallen in love with a country girl, went to her father—a blunt old far- mer—and, with a polite flourish, said, "Sir, I have come _ _ .
to ask vu for the hand of your daughter in marriage. The old man, looking at him in surprise, responded, "Her hand! Only her hand! Why didn't you ask for the

gal !" An edition, apparentiy unknown hitherto, of the New Testament in English has turned up, and is in the pos- session of far. Toon, the well-known bookseller. • It was printed at Dort by Catlin in 1601, "at the expensis of the aires of Henrie Charteris and Andrew Hart, in Edin- burg." It registers in eights, and is very small. only 31 by 1 inches. Canin printed an octavo Bible for Char. tens and Hart in 1601. and an octavo New Testament in 1603, both much larger than this volume, and having a • commentary on the marttin.—Atheyeton. When Captain Grose first went over to Ireland, his CUriousity led him to see everything in the capital worth ' seeing. In the course of his perambulations he one even- ing strolled into the principal meat market in Dublin, when the butchers as usual, sent up the constant cry. t I What do you buy, nhat do you buy, master ?" Grose parried this for some time by saying "he wanted nothing." At last a butcher started from his stall. eyeing Orose's figure from top to bottom, which was like Dr. Slop's in "Tristram Shandy," and exclaimed, "Well, sir, though yon don't want anything at present, only say you buy your meat of me, and you'll make my fortune." Do ANIMALS TAM TO ONE Aim mica ?—Among birds there is a universally understood signal of danger. In some cases it is the shrill scream of the swallow and swift; in others the repeated despairing cry of the thrush and blackbird; or it niay be the hiss of the tom- tit and wryneck ; the "pink, pink" of the chaffinch; the "cluck, cluck" of the farm-yard hen; but wherever or whenever it is heard, all the feathered tribe instantly seek some place of refuge. But quite apart from this Well-,known warning, there are numerous instances -which seem to he conclusive that birds also communi- cate their ideas to each other. One day. while sitting hidden in the garden, I observed a crow fly to a wood. pigeon's nest, which was in a tree close above me, and bring from it one of their eggs which was hard set. Carrying it in his beak, he flew to a neighbouring tree, 'toad proceeded to pull out the young one from the shell and eat it slowly. Presenty, another crow came sailing along on leisurely wing, and seeing what was happening, he alighted beside the thief, who must have explained everything very clearly, as, after a minute or two, the new corner flew straight to the wood-pigeon's nest, which was well hidden in the tree, and, notwithstanding • the cries and resistance of the parent birds, he soon ap- peared with the flecond egg, whiclOie ate with much relish on the grass a short distance from me.—Little

:F-olkst Magazine: TRE THRIFT OF THE WORKING CLAssF.s.—During the quarter of a century which has. just elapsed since the Post Office Savings Banks were established broadcast throughout the three kingdoms, the amount of money that has been saved through their instrumentality by the wage-earning classes, for whose benefit chiefly they were proposed, is simply marvellous, and speaks most elo- quently indeed for the providence of the people. In this .'period, over one hundred and seventy millions sterling has been received, and over one hundred and thirty mil- lions paid by these banks alone, with nearly fifty millions standing at present at the credit of their depositors. But .tothese extraordinary large figures there are, of course, yet to be added those representing the sums received, paid, and now at credit of depositors in the older or Trustee Savings Banks. Some of these banks were established in 181'7, but the majority by Act of Parlia- ment in 1836, so that necessarily they had the advantage over the Post Office Banks by reason of age and experi- ence. To show that they have done, and are still doing, a vast amount of good to hundreds of thousands of indi- viduals, one has simply to mention that since the system was first established, over two hundred Millions have - been deposited, and nearly two hundred and forty mil- lions, including interest, paid, while the present capital sum at credit of' over a million and a half depositors approaches nearly to fifty millions sterling !—Cassell's Magazine, for November. To EISIPLOYFRS.—I have so often advocated the great importance of providing interesting and improving books and periodicals for our servants, that I will not ' dwelt on the subject now; but lam certain if we could provide them with healthful recreations they would greatly appreciate them. The late Lord Derby used to take delight in watching his servants play cricket. There as One point that those interested in the welfare of ser- vants should bring before them—that is, the duty of thrift. No doubt a very large number of servants prac- tise great self-denial in order to support parents, and in some cases even distant relations. In fact, I believe that extraordinary virtues exist among servants; I have beard of so many cases of almost heroic self-denial among quite young men and women. But where there is no particular motive for saving, it is to be feared that servants are no more free than other people from tempta- tion to fritter away their money. MT. Granville Baker, of Hardwicke Court,Gioncestershire, on of Mr. Barwick Baker, the well-known practical philanthropist, has pub- lished for distribution a report of the workings of Aids to Thrift. The pamphlet explains the system he pur- sues, and when I mention that through his encourage- ment his butler—Who was a single man—saved nearly sixty pounds in three years, his groom forty-two pounds n fonrlyears, and his nursery-maid (out of wages rang- ng from eight pounds to fourteen pounds) saved thirty- eight pounds in nine years, it will be seen that the plan was successful. Mr. Baker used to mention the advan- tages of thrift to his servants, and generally found them ery glad to to advised.—Lady John Manners, in The 11 'item Qts it Rotron, RED, Oft. A. VISIT TO CROFT. BY Bnorrusat Warms. Well, mi friends, awd heeard so mich abeawt th',l pony le hearns un a lot moore bits o' strange seeti fort be seen at Croft, so one day last wick bein' led bi curiosity us mich us owt else, aw thowt awd her a ramble us far as theere un use mi own opinion o' that part oth' cnntry accordini to what aw seed missel. Aw started fro' th' Tooad-row, Chowbent, abeawt eight o'clock on th' morn o' last Munday, un thinkin' us Croft wur tother soide o' Manchester, aw seet eawt that direckshun. So after givin' eawr Sal sum good wards o' advice an leevin' her un mi noine nippers eighteenpence fur spendin' money while aw wur away, aw bid urn aw good mornin', un slung mi neddy away froth' heawse. Awd gon abeawt a theasund yards when aw met an owd pal o' moine. He / ses, "liullo, Jemmy! wheere yo' gooin' this toime oth' mornin'? Yo' favvurn drest up un gon eawt." Aw ses, "Awm ony gooin' as far as Croft fun, see th' pony wi' beams, but goodness knows what swat see afore aw see eawr Sal agen." He ses "B,eet, owd crate egg, un aw expect thall naer meet wi no bad luck on thi road." Aw thankt him, un seet off agen. ANY' hadn't gon far, heawever, when aw meets a lad un wench us fayvurt us iv they wur gooin' a gerrin' wed un mist them road to th' church, bur aw tuk no notice on urn un past on, bur, after awd gon past urn a bit th wench ses to th' lad," I say, Peter, who is that gentleman? He favours the Duke of Marlboro' to a tee. I see th' Duke at Windsor one time; he's the features of that gentleman to all the world. I'm certain almost it's the Duke.' Th' chap .sed nowt, but after awd heeard so mich abeawt aw thowt aw wudn't ler her her aw her own road, bur awZ tell her different, so aw bawls eawt,"Tha wants th' Duck o' 3fuldoon ; awm nowt oth' soart. Awm Jemmy Whims, troth' Tooad-row. Chovrbent, un awm gooin' t' Croft furt see th' pony wi' beams." Th' chap stared un sed, "Youre going to Croft! I'm terribly afraid you're in the wrong direction, sir." " Ger away wi thi," aw sed, "dust o think aw dunno th road to Croft when aw us't keep a butch- er's shop i' Croft, un carry aw th' beef us aw sowd away fro Manchester on mi back, un one tonne mi mother un me went to Manchester un boo pitched hersel up ith air en nobdys, naer heeard nowt on her sin. Aw wur seechin her ari a candle at twelve o'clock same neet i' Buttermilk lone bar cud kind nowt ony an owd deead cat us awd dreawned th' day afore. Bur, aw mum be gooin; swat user ger i' Croft iv aw keepaingin bike this, so gad day yo two." " Gud day, sir," Peter sed, an walked off. Aw went reel after that un aw 'audit on th' shores o' Manchester abeawt one o'clock un feeling rayther peckish i' mi insoide aw thowt awd goo un her sumtnut eyt. Aw wur lookin abeawt mi fur a aleheawse when aw seed a big place a bit higherup th' street, an i' this place aw went. PAW oppent th' door, went up a lung lobby bike, un went us aw thowt into th bar parlor, un takkin no noticeo nowt aw axed a swellish soart uv a fellow us aw thowt wur th' waiter "Eh, aw ses, bring us a, sheere o' stockin puddin un a point o' tit' best ale yo Imo iith heause ; awve travvellet fro Cho wbent this mornin, un aw think its toimefurt be hevvin summut eyt." Th' chap turnet reaund un favvart us iv hed bin frikkent deeath th' dayafore, un he ses : "My gad friend, what is it youre wanting this mornin ?" " Awve towd thi onct," aw ses; "Aw silent tell thi agen. Bur dust to see these pit clogs o moine theyll foind a road into thee if tha dusnt do as aw tell thi. Am aw gooint stop here aw day waitin fur summut to eyt? Art to goin t' fotch It me or nor?' So th' chap ses, "I'm afraid, my friend, you don't know where you are, talking in that impudent sort of a manner to a gentleman of my position." "Gem away wi thi," air sed, "Ass' ony axed thi to fotch me a Junk o stockin puddin un a point oth best ale. What art meytherm abeawt?" Th. chap laft an sod," My good fellow, youre in the wrong place altogether. Youre in the Bank of England, and I'm chief cashier. I think you had better be making your exit as quick as possible." Aw wur took as if awd bin copt wi prato wedge ith cockles o mi heart. In a bit aw sees th same chap wi a cupple o bobbys cumin up th lobby, ..c• aw bouts up the chim- ley eawt o'th road, welly frikkent to deeath. They aw coome in th' place, un looked up and deawn, under tit tables un in th drawers, un ever3rwheere, till aw begun wishin theyd be makkinther eggs-hit, us th chap sed. So in a bit one oth bobbies, with a vice bike a cracked washin pot, ses "Well, I think we had better be going. I'm afraid we've, missed our game this time, John." So th chap us cawd hissel casher see," I left him here. He was bother- ing something about stocking pudding and ale, and then finished up with using insulting language to me. I was afraid lest it was some raving maniac escaped out of an asylum." So th' bobby sed," Well, I see nothing of anyone now. I fancy he has sus- pected something of this sort, and gone out before we arrived. But, however, if he should make his unwelcome appearance again, kindly aquaint us of it. Good morning, sir." "Good mornin," th' chap sed, un off they went. Aw wur glad, too, awl tell yo, when they did goo, becose my throat wur full o smook. Aw gen urn tonne furt ger eawtsoide th' dam, un then aw coome flunderin deawn th' chimley us black us a nigger. When aw geet deawn aw begun scrapin th' Eut off mi cloothes, un th' chap fotched a basket eawt wi sum bread un ham in it an he towd mi fart help misel whoile he went ith next room furt soart sum Rappers eawt, bur aw knowd what he wantet furt do, so aw seet mi deawn fur a blarney till he'd gon eawt o'th place. Then, us soon us he'd gone aw bowlted through th' window in a back street un geet away froth place abeawt a moile, welly frick- kent eawt o mi moind. Aw thowt it ud bi th' best plan furt mak th' best o my road whom un jack th' Croft bisness up, un aw did do, an seet on th' road back agen. When awd getten to Thruteher's owd barn aw catchet mi, clog agen summut on'th road un flunderet deawn awth length o mi face, un mi brass flew abeawt iaw direckshuns. Aw piket misel up us wed l us aw cud an begun lookin fur mi money. It wur gerrin dark then so awd a job furt foind ony o my brass at aw. Awd bin lookin abeawt th' place for an heawr or moore, when it startet minim, so aw buttonet mi jacket closer to mi, un stuck an ewd shawl, as eawr Sal hut mi when aw startet, remand mi neck, an sect to lookin fur mi money agen. Ther wur a fielt at either soide o' th' road, un thinkin' us sum ud roll in it, aw made a road through th' hedge. struck a match, un begun mi search once moore. Aw wur lookin' abeawt when aw run up agen snmmut heheend th' hedge, "Heigh up," aw sed, "ger eawt o' th' road, while aw look fur mi brass as awve ,iost:' Awd no sooner sed th' words when B.w wur knocked abeawt 40 yards away agen a tree, so aw turnt back agen fart see gradelv whoa had bin so bowld us fart khock mi that fur, when behowd ! if it wart:a owd Sam Thrutcher's mule us had bin shelterin' beheend th' hedge. Aw thowt misel lucky us awd escapet wi' a bit or a kick. becose it wur nowtiest mule within five moile o' owd Sam's heawse. Aw war vary neer wed t through bi this, so aw left th' money on th' floor un went whoam. Aw geet theere abeawt nine o'clock that neet, un aw swore to eawr Sal us awd naer goo t' Croft agen. Aw towd her aw mi adventures un boo were fain aw crept through th' Bank winder, us boo sed if th bobbies ud

div.head: OUR LONDON LETITR.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETITR.

LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT. The speeches at the Mansion House last night fill several columns of the morning papers- But there is really nothing in them worth .a tithe of the space. Lord Salisbury was content to announce the fact that in respect of the Afghan Frontier and of the Suez Canal, the Conservative Government had brought to a happy conclusion lines of Liberal policy, which, wh9 initiated, were hotly 'opposed by the Tories. With respect to Home, Affairs, there was nothing new, though between the lines of his reference to them and the remarks of Mr. W. H. Smith there lurks confirmation of the rumour that next session, the Government propose, so far as lies in their power, to ignore the Irish question and proceed with other legislation. This is very brave, but very foolish; Lord Salisbury and his colleagues might as well get up early in the morning and at- tempt to hold the sun back from rising as burke the question of Home Rule. A Conservative Minis- try naturally has an enthusiastic welcome in that hot bed of Toryism, the Guildhall. There was no exception to this rule last night, and, as usual, the most reactionary member of the Cabinet was the prime favourite. It was a pretty sight to see Mr. Balfour bowing and blushing, whilst aldermen, flown councillors, and city gentlemen, who. had generously dined, vociferously cheered him. Ire- land was the subject about which Mr. Balfour is supposed to know most, and that was the one sub- ject which, save in respect of an incidental refer- ence, he avoided, contenting himself with making a few common-place remarks, complimentary to the ex-Lord Mayor. What wonld have been really well worth hearing is this exquisite person's -frank opinion about the average alderman; especially in his post-prandial state. It is a Ipng tithe since so melancholy a procession wended its way through the streets of London as the cavalcade which preceded the Lord Mayor on his way to the Law Courts yesterday. Sometimes, and on a fine day„ when bunting is abundant, when military uniforms. are about, and bands of music abound, London can put on a festive appearance which in its particular fashion need not fear com- parison with any city on the Continent. But, given a November day like yesterday, and the Lard Mayor's Show, London can claim proud pre-emin- ence for the unspeakable misery and depression of the situation. The crowd„where I saw it in Fleet- street, was really wonderful, men, women, and children standing patiently for hours in the muddy streets under the- ceaseless downpour of rain. Elsewhere, notably on the Embankment, what is after all the principal glory of the show, had faded. The procession, prepared for a fine day, went its way just as if the sun were shining,. save that with occasional comical effects waterproofs and wraps were invoked. The Lord Mayor's own coachmen looked particularly ludicrous with their gorgeous three cornered hats-enveloped in a thin covering of waterproof tinted green.. Host pitiful sight of all were the emblematical cars representing Commerce, Education, and Charity.. Poor Charity, in gauze and tights, shivered piteously, and everyone was glad t 6 knovS that as soon as the Law Courts were reached the Lord Mayor allowed Charity, with the rest, to' go and shiver at home. After all, the most striking feature in yesterday's display was the muster of the police; mounted 'lnd on foot. They showed, everywhere in overwhelm- ing numbers. The nevelty of this demonstration is now worn away for Londoners, who are hourly accustomed to see the streets patrolled by mounted police. The town, indeed, seems in a state of siege, with horsemen in military clothes standing motion- less, but watchful, at the corners of the principal streets, or pacing slowly up and downthe thorough- fares. With the advent to power of Sir Charles Warren, the composition and tendency of the police force has become increasingly tmilitary. For the present, since the promulgation of the edict forbid- ding public meetings in Trafalgar-square, the atti- tude of the police has been one of precaution. But we are threatened on Sunday with something that may develope into a net. The inconsiderable per- sons who have taken a prominent part in recent demonstrations in Trafalgar-square and Hyde Park have announced the determination to challenge the power of the police to exclude them from Trafalgar- square on Sunday. They invite the unemployed to assemble in their thousands and try conclusions ...with the police. The occasion is looked forward to with some anxiety, not because there is any organi- sation among the roughs,'but because there is sure to be a Crowd of idlers; and the police in London; as well'as at Mitchelstown, have a constitutional. knack of bringing on. a row. I very rarely look at the "'Daily Telegraph," life being too short and too serious for such dissipation of time. But yesterday I bought a copy of the paper, curious to see in what lofty language this journal would deal with the personal application of that autocratic police power which it has been urg- ing upon the Povernment, more especially in their dealings with Ireland. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Burleigli. a well-known and esteemed member of the "Daily Telegraph" reporting staff, had been arrested by the police in Trafalgar-square, and charged with being "a loose, idle, and disorderly person, intent on committing a felony." Looking over the paper I came upon the heading "Outrage on a British Subject." Ah l here we are. I thought. Now for a scathing denunciation of a Government which, by its acts, is occasionally a distress to good Dissentient Liberals. But the outrage here pro- minently dealt with had taken place in Fer- nando Po, and there was nothing about poor Mr. Burleigh. In another part of the paper, in emotionable type, there was a brief account of the proceedings in Tratalgar-square, where it was men- tioned by the way that "subsequently the repre- sentative of the .Daily Telegraph' was arrested and conveyed to King-street Station." That was all. Neither there or in editorial columns was there any comment on the proceedings. 1‘ he truth is now out about the Crown Prince of Germany, a.nd,it is finally admitted that he is in a critical condition. For, although this truth has only now found its way into the newspapers. it is familiar enough in private' conversation among Germans. More than a month since I was in Ger- many, and even at that time, when all seemed going on smoothly, I heard well-informed Germans pooh- poohing the optimist view taken by Sir Morrell Mackenzie, and declaring their conviction, founded upon the expressed opinion of German Bavanta, that what was the matter with the Crown Prince was cancer, and that fatal result was a matter at most of but a few months. It is believed in Germany, with what measure of truth I do not know, that Dr. Morrell Mackenzie was influenced in the view he took by personal representations made to him from the very highest quarter ,in this country. The Queen, the Germans say, insisted upon the impossi- bility of anything serious being the matter with her son-in-law, or any dire fate pretenting her daughter in due time rising to the dignity of Empress of Germany. The idea that a man of Morrell Slacken I zie's position would yield to any such influence seems preposterous. No royal favour that could be bestowed upon him would compensate for the serious blow his professional status would receive if his prognostication should be overthrown by events. However it be, and under whatever influence, con- scious or unconscious, Mackenie acted, it seems too sadly probable that he was wrong and the Germans were right. German doctors are now openly, saying that had their advice been followed, and an opera- tion been performed in the summer, the Crown Prince would now be out of danger.

div.head: 'HIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.
div.p: 'HIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.

Sir Charles Mike has -returned home from his notable reception at Constantinople ,and Athens, where he is recegnised as one of the greatest living English statesmen. lie is now, I believe, with Lady Mike, living in retirement, somewhere near Woking, meaning to return to town in Decem- ber. As far as the public eye is concerned, save in these accidental and unexpected manisestations in foreign capitals, Sir Charles Mike is as good as dead, though the house in Sloan-street is the centre of a circle of constant friends who include some of the best known people in London, who have not swerved from their faith in the innocence of a man who was once among the most popular and esteemed Englishmen. As for Sir Charles himself, he, with the assistance of his wife, is quietly and persistent- ly following up clues which both believe will event- ually result in his triumphant acquittal. The Board of Trade Returns just issued supply in- contestible proof of the reality of the improvement of trade. Over the ten months of the year which come under review there is an increase of im- ports of not less than nine and a half million; in exports of over four millions sterling. Compared with the gigatic totals, this is a moderate increase But it shows that the impetus is on the right side. The increase would havt been more still only for the blessed Jubilee. The one exception to the monthly improvement befel in June, when what had hitherto and has since been an increase in the imports shows a falling off to the extent of ok per cent This is of itself pretty good price to pay for the dubious joy of a jubilee; but it of course reprt- sents a very small proportion of the line which people engaged in trade had imposed upon them. I mentioned last week the pending action in chambers of the "Times" with the object of inter- posing *nab delay in the prosecution of Mr. O'Don- nell's action for libel., No report appeared in the newspapers, but I hear that the Times" gained the prayed for extension of time for lodging its de- fence to the claim. On Saturday, however, it will be imperatively required to produce the document which its legal advisers have had in hand since the 4th of August. In the meantime Mr. O'Donnell has instructed his solicitors to take steps to apply for an interim injunction against further sale of "Parnellism and crime," pending the trial ot the :tion.

div.p: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.

- - The luekiest "find" ever made in California was made by a man named Finney,. who "turned up" a solid lump ot gold near Downievilfe, 1866, that weighed five thou- sand ounces, worth 18.60 dots. per ounce, which would make the nugget worth £lB,OOO. This was the largest nugget of pure gold ever discovered. Heretofore the Australian nugget found in. the Ballarat gold fields has been considered the largest, It was valued at £15,000. This man Finney, or "Old Virginia,' as he was called, went to Washoe, California,. and there he made the great ' silver discoveries, where the- " Comstock " lode was Tocated, and where Virginia City, which was named after him, stands. He died in great poverty. He was cele- brated for his wonderful heard of hair, which was of a rich, dark brown in colour, full of widen tints, and 'which fell in heavy curls over ills stalwart shoulders_ He was very proud of his head covering, and always carried in his "outfit" a brush, comb; and small hand mirror, and whenever he made his "camp," while prospecting, would comb and dress his hair with great care. When misfortune overtook him, and he continued "playing in bad' lack "—as he termed it—he began to neglect his hairVand it became frowsy, began to turn gray, and fall out, so that a few years before he.died hewas nearly bald,. and his few remaining hairs were quitewhite. Had he added to his " outfit " Mrs. S. A. Alien's World's Hair Restorer, he might have retained his hair as long as he • lived,, for it never fails to strengthen and invigorate the hair,, restore its colour, and render •it soft, glossy and strong, It can be found at any chemist's or perfiimer's in theworld. It is the best and most agreeable hair dress- in,g. known. Try it.

NEW BOOKS, Szc. In/ the Greater Writers series, published by Mr. Walter Scott, we halve the "Life of Percy. Bysshe Shelley.," by Mr. Wr..Sharp. There has been a good deal of controversy over the‘writings and doings of the Poet Shelley, and there have been quite a number of lives and'irecollections of him. The volume before us preserves a judicial' tone, whilst stating, the main facts clearly. Mr-Sharp does' full jUstireto. the genius of our greatest-lyric poet,. and presenn,Shelley- in a light which makes hie. conduct con- sistent with his peculiar views and peculiar development 'of character. No one can rise from.the tup of this biography without feeling that Shelley was infinitely better than mury of his detractors, and that he is not to. be judged' by the narrow conventionalities,' of the' hour_ We can quite, understand how so many students have become fervent admirers of the writer of • * The'Olie to a Skylark," ".The Cloud,'? and "The Sensitiverilant."' Mr.. Sharp's life will tend to make Shelley more popular,. and lead to a stndyr of his matchless verse. ' The Bibliography is furnished, by Mr. 3. P. Anderson, of the British

Museum. "The Merchandise Marks Act, 1887, in its, relation. to. the cotton tradh," js a useful and opportune little work by Mr. H. L. Wright, 8.A.. of Preston. It ia publfehed by John Heywood, Manchester, and was originally issued at the request of the National Association of Bleachers. The Act is one of the most important as affecting trades of variouakind's that has ever been placed on thestatute book; and;.aathe cotton trade is so vast, it iinot sur- prising thatimmufacturers have so quickly bought up the first edition that a second, revisedand enlarged, has been published_ The scope and procedure of the• Ant are carefully—dealt with, and there is a special chapter, on its principles:. There is alist of cases cited, and' there is a capital index, besides the full text of the Act. Part 13-to hand of Baines's History of Lancashire, edited by Mh:..Taidas Creston, and published by Mk. john Heywood, is afr mine of valuable statistics. Appendix five gives afrlikt of the variou.s creations of orders-, &c., while the next appendix is devoted to the annals., of the cotton maintafacture. In brief, we have a history of the. trade. In vievr of the three million bales of cotton now being sent us from America, it is interesting to note that in 1765; the first' cotton imported into LiVerpool from America was five bags. Mention is made of a Royal Counnis.sibn being appointed in 1833 at the in- stance of Mr.. W,. Patten (now Lord Winmar/eigh) "to collect information on the condition of thildreis employed in factories!' Appendix 7 furnishes electoral statistics a Lancashire-brought down to the last electipn. "The Dictionary of Eriglish History" ia being issued in monthle parts (6d each) by Messrs. Cassell' and CO. It is editefra by Mr. S. J. Low, B.A. and Mr. F. S-Pulling, MA., and promises tobe an exceedingly interesting and valuable-book of reference. A large number of eminent writers have been Engaged to contribute to the work, which will be a record of the doings of the Ebglith nation at homeand abroad. A highly finished fao-sitnilk copy of MagnarCharta is given with the first. part,,and is in itself worth more than the price of the part. " The Quiver " fix November is the first part of a new and ertpirged series. There is to be no cliange in the price, although the letterpress is increased from 64 to 80 pages. The frontpiece is a beautiful coloured plate Good-bye tnthe old home." There is abunclance in the way of sketch,. story, and verse, and the illustrations are high.claes, `The Quiver" is now SO cheap, and so tempting, that it is sure to command a large body of new readers. fr "The Sea", (part 4) has for 'frontispiece a plate of the procession of Ships at the opening of thefrfiner Canal _

the procession of ships at A full account is given of the making ofr the canal, of which, there is also a bird's-eye view • and a portrait of M. de Lesseps. /n the chapter on Malta detariLts are given of the struggle between the Christians and the Turks, with illustration of the defence of Malta, in. 1.585. The reader is finally taken through the Red Sea to India and China, views being fiurnished of the more important places. 'lathe "Magazine of Art" for November, there is a powesiuletching of the powerful picture "Fleeced," by Mr. Seymour rilleaß, A .R.A. There are several engrav- ings of other pictures by this eminent hand, with a por- trait and a sketch of his career. An article on the Har- bours of New Zealand is effectively illitstrated ;,,and the same may be said of the racy paper on "Irish Types and Traits "by Katherine Tynon. The artist, H. Hel- mick, is alive at every point in hitting off Irish charac- ter. There are Some charming bits of "Exmoor," with letterpress by Mr. John Fortescue. There is a full plate illustration of Frank Dicksee's "Adam and Eve,' and another of "The Dice-Throwers" by IVlurillo. Cassell's Magazine for November is a good averaga number. "Curious Corporation / Customs" is the title of a very interesting paper. At Congleton, in Cheshire, we are told the burgesses had at one time a remarkable predeliction for bear-baiting. "The bear having died, the Corporation pre orders to sell their bible in the year 1681 in order to purchase another, which was done, and the town was no longer without a bear." Happy Con- gleton !—ln "Little Folks" the serial stories "Aunt Clotilda's Guests," and "The Boy Hunter's of Ken- tucky" are continued with increasing interest; and th#re are plenty of short stories, Rm., of a really pleasant kind. The current issue of "Cassell's Illustrated Shakespeare" finishes the first volume which includes all the comedies. part: 46 of the Encyclopcedic Dictionary continues the letter L, but so exhaustive is the treatment of each word that the part does not by any means exhAust it. The November issue of "Familiar Wild Flowers" includes coloured plates of the bindweed and the flowering rash. Part 1.8 of "The Life and Times of Queen Victoria" has for frontispiece a full page envraving of the Queen keep- ing halloween at Balmoral. TisieM are other fine engrav- ings; and the period covered is from 1868 to 1870. The House of Surprises" is the title of the "Little Folks" Annual for 1888. It is written by Mr. L. T. Meade, and it is a really first rate story; natural, full of incident, and healthy in tone. Cassell's Illustrated Almanac for 1888 is, as usual, a capital sixpennyworth. It overflows with useful information, and is, besides, an excellent picture book.

CHAPTER VIII. THE POLICEMAN'S DISCOVERY.
' More than three hours had now passed since Richards had started for Tavistock. It was about _ _

half-past nine when the dead silence all around the house was at last broken, and the two women in their mournful watch beside the parlour fire heard the welcome sound of carriage wheels drivino, up to the 0 0 farmhouse. "The Lord be thanked, there's Riehards at last ! " cried his wife, , starting up from her chair. "And I do hope he has brought the doctor, and the police with' him. I'll go and unfasten the front door." In another moment the doctor, Mr. Prior, a grave and kindly-looking middle-aged man, entered; and Anne rose to receive him, feeling as she did so,' stiff and benumbed, as if she had lost the fail 'se of her limbs. Mr. Prior spoke to her a few gentl4 sympathising words, and asked her a few questienS, to Which she replied with perfect calmness; only her lip i quivered a 'little when she told him that her brother had not yet returned heme, and that she was very anxious about him, as he was out on the moor. Then Anne held the lamp with a steady hand, while Mr. Prior examined the wound on the dead woman's forehead. "Death was instantaneous, and she did not suffer any pain, I am thankful to' say," he remarked presently. "She was shot by a small bullet from a pistol, I should say. ,The murderer' who- ever he was, probably took the pistol away with him, but Watkins, whom we have brought with us, had better come is now, and make a thorough search. I hope you will not find any , valuables stolen, Miss Derrick, though, no doubt, you care little about that, now." Watkins, the village policeman, was then called into the room. He entered; his sense of dignity and,importance heightened by being summoned for the.firist time in his life to deal with the chief crime in the calendar, but when he saw the dead woman lying on the sofa, pretty Susan Derrick, , whom all the men in the place admired, and with whom he had sometimes exchanged &friendly greet- ing, then his official position was forgotten for a moment; be took oft his helmet reverently,. and the tears almost came into his eyes.. Anne began, by telling him what, gave her a freezing shiver to recollect, that she had t ome into close contact with the man who in all probability was her sister's murderer,and that as she had entered the hall in the darkness she had actually laid her head upon his arm. . "I can feel it now," she said, shuddering. "lean feel his coat-sleeve." "And what did it feel like, Miss Derrickt" asked the policeman, "'have you any notion, or. did Wall happen too quick br ?" "I have a very clear notion," aeswered Anne.. "It was a good thick cloth Coat, like any respectably- dressed man might wear; it was no ragged' tramp that I laid my hand on." "Mr. Derrick has not come home yet, I under stand ? " Watkins went on. "That's unfortunate ; should all have beenliad of his help. Well, I sup. pose, Miss, I had better go round the place. now and make a thorough search, to see if we can find any trace of the criminal. It's a pity so muck time bas been lost, but it can't be helped, of course. I'll have a look round this room first, ' and the policeman resumed his professional air, and glanced all about him with knitted eyebrows. 'Did you notice anything particular when you first came in, Miss Derrick, was anything gone or out of place ?' was there any sign of a struggle ? " "The room is exactly as I found it," replied Anne. "I have taken care that nothing shoullbe touched before you came." Watkins then made a careful survey ok; the parlour. "There's nothing out of the common way to be seen here. You don't miss any article, do you, Miss Derrick? Please to open that cupboard Were and see for yourself." "There's nothing gene," replied Anne, as she , threw open the door a the corner cupboard. and displayed a :listening little hoard of plate therein. "See, there's the teapot and the cream pig andithe spoons and the mug, all the real silver we have, quite safe, I don't see what else there is for athief to take. We keep very little money in the house. What there is,/ is in this drawer," and Anne, un- locked a draWer -in the old-fashioned brass-handled bureau. There was a large leather purse inside: She counted over its contents,and found them untouched. "He must have been disturbed by your coining home, depend upon it, miss. But 'tis a strange businesso do,n't look altogether like an attempt at, robbery, somehow," the policeman muttered, with a perplexed and dissatisfied look. "We'll try the other rooms now, and see what we can make of them."

" I will ask Mrs. Richards to bring you some refreshment, whilst I go round the 'house with Watkins," and Anne turned to Mr, Prior with all her gentle courtesy. "Thanks, Miss Derrick, I could not think of troubling you; and will you not remain quietly here, and allow me to go round the, house with the policeman? I am arur,..ons you should be spamd as much as possible." - "We will, all go together then, Mr. Prior," replied Anne. "I Will leave no stone unturned to discover • my sister's murderer." ' Let me carry the lamp," said the doctor; anxious • to he of some service to. Anne, whom he pitied pro- foundly, and all the MOTO because he'llacli, as well ras Watkins, an uneasymonsciousness that there was i something more in the matter than an attempted t robbery. So they left the parlour, Anne and the policeman, and the doctor carrying the lamp, while Mrs. ! Richards resumed her post of watching beside the corpse; there was arninstinctive feeling that it must not be left unprotected. The kitchen, pantry, dairy, and them the bed- rcsmis were examined—all without result. They came downstairs again in gloomy silence—silence which presently was. broken by the pelicerman. "Your . sister waa just going, to be married to Cap- tain Stambridge, so I've heard. Could there have been any other party—excuse my mentlening of it, Miss Derrick—anybody that was jealons, do you think? Such things do happen. Or is there anybody that has had a quarrel with your sister, do you know ?" "Certainly not," replied Anne;: and the next moment her heart gave a sudden ihrek for she re- membered what Susan had saia, onli this morning— but what years it seemed ago !—about a quarrel with Stambiidge, about the engagement being broken oft Could it be that he, mad with passion and despair, for, middle-aged man as-he was, he,, had a strong passion for Susan, Anne felt sure—couldit be. that he— She tried to drive away the thought as a wild, un-.' reasoning fancy, and to return to the practical work of searching the house. "There's now only my brother's little room that we haven't been into," she said;. "but there is nothing there they would be likely to steal." * The doer of Martin's smoking-room stood open. They entered—and then Anne uttered a, sudden exclamation. "See there there is a chair thrown down !" She pointed to one lying on the floor. Mr. Prior held up the lamp, and they all looked eagerly around, but if indeed the fallen chair was a sign of any struggle there was no other. "No, there is nothing to 1); found here ; " and Anne turned away, discouraged that after all their search they had not lighted upon the smallest clue to the mystery. " Ah, what's that ?" came a cry from Watkins. He darted towards a table which stood against the wall —a table strewed with papers from under one of which something dark peeped out. Watkins clutched it, and held it up in triumph. It was a small revolver. " Here's what did it, sure enough! Look here, sir," and he showed it cautiously to Mr. Prior (Anne being only a " female," could not, so he thought, be expected to have any understanding of firearms). "One chamber has been fired off, and not so very Ion" ago neither, and the rest are still loaded. We hue got a clue now, and no mistake But though the policeman did not think it worth while to thew the revolver to Anne, she saw it, and—site knew whose it us. She had enough presence of mind not to utter a single sound; she merely turned and walked steadily back to the parlour and seated herself again by the fireside. Mr. Prior followed her and said, "My dear Miss Derrick, if there is really nothing more I can do for you tO-11441A, I think I had better be Ariving home again. Watkins will remain in the house until your brotl%r conies home. I will see the Coroner the first

thing.. to-morrow morning. But how ill you are look-, ing, and no wonder. Let me prescribe for you—have an egg beaten up with a little brandy, and then go to bed at ouce." " Not before Martin conies home," Anne tried tc say, but her lips felt paralysed and she could hardly utter the words. ' At that moment she heard—for though she could scarcely speak, yet all key senses seemed pre- teinattrall7 ticilteafie heard the ' sound of horse's hoofs coming into the farm-yard. she sprang up, flew to the house-door, and threw it open. "Martin—Martin—you have come home at last 1" The newly-risen moon made visible the darkness without; Anne could just distinguish her brother as he sprang off his iron-grey horse; then Richards, lantern in hand, led off the horse to the stable, and Martin came towards the house. He started back amazed, for there he saw, not only his usually calm sister Anne, with a deadly white face, leaning against the hall table as if she were ready to faint, but behind her appeared the stern and serious faces of the doctor and the policeman, who are always alarming officials to be seen in one's own house. . "Why, what in the world is going on ?" cried the young farmer, looking rather pale and bewildered, as he cafne out of the darkdess. Mr. Prior was the first to answer, and very gently and feelingly he broke to him the terrible tragedy which had, taken place in his house that evening. Martin listened without moving or speaking, while Anne, for the first time breaking- down a little, held him by the arm and hid her face on hi shoulder. At last Martin gave One long shuddering sigh. " Ah, poor "girl, why' did She ever come to this 'accursed house ?" .he , muttered between his teeth. Then he asked abruptly—" Where is she? I will go and see her," and with - his arm round Anne's waist he moved towards the parlour door, when the policeman stepped forward,-held out the revolver, and said-- " I found this just now, Mr. Derrick. Do you happen to know who it belongs to ?" Martin glanced at it over his shoulder. is mine, certainly. What of it?" "Yours !" cried Mr. Prior, with a great start., " One of the chambers, has lately been fired off, fiat's all," said the policeman.
"Why it

CHAPTER IX. BROTHER MD SISTER. There was little sleep for the household at Roevtor Farm that night. The doctor and the policeman had departed, and Anne and Martin had between them carried their sister upstairs and laid her down on her lied. It was long past midnight when Anne went downstairs again to the parlour, where Martin was sitting sinoking, deep in thought by the fire. "My dear Anne, I hoped yrai were gone to bed," he said, starting a little as shessaine in. "It would be no Use, I couldn't sleep. I knew yen were still up and I wanted to see you again." ' She seated, herself beside her brother. Martin held. out his hand to her; and they clasped hands for a moment in silence; then he went on smoking, and. nothing more was said forsome minutes. At last Martin brain, "I have been sitting here' thinking till lam ''almost dazed. You see, if it had: been nothing but an ordinary house-breaker he would have taken what fee/ little valuables we have, and not have injured the poor girl, beyond per- haps tying something over her mouth, and locking her up in a cupboard to prevent her giving an alarm arid so forth. There. is something beyond ordinary crime here, something we can't fathom at present." "-I would give every farthing I have in the world —4 would give my life to find out who did it," cried Anne, with sudden passion, and then again she took Martin's hand , and clutched it tightly. He looked itt, her with a sad; steadfast, com- passionate glance, and; ,answered, "Anne, what I am afraid of is, the -police won't look far enough afield to find the real eriminal, it will come much easier and simpler to them. te look near home." , Anne'slips moved, hut she made noaudible answer, and he went on. "My dear girl, I know what is in your mind; let us speak out plainly, and say all we have to say about it. That was n' revolver, as you know, and it had just been bred off. It is a horrible tbinzto think that she came to her death through anything of mine. But that's not all. I have been ruileaaway over the moor, and I doubt if I have seen a living soul since 3 o'clock this afternoon. I was late in. getting home to-night because- of the fog. I lost mar way altogether once, and I was forced to keep in: the track every inch of the way when I had foundit again. So nobody can say where I have been all the evening, and an alibi is out of the question. Our tumbles are not all over for you and me, Anne." " Oha MartitiPshe said in &choking; voice; "how can you take it so quietly ? " "Don't you see—l am innocent now. I was not then—at least, I was innocent of all intentions of course—only I did it, that's all the- difference. Ah, it is pfairt I have not suffered enough. yet for that nights-work. I don't think there' has been a day these two. years that' I have not had the thought of Dick Lawson heavy on my mind; but still, you see, it has not been enough. I was let,oft before. I shan't be this. time. Fate or Providence,. ocwhatever it is, won't let use alone vet awhile." "What have we done that there should be such a curse upon us ?" and then Anne • struggled to speak more calmly. . "Martin, you are talking nonsense. Would anybody in their senses suspect you had a hand- in this—you, your own sister ! What has that—that dreadful misfortune cstours to do with it ? Everybody knows that that was an accident." "And yet, on account of that ascident, as you call it, everybody has fought shy of ma ever since." "But what would they imagine-your motive to be now ?—Your own sister," repeatei? Anne. tSA, quarrel between us probably—you know they give me the credit of having the devil's own temper.' Anne could not deny that such was Martin's reputation. Yet to bear him state the fact so coolly Made her feel a little resgess and impatient. "I think We must be both of us mad to sit here talking like this—and I am sure enough has hap- pened to-night to turn our brains. Our poor Susan ! ' They remained silent for somesminutes after that, then. Martin rose abruptly. "Yon had better try to get some rest now, 'Anne.. What you have gone through to-night I and I away; not here to help you Here's your candle," and he lighted it and held it out to her. "You may be able to sleep, perhapss'now that we .have had it out together, and I have tolel you 1 know what is. befoze use, very likely, and I am quite prepared for

"-Martin," she said, feeling as if her heart would! break, "why do you talk so?: I can't bear it." "It's well to look the worst in the face. And it's. you I am thinking of, if yom should be left all alone by-and-bye, my dear. All the same, I can't see that they have any evidence against me, except the re- volver, and the fact that I can't get a single witness- to- prove where I was all the evening. But it's a case of give a dog a bad name,' &c. People won't care to rook any further—it will seem most natural to, suppose I did it" Life went on much as usnal the next two days at Row-tor Farm, even though the shadow of a mysterious crime hung over it. Martin had his work on the farm, Anne had her household, her dairy, and -her poultry to attend to. The undertaker came from Tavistock to arrange for a funeral in the house where a wedding was to have taken place in a few days' time; and a messenger came from. the Coroner to give notice that the inquest was to be held on the following Monday afternoon. Mr. Prior, in his compassion for Anne, had done every kindly office for her that was possible for him to do. He had promised to see James Sta.mbridge, and to break to him the dreadful tidings of his be. trothed's violent death. All Saturday and Sunday Anne was expecting him at -Row-tor Farm, as was only natural. But the hours, passed on, and nothing was seen or heard of hini. "It is most extraordinary,* said Anne to her brother at tea-time'i.Sunday evening, "that James Stambridgp has never been near us. I am getting quite uneasy about him. Could you go and see him this evening, do you think, Martin?" Martin made no reply for a few moments, then," "No, Anne, I don't think I can,."' he answered gravely. • "Why not ?" she asked, half under her 'breath. Something in Martin's tone seemed to give form to the vague horror in her own mind. "Because he probably thinks the very worst that can be thought of me.' "Are you sure it's not the other way?" she whispered, almost afraid to speak her thought aloud. "Well, I have turned everything I can think of over in my own mind. Everything seems unlikely— that and everything else. It is just barely possible, and that is all I'll venture to say. At all events, Stain- bridge knew where to find my revolver. I re- member pointing it out to him one day, and saying in a lonely house like ours, it might possibly come in handy some time ot other, though its not once in a dozen years that we hear of a house- breaker in this part of the country. However, we shall all know a little more perhaps when tho Inquest is over." " The inquest another inquest, " muttered Anne, with a shudder ; and again came the bitter thought —"What had they done? this brother

anu taster, nomeiy, nara-woriong 101 K, wno naa never over-reached their neizhbours. or driven a hard, bargain with the poor, or ili-usen a damn animal ; what had they done that the shadow of crime should for ever dog their footsteps and darkeD their good name Z."
(To be continued.)

When the ancient empire of Atahualpa existed in all its %tory, and before its overthrow by the rapacious Munro, the extraordinary virtues of the "Pearl of South America" were as well known to the then natives as to the Peruvians of the present day. indeed, its great and admitted worth led to its being used in all public ceremonies as ah acceptable offering to their deity—the Sun God. The leaves of this marvellous shrub, when ready for market, are transported on m'ules up the steep mountain sides, across the icy and desolate plateaux, and throokk the passes of the Bolivian Andes mountains, many of them 13;000 and 14,000 feet above the level of the sea, and then dowstwards on the other side of the mountains into Peru for shipment tram the port of Callao (Lima.) And so terrible is the Icy rigour of the climate amidst the lofty heights of the Moneta:ism, especially of the icy plateaux of Lipes, that the Muleteers find the chewing of these leaves alone enables them to withstand the icy rarefied air, and to support the long night- watches to prevent the mules they are transporting to Peru from straying. Several natives, who, never allowing a day to Pass without chewing the leaves of the "Pearl of South America" at least three times daffy, attained the truly patri archal age of 130 years.

As the ordinary food of the native Peruvian consists almost exclusively of roasted maize, barley, or seeds of the guinea. *which are eaten without any addition, they suffer with fre- quent and obstinate obstructions and derangements of the di- gestive system, which are entirely cured by the use of " TEAM PEARL OF SOLITE AMERICA." Dr. Weddell says that the natives, while chewing the leaves pass Whole days in travelling or working without food, but they nevertheless eat freely In the evenings. With another extract from the Australian Bark, Atstonia,'Conl stricta. or wonderful Queensland Fever Bark, which with all the nerve and stomachic stimulating power of Quinine, pro- duces neither headache nor other ill-effects. With another from the if Purshiana, the unequalled power and yet Withal permanently efficacious effects, of which on the liver and bowels, has led to its recent adoption by eminent British medical authorities.; these rare and valuable medicinal ex- tracts, together with others of almost equal worth and potency (of which want of space will not permit of our particularis- ing), have been 'united In one preparation, and form a medi- cine of almost marvellous efficacy. This curative remedy, is a stomach, a liver, a brain, and a nerve stimulant, and im- parts to these organs and all their functions, a sense of strength and ease in the performance of their allotted duties, which is as astonishing as it is delightful to the patient who has hitherto been a prey to the almost innumerable and dis- tressing symptoms of intestinal disease.
