R. H. M. STANLEY'S EXPEDITION. Sr., PAUL DE LOAIMA, FrirDlY.—The latest intelli- gence received from Mr. H. M. Stanley's expedition is deed August Bth. At that time the expedition had left the camp established by Mr. Stanley at about eight days' march from the MabOdi country, and was advancing direct towards the western shore of the Albert Nyanza, Mr. Stanley had experienced considerable difficulties in consequence of the fatigue of his men, which ultimately became so serious that, owing to the men straggling, the expedition was scattered over a distance of several kilo- metres. Mr. Stanley, Moreover, had to negotiate with some of the most important chiefs of the district through which he was passing in order to obtain fresh victuals, the consumption of food by the expedition being very large. The natives, however, showed themselves well disposed to meet all Mr. Stanley's requirements. After halting for three or four days at a fresh camp in order to reorganise the expedition and rest his men, Mr. Stanley continued his march towards the interior, leav- ing a guard of 30 men at the camp. On artery' ing at the west shore of the Albert Nyanza, Mr. Stanley intended establishing himself in a new halting pilace on the slopes of the extremely fertile mountains 'which, according to native information, border that portion of the lake. He would thence despatch a small advance guard towards Wadelai, by way of the Nyanza, in the steel whale beat, which, partially ta'ken to pieces, is still being conveyed by the expedition. The direction of this mission would pro- bably be intrusted to Lieutenant Staers, who was still withthe van of the expedition, and was in good health. This plan was, however, subject to modification, either because Mr. Stanley previously received direct news from Emin Pasha, which up to the time of the despatch of the foregoing intelligence lie fully expected, or on account of the great sensation produced by the expedi- tion in the country. Mr. Stanley had alreaav learnt that Emin was in OA health, and that the country to the south of the Albert Nyanza had been greatly tran- quillised.
THE EUROPEAN SITUATION.-THE TRIPLE ALLIANCE.-AFFAIRS IN BULGARIA.

Count Kalnoky, the Austro-Hungarian Foreign Minis- ter, gave some explanations on foreign affairs on Satur- day to the Hungarian Delegation. He looked upon the fact that foreign interference in Bulgaria had been averted as a considerable acMevetv,ent. The Government of -Vienna had not yet been able to enter into relations with Prince Ferdinand, but they would continue loyally striving to advance the interest of the Balkan peoples. The Austro-German alliance had been a blessing to the world; and the adhesion of Italy and the practical iden- tity of England's aims were gratifying factors. pant Kalnoky dwelt upon the importance of maintaining friendly relations with Russia as a fundamental condition of the establishment. of a trustworthy European peace..

Sr. PETERSBURG, 111(nmAy.—The seMi-official Jouraa/ (le St. Peterxbury, commenting upon Count Kalnoky's speech, says his view of Prince Ferdinand's position differs from that entertained by , which has never recognised the validity of his electir .1. AMERICA.—WARD BEECHER'S SUCCESSOR —THE DYNAMITARDS.—THE CON- DEM-I,Mb ANARCHISTS.
NEW You, FRIDAY, NLORT.--TDR AdViSOry Committee of Plymouth Church have decided to call upon the English minister, the Rev. Mr. %thy, to succeed the late Mr. Ward Beecher.

CHICAGO, SoftPar.—A searcipof the cells in which the Chicago Anarchists are confined \VP; made to-day, when six loaded bombs, concealed under newspapers, were found in the cell occupied bv inigg. The news of the discovery spread rapidly, and a marked reaction of feel- ing among those who had hitherto been in favour of the prisoners, was at once apparent. The discovery has caused the adoption of extra precautions regarding visitors to the condemned men, and the receipt of news- papers or presents. How the bombs were introduced, and with what object, is unknown. The 'general suppo- sition, and the only apparently reasonable one, is that they were intended to destroy the gaol and its inmates. NEw Yortx, MoxPer.—lt as just become known that Engle, one of the condemned Anarchist, attempted suicide, by drinking laudanum, on Aunday morning. He was discovered suffering from its effects, and was placed iin the hands of the prison •floctors just n time to pre- vent a fatal result. He was restored by the ordinary methods.
ARRIVAL OF MR. CHAMBERLAIN IN NEW YORK.

• NEW Yoga, MQNDATI JAW. -Chamberlain 'MIS besieged by the reporters when he landed, and about 20 went to his hotel and there awaited his arrival. In conversation with them he said he was not accompanied by two detectives. That story, like many others, was untrue. Be also said: "As to the fishery business, I do not expect any difficulty in the settlement of it. I have not mapped out ant' plan on the subject for the Conference. I think it would be disgraceful if two friendly nations could not settle amicably a matter of this kind. Ido not expect there will be any difficulty with the Britislr House of Commons in the matter. Of course, whiletheoretically I have full power, anything II may agree to will have to be ratified by Parliament, but I do not expect there will be any difficulty in that respect. Now, with regard to your questions as to Irish matters, I must beg-to be excused from answering them or expressing any Opinion on political questions. From the time of my leaving Queenstown I became a diplomatist charged with a diplomatic mission on behalf of the British Governmest. and it would be indelicate, far me therefore to discuss or express any opinion on any controversial subjects of a political nature." FRANCE .—THE MILITARY SCANDALS: ANOTHER GOVERNMENT DEFEAT.

PARIS, Satvansx.—The Chamber discussed again to- day the question of the nomination of a committee to Inquire into_ the Wilson-Carl matter. M. Wilson him- self was not presilmt. The sitting was a very stormy one, owing chiefly to the vicilent speeches of several Monarchist deputies. Of. these 'MM. Hendry d'Asson, Cassagnac. and Cuneo d'Ornano 'vigorously attacked M. Wilson, bringing openly, and in the most unrestrained manner, serious accusations against the President's son- in-law. M. Rouvier again spoke•vehemently against the appointment of the comtnittee,..giving similar reasons to those which he had previously brought forward. His speech wiKan excellent one, and marked by vigour and courage. It did not, however, save his cause, and on a division the Chamber voted the inquiry by 445 against 84. The result was received with boisterous demonstra- tions 'of satisfaction by the Opposition. PARIS, MONDAY.—The trial of General Caffarel and Mesdames Limouzin and Rattazzi, General Count d'Andlau, a member of the Senate, and others, com- menced before the Correctional Tribunal to-day. The accused are charged with fraudulent proceedings, or attempts to swindle. General Count, d'Andlau did not put in an appearance. The address of the prosecutor did not reveal any fresh facts. ILLNESS OF THE GERMAN CROWN PRINCE.

BERLIN, MONDAY.—A telegram from Sir WIWI MAC- kerrnie, dated from San Remo, states that the German Crown Prince's general health is excellent, but the local complaint has assumed an unfavourable character. Although there are no symptoms indicating immediate ' danger, Sir Morell Mackenzie has invited Professor Schroeber, of Vienna, and Professor Krause, of Berlin, to go to on Remo. The Emperor has instructed Prince ' William to proceed to San Remo to obtain a detailed verbal report. • BERLIN, TUESDAY.—Professor Bergmann will perform the operation on the Crown Prince, should one be deemed necessary. The Emperor William is steadily improving, .but is much worried by the reports ef the Crown Prince's sickness. A second telegram from Berlin, dated on Tuesday, states that private telegrams from San Remo represent the state of the Crown Prince as rather alarming. Queen Victoria has telegraphed repeated inquiries as to the condition of her son-in-law, which Sir M. Mackenzie is said to have answered in a rather discouraging tone. The new growth or the swelling in the throat is stated to be lower down than before, more malignant-looking, and triore•difficult to operate -upon. Prince William left on Monday for San Remo, accompanied by several Berlin doctors, who were to be joined at Frankfort by Dr. Moritz Schmidt, another famous specialist. In the course of , Monday, Prince William had two interviews with Professor Bergmann, who formerly attended the Crown Prince. fhe people of Berlin are very uneasy, but the truth is not yet quite clear. The Prince of Wales, who is now at Sandringham, is in frequent communication with San Remo. In an inter- view which Sir M. Mackenzie gave,. a fortnight ago, to a representative of the Press, he stated that he would not visit the Crown Prince again for some time, unless specially sent for. BERLIN, Tunrisner MORNlNG.—Professor Bergmann will shortly publish a full and detailed account of the Crown Prince's malady. It appears to be finally decided that an operation on the throat will be performed, and preparations are being made at the Palace for that pur- pose. His Imperial Highness is expected to arrive in Berlin on Friday night. ,A telegram received from San Remo at the Foreign Office to-day confirms all the fears hitherto entertained with regard to the serious state of the Prince. SURRENDER OF AYOUB KHAN. a TEHERAN, THURSDAY .—Ayoub Khan, who has for a long time past been in hiding near Khaf, has voluntarily surrendered himself to the British agent at Messed. EARTHQUAKES IN NORTH ITALY. A Central News telegram dated Rome, Thursday morn- igg, says :—Serious shocks of earthquake have been felt during the night at various places in the northern pro- vinces. Accounts reach this city from Ravenna, Bo- logna and Venice, all of which state that the shocks have been Very decided and alarming. It is not reported, hewever' that any lives have been lost. The Rivers Po, Reno, and Panaro threaten serious inundations. '

As a result of the consultation last week, between Lord Salisbury, Mr. Matthews, and Sir Charles Warren, it has been resolved that no public meetings shall in future be allowed to be held in Trafalgar-s4uare. Hurley Flour Mills, Great Marlow, were destroyed by fire on Monday. The damage is estimated at several thousand pounds. ,

On Monday, an elderly man, named James Pegg, platelayer, on the Midland Railway, was knocked down by an excursion train from Nottingham to Manchester, just outside Derby station. His head was out off, and his body frightfully mutilated. The deceased's home was in Derby.

The miners of Fife and Clackmannan unanimously agreed on Monday to support the national scheme for the restriction of output by working only eight hours daily, taking a weekly holiday in districts, and one week's annual holiday simultaneously throughout the king- dom.

An easterly gale prevailed over the Tyne and along the Durham and Northumberland coasts on Monday, accompanied by heavy rain. Several vessels had to put back for shelter. During a gale on Sunday, the schooner Livingstone, of Newcastle. went •ashore at Dungeness. The crew, except one man, was rescued by a lifeboat. About mid-day, on Sunday, the body of one of Mr. Assheton-Smith's gamekeepers, stationed at Llanberis, was found in the river near that place, close to the waterfall. His hat and coat were subsequently found in a wood close by, having been torn to rags, evidently in a severe struggle. He was last seen about ten o'cioek on Saturday night.

SCTICIDR OF A RooxmAxEn.—Charies Middleton Cox, a bookmaker, has committed suicide at his residence, Cat- ford, by shooting himself with a shot-gun. The deceased was awaiting his trial at the Shrewsbury Assizes this week on a charge of fraud, and on Saturday he should have proceeded to that town to report himself, in accord- ance with the terms of his bail.

Esiranatiori.—.Since the Ist of January 358,715 persons have emigrated from the United Kingdom to places out of Europe, as against 295,510 in the corresponding period of last year. The English numbered 149,861, the Scotch 30,770, and the Irish 74,898, the remainder being foreigners. During last month 32,749 persons emigrated, as against 27,589 in October, 1886. KILLED BY A Bartzu EXPLOSION.—An inquest was held on Saturday, at a half-way house near Ely, on the body of James salmons, steersman on,a traction engine, the boiler Of which burst on Wednesday evening. The driver, named Kidd, was injured. The boiler had just been re filed, and the driver had turned on steam to start when the explosion occurred. Verdict, "Death from the ex- plosion of a boiler." Tits LATE SIR GEO. MACFARREN.--The funeral of the late Professor Sir George Macfarren took place at Hamp- stead Cemetery on Saturday afternoon, in the presence of a large number of spectators. The Royal Academy of Music, the Royal College of Music, the Sacred Har- monic Society, and other bodies were officially repre- sented. A memorial service in Westminster Abbey fol- lowed that at the grave.

PROPOSED INDUSTRIAL EXHIBITION TN Box:rm.— A movement is on foot among influential tradesmen in Bolton, for establishing a permanent industrial exhibi- tion in a capacious gallery of the Market Hall in that town. Various industries and trades might be advan- tageously shown, and it.is believed the Corporation, to whom the market belongs, will give every assistance. The movement would be a valuable adjunct to the pro- posed local technical institute.

At Barnet, On Monday, Ed. Allen, a 'signalman in the =Ploy of the Great Northern Railway Company, at Fottei's Bar, was committed for trial on n charge of hav- ing ,caused poison to be administered to William }lecher, another signalman. It appeared that there had for some time been quarrels between the parties, who occupied the 'same signal box, and that, as alleged, last week Racher found that chloride of zinc had been mixed with the water he had to drink. DESTRUCTION OF A CHURCH BY FlRE.—Panbricie Free Church, at Carnoustie, near Dundee, was destroyed by fire on Sunday. The church was heated with a hot air apparatus on account of the stormy weather, but nothing wrong was noticed at the end of the forenoon service. Half-an-hour afterwards, however, flames were seen bursting from the east wing, near to the furnace. Not- withstanding strenuous efforts, the building was gutted. The church was in good order, having been fitted up only a few years ago at considerable cost.

• WriormstE SMOOOLINO ON A ROYAL YACHT.— Another extensive seizure of smuggled cigars and to- bacco was made on the Royal yacht Victoria- and Albert. Into on Sunday, a largo number of boxes of cigars and •cases of tobacco being concealed in the hammock-room. 'The men's leave was, stopped, and an investigation ordered; but the crew disclaimed the ownership.. On Monday, however, a coxswain, a rigger, and a blue jacket claimed the contraband goods, and the affair. which is creating considerable excitement, was referred to the authorities. A POLICEMAN COMMITTED FOR EXTENSIVE THEFTS.-- At Bolton Police Court, on Monday, Solomon Newby. market policeman, and an oli Corporation servant, was ,charged with plundering the stall of one of the tenants. A quantity of game. seven couples of rabbits, and a large number of poultry were missed, and the prisoner, having had possession of the keys on Friday, suspicion fell upon him. it detective was set to vestal, and on Saturday morning he discovered prisoner engaged in skinning the rabbits in one of the market vaults. He was committed for trial. BIGAMY AT WIGAN: HEARTLEYS CONlM7CY.—Richard Ireaincl, labourer, was on Monday committed by the Wigan macistrate-s for trial at the Liverpool Assizes, for bigamy. The prisoner was married at Bury, but left his wife and two children, who had to go into the Work- house. At Wigan, in September, he married another girl, .under another name, but left her in a month. He went to Bury and WAS apprehended under a warrant for main- tenance, and sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment. The second wife gave information whilst the prisoner was in gaol, and he was afterwards given up to the Wigan police.

DEATH OF LORD WOLTRRTON.—Lord Wolverton died on Sunday, at the Bedford Hotel, Brighton. Be attended Levies races on Friday, and Plumpton steeplechase on :Sattirday. He was seen on Sunday mortern,g by his valet. and took a bath, and afterwards shaved. Two hours later, as he did not come down, his TOOTO was entered, and he was found dead. The deceased, George Grenfell Glynn, second Baronet Wolverton, WRS born 1824. and sat for Shaftesbury as a Liberal, frotnlBs7 to 1873, when he succeeded to the peerage. He was joint Secretary to the Treasury, 1868 to 1875, and afterwards Postmaster- general. He was a partner in the Metropolitan banking firm of Glyn, Mills, Currie, and Co., a deputy-lieutenant of London, and a justice of the peace for Dorset.

A 'LONDON TRAGEDY: A REJECTED LOVER. —On Sunday night, a young conple were promenading Harley-street, in the. West End of London. Nothing strange had been observed in the man's demeanour, when he stopped suddenly, drew a pistol from his pocket, and fired at the girl. She was wounded, and, dropping to the ground, lost consciousness. The man then placed the weapon to his own head, pulled the trigger, and dropped dead. The injured girl was then taken in a nab to the hospital. Further inquiry shows that the deceased was a furrier named William Jenkins, 19, of Gravel lane. Southwark, who for sometime 'had been keeping company with Ada Newman of the same age, domestic servant, at 125, Harley-street, but the engage- ment had been broken off.

Oriartam Corrox BPYING COMPANY.—The twenty-fifth quarterly meeting of the uldloun Cotton Buying Com- pany was held at Oldham on Saturday evening, when there was a large attendance of members. Mr. Thomas Henthorn, who presided, said that for the year just com- pleted the company had sold over 97.000 bales, repre- senting a turnover of nearly £1,000,000. and that if the limited companies of the district would give them half their bt6itiess tl,ev would have a position in Liverpool which no organisation could assail. The balance-sheet was adopted, and a bonus of 6s. per £lOO to members and 3s. to non-members declared. A discussion ensued as to the position held in Liverpool by the company, and the manager stated they had the largest and best selec- tion of cotton of any house in pverpool, whilst on ac- count of their financial strength they were able to do business in many cases on better terms than ordinary brokers.

• FATAL EXPLOSION OF GIINPOWDIO2.-.—The Kerala] Vale Gunpowder Works were on Monday the scene of an ex- plosion which caused considerable damage and loss of life. A terrific noise was heard coining from the neigh- bourhood of a large building called the press house, used for compressing guri.i.)owder by hydraulic power into cakes. This house was entirely demolished, large blocks of stone being blown long dirtances, and blocks of timber were found 150 yards distant. At the moment of the explosion, it being mealtime, only two men were in or about the press house. One, named William Dunstan, was engaged in moving the powder from the house to a cart that stood at the door, and another man, named Parry, was in charge of the horse and cart in front of the building. The latter was found to be fearfully burnt and shattered, but at. the Truro Hospital, whither he was removed, hopes are entertained that he may survive. The body of Dunstan was blown to pieces. Ile bas left a family of nine children. WRECK OF A PASSENGER STEAMER: EXCXTING SCENES. —The total wreck of the Australian passenger steamer Perth, is announced in despatches receivedsby the last arriving mail from Melbourne, and from which it appears that the boilers of the steamer exploded just after she stranded, injuring several of the crew. The Perth belonged to the Adelaide Steamship Company, and was going from Ashburton to Carnarvon. .When about midway between the places she got ashore on a reef near Point Cloates. There were a good number of passengers on board, and when they realised the seriousness of the disaster there was naturally much confusion. Just then the boilers of/the steamer burst with a loud report, and the confusion and excitement amongst the passengers were then alarmingly increased. Several of the firemen who were near the'boilers were badly injured. Order was eventually restored, end the passengers, both ladies and gentlemen, behaved with the greatest coolness and bravery. This resulted in all of them being safely landed. Subsequently a number of the passengers set out in a small boat to the North-West Cape, and were fallen in with by the steamer Australind, and taken on board. When the news of the 'disaster reached Perth two steamers were despatched to the assistance of the passengers and crew. When the Australind left, the shipwrecked people had plenty a provisions with them.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.
GENERAL NEWS.

The Board of Trade returns, issued on Monday. show that the imports for October increased £1,495,908. while the exports increased £511,378, compared with the same months last year. For the first tea months of the year the imports showed an increase of £9,485,869, and the exports an increase of £4,094,822, compared with 1888.

At Notts Assiz.es, on Monday, Wm. Dykes admitted hav- ing bigamously intermarried Elizabeth Taylor, last April. The prisoner lived unhappily with his first wife, who left him to live with another man. He became intimate with another woman, and his wife told his paramour that she had married again, and that she ought to make the prisoner marry her as well. The Judge characterised the prisoner's wife as an abandoned woman, and ordered the prisoner to come up for sentence when called upon. MR. SPURGEON AND TR/ "DOWN GRADF.."-011 Sunday, Mr. Spurgeon, who leaves for the Continent this week, referred, at the Metropolitan 'Tabernacle. London, to charges which he has made against ministers of being theologically and spiritually on the down grade. De- scribing his conversion. be said he had clutched at the vicarious atonement of Christ, believing it to be his last hope. Did any one of them wornr'sr that he should fight for it? Would not any one of them fightfor their wives and children? The vicarious atonement was everything to hint, more than wife'or children; for without it be was damned. • Tim 112XTRORPE COLLISION: CULPABLE NEGLIGENCE.— Charging the grand jury, at the opening of Yorkshire Winter Assizes, at York, on Monday, Lord Coleridge refused to the charge of manslaughter preferred against the driver and fireman of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire train in the Fiexthorpe disaster, which he said arose from what in law was termed culpable negli- gence. No man could define what culpable negligence was, but it would rest with the grand jury to decide, after examining the depositions, whether the men had been guilty of what was really culpable negligence. If so, they would find a bill, end, as in most cases, the amount of punishment would be left with him. RAILWAY ACCIDENT.—NARROW ESCAPE OF PASSEK- GERS.—Ati alarming accident happened on the Cambrian Hallway on Monday morning. As the mail train leaving Whitchurch at 2 6.5 was slowing about 200 yards from Ellesmere station the engine left the rails at some points, and 14 trucks laden with goods were precipitated down an embankment. Owing to the breaking of the couplings three passenger coaches containing four passengers, a brake van, and two cattle waggons remained on the rails. The passengers had a very riarrsiw escape. The perma- nent way was considerably claninged. The engine ploughed along it for seventy yards before it was. stopped. Most of the trucks were smashed to pieces. A MODEL " SALVATIONIST."—At .Heanor, Derbyshire, on Monday, a young man named Hy. Houseley was bound over to keep the peace for sending the following letter to a female captain in the Salvation Army named Eliza Elliott:—" Dear Captain,-1 just write to ask you a favour. I want to know if you will marry me, as I have taken a fancy to you. If you don't agree with my favour it will be worse for you. I either mean to marry you or murder you. If you say no I mean to do or you, so you can order your coffin at once. I know I shall have to be hanged for it; but I don't want to go to hell by myself; f.want you to go with tne. Prepare to meet your God. From your comrade, HARRY Houseurr." RECEPTION OF A Pnertisr.—An immense reception was given to ,T. L. Sullivan, the American cliampion, on his arrival at LiverpooionSunday in the Cunard steamer Cephalonia from Boston. The champion pugilist was met outside the harbour by a special tug chartered by his admirers. As he disembarked at Liverpool' landing stage from the tender some thousands cheered Sullivan with the utmost enthusiasm, and it was deemed advis- able to form a bodyguard, so that the champion might make his way to the four-in-band which took him to the Grand Hotel. Attempts were made to unyoke the horses, for his admirers were ambitious of taking their place, but from this they were dissuaded, and the hotel was safely reached, where a levee was held, attended by a large number of Sullivan's admirers. Sullivan's party left on Monday for Euston. The Customs claiming duty on the champion's belt (which is made of gold, and studded with diamonds), it was left in their possession pending negotiations.

_ THE . DUKE ON CAMBRIDGE AND THE VOLUNTEEHS.— The Duke of Cambridge attended a gathering of London Volunteer sergeants on Saturday evening. In the course of a short speech his Royal Highness said that the Volun- teer force had attained a high degree of efficiency, and that the nation which produced such a force without conscription was in the best position to carry out the object for which it was created.—Early in the evening the following telegram was sent to the Queen at Bal- moral :—" Seven -hundred sergeants of London Volunteer regiments, assembled specially to commemorate the Jubilee year of your Majesty's reign, respectfully offer their most loyal and sincere congratulation, and also their earnest wishes for your Majesty's continued good health and for every blessing you may desire." The reply was as follows The Queen is sincerely gratified by the conpratulations of sergeants of the Volunteer Corps, and desires her best thanks to be returned for their good wishes?' THE LONDON SOCIALISTS AND LAND REFORM. A deputation of the English Land Restoration League attended the unemployed meeting in Trafalgar-square on Monday. The speakers being cautioned that imme- diate arrest would follow violent language, Mr. Saunders asked the people to keep quiet. If they accepted the League's plans they would all get double wages. Money was wasted by the Government in paying high wages to those who did little work. The principle of judicial rents in Ireland should be applied to English tenants. Work- ing men of small incomes should be exempted from rents and taxes. Ireland obtained her advan- tages by sending men to Parliament to look after her interests. They ought to do the same. For- merly the land paid the taxation of the country, and it should do so now. In London land was worth £418,000,000 and houses £212,000,000, and taxation was 2.500,000 on land and £7,000,000 on houses.—The Rev. S. Headlam said if Jesus Christ came to earth again and attended Trafalgar-square, he would soon be arrested. The men there had a right to ask for work, and they had a right to ask for what the landlords had stolen. He entreated them to commit no violence on Lord Mayor's day.—Rain fell heavily the whole of the time, but 500 Or 600 re- mained until the speeches finished, and then dispersed. of AnGudowonn,RB IDDryDASXOCarE alTl;lyirta Pennyi sp erdal cl eetff. e ete d Softens by theaten sro —Advt. THE CRIMES ACT.

tX siil enuri-tiiicierrtiiefaiiiees—Ae-t-was held on Mon- iltiy at Mints!), when abont4 38 persons were charged with unlawful assembly and attacking the police on the occasion of the recent evictions, by Captain Vandeleur, of kir. James Clancy and his sub-tenants i Vandeleur- street, Kilrush, for non-payment of ground rent. Mr. Clancy was first charged with holding illegal possession, and the court sentenced him to 21 days' imprisonment, with hard lab-ur. A charge of intimidation against another defendant was dismissed, and the court then adjourned. . At Woodford, on Monday, four men were charged with resisting evictions on the Clanricarde property, on the 20th of October, and were sentenced to five months' imprisonment. Notice of appeal was given. Mr. Martin M. Egan, brother of the Rev. P Egan, parish priest, and a Man named Devine were charged with conspiraty. Mr. Egan delivered a speech on the 12th of August at liallinaskell, and was summoned with three others, but refused to appear. Devine was arrested, and Mr. Egan subsequently surrendered. The Bench decided to ad- journ the case till the other defendants were arrested, but accepted baiL

div.head: 11{ELAN.1).
div.p: At Armagh. on Saturday. the magisterial bench re- turned Thos. Monaghan to the next assizes on a charge of the wilful murder of his wife at Banbrook Hill on Wedne.sdriv night last. It was stated that the pair had been drinking, and that the prisoner was seen beating his wife with a stick on account of her having secreted a bottle of whisky for her own use. On Monday, the Dublin assessors, Mr. Mc.lnemey and Mr. Hart:, differed as to the right of Mr. Sexton, M.P.. to the municipal franchise, which involves his qualfication to he Lord Mayor next year. The Lord Mayor held in favour of Mr. Sexton, who was rated jointly for t National League offices, but r..sided at 20, North Frederick-street, where the objection contended he was only lodging. There will bean appeal. The Royal Commission on Irish Public Works which, under the presidency of Sir T. Allport, has been taking evidence in Ireland, met on Monday at the Treasury. It is stated that the commission is now engaged in con- sidering its final report upon the fisheries, harbours, and railvrays, the subject of drainage having already been dealt with. The report, which will be most important as bearing upon the present condition of labour in Ireland, will be ready for publication by the end of the present year. At a meeting of the Dublin Corporation, on Monday, Mr. Sexton, M.P., proposed that the Council should ad- journ without transacting the ordinary business, as mark of respect to Mr. William O'Brien. He said he had been horrified by the reports of the cruel and barbarous treatment Mr. O'Brien had received at Tullamore Gaol. The Government tried to break Mr. O'Brien's gallant Spirit, but failing in that they determined to take his life. Another member of the Council said there was no- thing in his experience to equal the abominable treat- ment of Mr. O'Brien. The Council adjourned.

THE IMPRISONMENT OF MR. O'BRIEN. \ Since the committal of Mr. O'Brien to Tullamore Gaol , he has been allowed to wear his own clothe.s, and, as is known, he had previously expressed in the strongest manner his determination to resist the enforcement of the regulation which orders the wearing of the prison uniform. On Saturday orders were received by the governor of the gaol to compel Mr. O'Brien to wear the uniform. Acting on the directions received from the prison authorities, the governor proceeded, on Sunday morning, to carry out the rule which directs that all prisoners be dressed in prison garb. The governor having intimated his instructions on the point to Mr. O'Brien, that gentleman reiterated his determination to resist to the utmost of his power the change of his own clothing for that of the prison. Matters assumed so serious an aspect that the medical officer of the prison had to be' communicated with, and he, having ex- amined into Mr. O'Brien's condition, directed that no force should be used to compel him to put on the prison garb. Respecting Mr. O'Brien's imprisonment, the Freeman s Journal says i—There is no rule empowering prison au- thorities to forcibly dress a convict in prison garb; but a diet of bread awl water is provided as the punishment of contumacy, and the governor of Tullamore gaol has enforced this rule—acting under instructions—against Mr. O'Brien and Mr. Mandeville. On Sunday, a crowd assembled round Tullamore gaol, numbering, it was said, 8,000 to 10,000 persons. They were accompanid by bands, playing "God save Ireland," A erUnson hand- kerchief, which was waived from the cell window, was presumed to be Mr. O'Brien's, and was vehemently cheered. . _ _ _ _ . -

Mr. Wm. O'Brien was transferred on Tuesday to the Infirmary department of the Tullamore Jail, by direction of the medical officer. It is stated that although Mr. O'Brien has been in prison less than a week, his health had already commenced to break down, and the prison doctor deemed it advisable to exempt him from the rigorous and monotonous discipline to which prisoners in good health are subjected.

div.head: WARE AliT AGAHCST MR. COX. M.P.
div.p: THE WARE AliT AGAHCST MR. COX. M.P.

Mr. Cox, M.F., has up to the prwent succeeded in eluding the police, wh6 are on the alert, in their endeavour to execute the warrant issued-against him, for an alleged offence under the Crimes Act. He was in Longford on Friday, and proceeded thence into county Leitrim. He declined to remain at Carrick-on-Shannon on Sunday, as he observed he was "wanted," and be left by boat on the Shannon. He was followed by the detectives to a station on the Midland and Oreat- Western Railway, but a friendly signal caused his rapid disappearance from its preciirts.
COLONEL KING-HAR?dAN AND P. J. SHERIDAN.

P. J. Sheridan, writing from Monte Video, United States, under date September 28th, to the Freeman's Journal, repudiates Colonel King-Harman's assertion that when he conteited Sligo in 1880, Sheridan offered for a certain sum of money to come forward as a Nationalist, and split the Nations list vote. Sheridan says he de- nounced Colonel King-}Farman tutone of the most mer- ciless rack-renters in the country, and worked up public feeling against him to such a degree as to make his elec- tron impossible, without the Nationalist aid. The lead- ing Nationalists and himself secured Councillor Genty, of Leeds, son of a Sligo tenant farmer, as a candidate; but ultimately Mr. Sexton's candidature was urged. Notwithstanding repeated protests, it was resolved to nominate himself (Sheridan), when no influence outside the National ranks would have prevented his, return but be told his friends he would ask the Sheriff not to take his 'name. Challenging Mr. Molony, the colonel's agent, he adds : I did, however, write a letter to Col. King-Harman, in reply to one de- livered to me in my house by Col. King-Harman's elec- tion agent, Mr. Michael Moloney, of Sligo, in which the colonel offered, over his name, to pay a certain sum of money to the county treasurer of the Fenian organisation. or to any one I would name, if I secured him the sup- port of the Nationalists or Fenians, or as many of them as would ensure his return to the House of Commons. In my letter, I told Colonel King-Harman that if he handed over.to a man whom I would name the price of 500 stand of arms then, and 500 more after his return to Parliament, I would ensure his return to the House of Commons—not by offering as candidate my- \ self, as stated by Colonel King-Harman, but by getting the Nationalists of the county, or the great majority of them, to " plump " for him. These terms CoL King-tar- man, in a second letter (delivered also by his agent) refused to accept, but did agree to pay for 1,000 stands of arms after his election was secured, which terms I refused to accept, and there ended the negotiations. This decision I arrived at after mature deliberation, believing, as I did, that an exasperating Tory would keep the public temper in better form than a half-anxious and a half-reconciled subject of the Crown, as Mr. Sexton was then repre- sented to be. Now, however, I think differently of Mr. Sexton, and admire his hip-and-thigh chastising of Go- vernment officialdom, and his brilliant advocation of national independence, as much as any man in Ireland. SHOCKING MURDER BY MOONLIGHTERS. -

Early on Tuesday morning, a brutal murder was com- mitted by a party of Moonlighters, at a small farmstead, at Liscahane, near Ardfert, in the county Kerry. The farm was held in tenancy by Patrick Quirks, aged 75 years, who had taken the holding, after it had remained direlict for about two years. Mrs. Kirkby, Quirke's daugh- ter, whose husband got into difficulties, and had gone to America,had been evicted from the farm at the beginning of that period, and about twelve months ago, old Quirke had taken it at a greatly reduced rent, the arrears, due prior to his daughter's eviction, being forgiven. He continued to work the farm in the interest of his son-in-law, who was expected to return soon from America, and two of whose children were in the old man's charge. The house, in which Quirke and his family dwelt, is a miserable cabin. At about five o'clock, yesterday morning, a knock was heard at the window, and on Quirk answering it, he was informed that his cattle were tres- passing in the inangolds• of one of his neigh- bours. He replied that he would get up, and immediately did so. A few minutes afterwards a shot was fired through the door, and two men, one of them armed with a double-barrelled shot gun, entered the kitchen. Quirke was by this time dressed, and was just coming into the kitchen, when one of the moonlight- ers said to him "Paddy, pay no rent 1" He replied, "I'm willing te do anything you want." The speaker said they would swear him, and Quirke's wife an old woman, who had now appeared, questioned their right to do so, saying they were neither magistrates, policemen, parsons, nor priests. The ruffian, who acted as principal in the affair, then replied, "We'll soon let you see," and thereupon discharged his gun at his aged victim. The shots took effect on the upper part of both the old man's thighs. He did not fail, but cried out that he was killed. Another shot was then fired, which struck Quirks on the shin. From the nature of the wound it is evident that the muzzle of the gun from which the first shot was fired must have been plaeed quite close, for there is a hole nearly an inch and a half in diameter through the trousers, and the inner portions of the flesh and shin bone are frightfully shattered, the bone being laid quite bare, and the arteries of the leg severed. • Pilled with terror, the old man's wife became powerless, and for some time remained in a semi-conscious state, whilst her husband lay in helpless agony on the ground. Is soon as she could control her deranged faculties she gave the alarm to the neighbours, and messengers were despatched for a doctor and a priest. Before their ar- rival, however, Quirke had succumbed to the shock arid hemorrhage, having lingered in extreme suffering for about two hours and a half. Mrs. Quirke states that she believes there were only two men engaged in the outrage, and that they were both young. The country was immediately scoured, and several arrests have been made, though the guilt has not yet been fixed on any individual. The motive for the crime appears uncer- tain, but the theory of the police is that the murdered man's neighbours were averse to his taking the farm, for the simple reason that they were thereby deprived of the benefit they derived by using it as commonage while it was derelict.

div.head: CRIME AND CRIMINALS.
div.p: CRIME AND CRIMINALS.

At Tha mes Police Court, on Monday, five Spanish sailors were remanded on a charge of stabbing to death, on Ratcliffe-highway, on Saturday, a man, name unknown. During a brawl, on Saturday night, in the East End of London, a Spanish sailor, when being pursued by a crowd, turned and drew his knife, and fatally wounded a man in the groin.

At the Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, Thos. Lowry, who had been convicted on the previous aay of the man- slaughter in flulme of a woman with whom he lived, was brought up for sentence. Mr. Justice Day said he could not understand why the prisoner had not been in- dicted for murder, and upon the evidence that had been given against him he should have been well satisfied if the jury had upon such an indictment found him guilty. The offence was one of the worst he had ever had before him, and he sentenced the prisoner to penal servitude for twenty years. On leaving the dock the prisoner said he was "as innocent as anyone in court," and he had not had a fair trial. i On Saturday, at Nottingham Assizes, Arthur Ludlow, a shoemaker, was arraigned for the murder of his daugh- ter, aged 11. On the morning of the 9th of September. prisoner went to the Nottingham Police Station and gave himself up as a murderer. He gave a minute account of having cut his little girl's throat with a knife used in his trade while she was asleep. He added, "I intended murdering both of them, but spared the boy on account of his mother." Under the direction of Baron Iltiddleston, the jury returned a verdict of guilty, accompanying it with an expression of their belief that prisoner was insane. The prisoner was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure. James Jones, 22, of Eign Hill, was charged before the Bideford city bench of magistrates on Saturday with the burglary at, the Knoll, Tupsley, and with murdering Mr. Philip bollard. on the 20th October. Eviden was ad- duced, alleging that the prisoner admitted to Detective Donovan that he and a mate came out of prison together on the 18th, and walked to Ledhury, where' he bought a screw lever for his mate. They then took a train to Wit hipgton, new• Hereford. Jones admitted re- turning home on the fo...wing Saturday, and was then asked by fli • officer about his tnato. He said, "Hare You not arrested him?" A screw lever wes found in the bed af the murdered man, It was intimated that the police had important evidence forthcoming, and a remand was granted. _ __

PRPSENTATIONS.—On Tuesday'afternoon Mrs Gladstone presented Mr. William Brown, Mayor of Chester, at the Assembly Hall, Holywell, with his portrait, given by the Welsh Flannel Manufacturing Company. Mr. Gladstone was presented with a roll of Welsh-Flannel. MR. WOODALL, M.P., AND WOMEN'S SUFFRAOE.-Mr. Woodall, M.P., presiding on Tuesday at the annual meet- ing of the Manchester National Society for promoting Women's Suffrage, said that the subject had now passed out of the stage of derision and contempt, and a majority of the members of the House of Commons were in its favour. The House of Commons, however, was impo- tent for progre.ss, except in the case of strong pressure of public opinion; but he had good hopes that in the en- -suing session they would get such a pressure of opinion as to enable them to carry a bill. Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength Is unequalled.--ildrt.

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., addressed a Liberal meet- ing at Innerleithen, near Peebles, on Monday. and said if the common law were administered in England or Scotland as the Crimes Act was being administered in Ireland, there would be a revolution.

A meeting of the Conservative members °Utile Senate was held at Cambridge on Saturday, to select a candi- date for the representation of the University, in the room of the late Mr. Beresford-Hope. Professor Stokes was unanimously adopted as the candidate, and an election committee was appointed. Replying to the letter of a Warwick correspondent, Mr. J. W. Sleath; who called his attention to the recent Protectionist meeting at Warwick, under the presidency of the High Sheriff, the Right Hon. John Bright says The Fair-traders or Protectionists are in a muddle. During our great agitation their arguments showed a mass of ignorance and a confusion of ideas. They seem no wiser now, and facts and arguments are lost upon them. _ .

Mr. Gladstone, while refraining from expressing an opinion on the case of a gentlemau named Byrne, who was recely removed from the commission of the peace by the Irish Lord Chancellor, says that at the present time the arbitrary and even illegal proceedings of the Government, through their officers. are such as to re- quire a careful and *dons examination of all parts of their conduct which bear upon the liberties of the people of Ireland.

The Marquis of flartington, writing to a correspondent who drew his lordship's attention to the recent speeches of Sir George Trevelynn in North Wales, states that he entirely coincides with the view that it is completely erroneous for Sir Geooge Trevelyan to say that tha objections raised against Mr. Gladstone's Home Itulll scheme are merely "hairsplitting and higgling," but that the Unionist party is fighting for a great principle, and that it is still far from clear how mnch or how little of the old bill Mr. Gladstone is yet prepared to bring for. ward.

A circular letter has been issued by Mr. A.lllingworth, M.P., to the Gladstonian members for English consti- tuencies inviting them to take part in one of two depu- tations which it is intended should visit Ireland this month and next. Mr. Illiagworth defines the objects of the stisit as being to give assurance on Irish soil ot the unfaltering support of British Liberals for Mr. Glad- stone's scheme of Irish self-government, to encourage the Irish to patience and perseverance in their constitu- tional struggle. and to realise on the spot the views and feelings of the Irish people. The majority of the mem- bers addressed have forwarded replies supporting the
.. project. The Liberal Association of the West Division of Edin.

burgh met on Monday to consider the vacancy in the division caused by the resignation of Mr. Buchanan. who has adopted Home Rule views. By a majority of 35 to 10 votes it was agreed to adopt Mr. Buchanan as the Gladstonian candidate for the division. The minority of Liberal Unionists then left the meeting. Mr. Buchanan, who was introduced to the meeting, said the course he took two years ago in joining the Unionists caused him great pain and long consideration, and it was only after considerable deliberation that he came to the resolution of a few weeks ago. But since he came to that resolu- tion he had not had one moment's regret at having done so. They had a hard fight before them, but they in- tended to be victorious. MR. CHAMBERLAIN'S PARTY OF FIVE. On Monday, Sir W. Lawson and Mr. W. Abraham, member for West Limerick, addressed a crowded meet- ing at Cockermouth, held to condemn the Irish policy of the Government.—Sir W. Lawson said they must take a good look at Mr. Abraham, because they would not have a chance very long, for if things went on at the present rate the whole of the Irish members would be shut up in gaoL The Tories were very eager to succour every oppressed nation except Ireland, and why? Because England was the oppressor, and that made all the difference. Though it was foolish to prophesy. he ventured to do so. and it was that before long, in spite of all the coercion of a Castlereagh, or the ballets of a Balfour. Lrehuid would get its freedom. Speaking of the Dissentient Liberals, he said he did not call them Liberal Unionists, but Liberal Coercionists. It was evident that Mr. Chamberlain's party consisted of only five persons—his brother, his brother-in-law, and his shadow, Mr. Jesse Collings. He had forgotten who the other two were, but doubtless they were the shadows of the shadow. If England did its duty, and was true to its principles, in a very short time the cause of the Irish would have a glorious victory.

div.head: CABINET COUNCIL.
div.p: CABINET COUNCIL.

A Cabinet Council was held at the Foreign Office, on Monday, from which Lord Ashbourne, Sir Michael Hicks- Beach, and Lord Stanley of Preston were absent. The Cabinet sat two hours, ministers separating at 2 30. The business transacted L j Ministers had reference to the measures which are in course of preparation for in- troduction next session. Some of the measures which were dropped last session will be reintroduced, and other new bills are so far prepared that they may be said to be now almost complete. The most important measure before Ministers was the Local Government Bill of Mr. Ritchie, which, it is understood, will be a very comprehen- sive measure. The Committee now sitting to readjust the boundaries of local authorities under the Local Govern- ment Boundaries Act will, it is understood, have its report framed before the business of next session has progressed very far, and the passing into law of the Commissioners recommendations will make Mr. Ritchie's bill, which is nearly complete, operative almost imme- diately that it becomes an Act. Irish affairs also occu- pied the attention of Ministers, but the Press Association understands this was in connection with prospective legislation rather than in connection with Acts at present in operation.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.

On Saturday, an unusually large number of Irish- men arrived in Eccles and Patricroft fr.)ra different parts of the country, evidently in expectation of finding work in cutting the Manchester Ship Canal. Every preparation for the actual cutting has been made in the Eccles and Barton districts, and also at Irlam and Cadishead, in which districts men have latterly been engaged staking out the line the canal will take, and also the deviation of the Cheshire Lines Railway between Flixton and lrlam. and also the measurements for the" proposed diversion of the river Irwell at Barton and on to Irlam, at which places the river takes a zigzag course. The measure- ments for the proposed diversion of the Bridgewater Canal, so as to allow of the construction of the pro- posed swing bridge at the aqueduct over the Ship Canal, were taken some time ago. Owners of pro- perty have also been communicated with by the Company, and it is generally anticipated that an early commencement will be made with the works.

The first meeting of the shareholders of the _Eccles and Patricroft Ship Canal Share Society was held last week.—Mr. R. Spary, Chairman of the direc- tors, said the society- numbered 374 members, holding 763 shares, and the average weekly payments amounted to £.38 3s. A sum of £935 had been paid into the bank, and £1,875 by the bank to the Ship Canal Company, the deficiency, which was not a very large sum, being guaranteed by the trustees. Only 32 members had been in arrears, the majority ef whom had since paid up their subscriptions. At the meeting of the Stockport Town Council, on Wednesday, Colonel M'Clure, in supporting the proposal to re-elect Mr. Joseph Leigh as Mayor, said the position which tllat gentleman held with regard to the Ship Canal was a very great encour- agement to the Council to elect him. Mr. Leigh was on the Board of Directors, and 'one of the managing directors of the Bridgewater Navigation portion of that great undertaking. They felt that this might be of great assistance to the town.—(Ap- plause.)—After his re-election, Mr. Leigh said he should be guilty of no breach of confidence when he told them that in a day or two the ground would be broken and an army of men would be at work, and that under the able, experienced, and ener- getic contractor, the work of the Ship Canal would very soon be rapidly carried out in such a way that would show to the world in general that within the time specified the Ship Canal would be an accomplished fact. (Applause.) The bringing of ships up to Manchester would be a par- ticular advantage to towns so near Manchester as Stockport.

Two railway workmen fell into the Farg, in Perthshire, on Tuesday night, and were carried away by the swollen stream and drowned.

The weather in London was continuously wet on Wed- nesday morning, seriously marring the pleasure of those who turned out to seethe Lord Mayor's show. The route was lavishly decorated, but the various banners and other devices were seriously affected by the rain. _ .

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.
LANCASHIRE and Cheshire are pretty well in- tersected with canals, and in view of the formation of the Manchester Ship Canal—operations in con- nection with which have at last been commenced

—a new work on" The Law Relating to Canals" cannot but be of interest to many of our readers. Additional interest attaches to this important volume—one of over 350 pages—from the fact that it is from the pen of Mr. ROBERT G. WEBSTER, ' M.P. for East St. Pancras, who is the son by her first marriage of Mrs. QuEwErr, the wife of the
RECTOR OI WARRINGTON. Mr. WEBSTER is a bar-

, rister-at-law, and has acquired repute as the author of "The Trade of the World." The work before us affords every evidence that he has thoroughly mastered his subject. We quote the - title Page, by way of indicating the scope of the book; it is as follows :—"The law relating to canals, comprising a treatise on navigable rivers and canals, and including all legislation to. the close of last session of Parliament, together with the pro- cedure and practise in private bill legislation, with a map of the existing canals in England and Wales." The introductory chapter is one of some fifty pages, and is of great interest from the mass of information which it contains, and from the manner in which it deals with present-day pro- blems with regard to canals. Mr. WEBSTER has a , -strong opinion as to the economy of. water car- riage, and raises a point which is well worth con- sidering, and that is whether it is possible for Railway Companies to continue to make reduc- tions in the cost of transport, and \ yet earn satisfactory dividends. He observes • , that from experience obtained of water carriage in France, Belgium, and America, 'there appears to be a consensus of opinion in these countries that water transport offers greater faci- lities for cheapness of transit than any other mode 'Of carriage in use, and this under conditions which are at presext by no means perfect." The princi- pal points, in his view, that require attention in the English canal system are 1, improvements in con- ' struction ; 2, amelioration of administration;

and 3, control of supervision. As to the mileage of our canals Mr. WEBSTER says : Taking canals alone, and excluding the navigable rivers, Thames, Severn, Wye, 'and Ifumber in Eno.- land, the rivers Clyde, Forth, 'end Tay and the Cale- donian Ship Canal in Scotland, and the Shannon and other navigations in Ireland, there are, I find, of ,anals owned or controlled by railway companies in tngland and Wales 1,333 miles, in Scotland 8.5 miles, whilst the length of canals independently Owned by other than railway companies is, in Eng- land 2,372 miles, and in Ireland 164 miles, giving a general total of 2,530 i miles, of which total 1,510 miles, or more than one half, are owned orcontrolled by railway companies. It seems that one of the great-difficulties in the Way of the amalgamation of canals is that many of the connecting links are in the hands of the rail- Way companies, who are anxious to lessen rather than increase the competition of canal traffic, and Cannot, tlerefore, be got to make improvements in the links with a view to through traffic. Cheap transit, in the present struggle for existence, is, however, of vital importance, and it may be that Parliament will have to step in, in the end, and clear the way. Touching the question of foreign com- Petition in relation to canal traffic, Mr. MEYER, engineer, of Liverpool and Berlin, is quoted as say- mg—" There is no dbubt that inland navi-

gation, as it is being developed in Germanh Prance, Holland, Belgium, and Rubsia, is becom- ing of immense importance and value to the trade, ' and industries of those countries." ' Mr. MEYER adds that in his opinion "about 250 miles of modern canal to unite the great centres of industry to our seaports would do more for the good of the country than any other number of competing railways, and it is a matter of regret that sufficient means can- - ,11°t be found to demonstrate this practically." Mr. vv eSsTER, in enlarging on this phase of his sub- t, quotes also the evidence of Mr. GEORGE oons, of Warrington, given in connection with die Manchester Ship Canal Inquiry, to the effect that Germany can send wire to London for ship- to Australia, for us. 6d. per ton, whilst it _c°6t him 17s, 6d. per ton, from Warrington to .4°11(1°11* Germany could not produce cheaper
ININIMNOM

than England, but beat her in cheapness of tran- sit. Following on the introduction to the work, we have in chapter I a carefully prepared sum- mary of statistics, relating to canals; chapter ll' 'deals with the jurisdiction of the Railway Com- missioners under the Railway • and Canal Traffic Act, 1873; chapter 111 is devoted to private bill legislation; and chapter W to special cases relating to canals: There is beside an appendix which sup- plies a list of Railway and Canal statistics and orders; and a "Table of cases and private bills." It will thus be seen that Mr. WEBSTER'S work is one of the first importance, the value of which is not lessened by a knowledge of the fact that near- ly forty years have elapsed sincethe last publication of a treatise on the law relating to canals.

A Liberal Club for Widnes was formally opened, on Monday, by Mr. E. K. MusrzAzT, president of the Liberal Association for the Widnes Division. Such a club is certainly needed in Widnes, and it is to be hoped that it will prove equal to the high expectations that have been foriaed of its value !is a political institution. Excellent advice was given to the, members as to the necessity of keeping the management of the club in their own hands, and of making it self-supporting. Mr. MusrnArr spoke very plainly on this point. He said: "If they had to go to gentlemen who had long purses, and very posssbly not as good and sound political opinions as the members—if they had to go to gentlemen and ask for assistance, those gentlemen generally asked for some return." This means, we take it, that they might be asked to 19wer the flag, and show a leaning which would not be Liberal. There can be no question that there has been too much coddling of working-men at political clubs. This is all very well for the Tories--it is quite in their way to patronise people in order to make use of them—but Liberals should be above manoeuvres of this kind. Let those who gather together for club purposes deal with the club income as they do' with their own; let them live within it, if they would be independent. A crust of bread and liberty is more to be prized than a banquet with slavery. Once let the idea get abroad that a olvb exists in the interest of Mr. So-and-So, and that he ought to keep it going, and it is not too much to say that all true life is gone out of it. If men, whether Tory or Liberal, cannot come together without having to depend, in the main, on rich men, they had better stay at home and talk politics by their own firesides. It should be the business of a club to so stimulate and formulate opinion that a candidate for Parliamentany honours would be disposed to go to it rather than the club go to the candidate. This is what Mr. Mrrsrnerr evi- dently had in mind when he said the members of the Widnes Club should be able to vieiv the con- stituency and say how they would be represented. This may not be a high ideal, but we fear hat very few clubs act up to it. At the average political club, the regular -attendant sees less of politics than of the Three B's—beer, 'bacca, and billiards. They. are entitled to their place, of course; but should not be allowed to take 'posses- sion, so to speak, of the whole shop. If club-men are in earnest -about politics they will make provi- sion for politics being discussed; and we are quite sure that no political chill can better fulfil its mission than by taking steps to ensure that the questions of the day shall be debated, at least dur- ing the winter months. Granted that there is a difficulty in getting opposition on some issues, there are others—such / for instance as land reform, and free education upon which there is greater diversity of opinion. And why should an arrangement not be made for a Liberal Club challenging a Tory Club to a de- bate, or vice versa—just as is done in the matter of billiards and bowling? It is to be hoped that there can be such a thing as a friendly discussion as well as a friendly game. It woula be the means, we cannot but think, of making opponents better acquainted with each other, and of ensuring mutual respect. It is true that the Tories have not hitherto encouraged the exercise of thought; but a change has come even over the spirit of their dream, and when we see leaders like Lord RAN.. DOLPH CHURCHILL advocating free education, we may be quite sure that the old order is giving place to the new. At any rate the experiment is worth trying. Political clubs, whether Liberal or Tory, should be centres of political activity and of political intelligence, and when they get to doing their duty as they ought to do, there will be a friendly rivalry amongst them, as there should be, in the advocacy of those measures which will beat promote the greatest happiness of the greatest rfumber.

Some pertinent and interesting observations on education were made at Crewe, on Monday, at the annual meeting in connection with the Union of Lancashire Institutes. The necessity of making provision for technical education was strongly urged, and there was some sharp criticism of the defects of the Technical Education Bill recent- ly brought in by Government. Enthusiasts in matters of this kind are usually ahead of public opinion. It should be remembered, however, that Parliament is like water in that it cannot rise above the level of its source. The section of the bill which left it to fifty ratepayers to render the act inoperative in a particular district—if they thought fit to exercise a veto—was certainly a bad one; but, as Mr. MTAREN, M.P. afterwards remarked, it is not unlikely that the clause would have been struck out, if Parliament had gone for- ward with the measure. Mr. J. H. REYNOLDS, secretary to the Manchester Technical School, suggested that a simple way of raising funds would be to empower Corporations to levy more I than a penny in the pound under the Public Lib- 1 raries Act. But we question if this would be a I prudent course to take. Men, like Mr. BEYNoLes, who are in earnest about technical education might find that, if money was raised in this way, it would be frittered away in miscellaneous expendi- ture. As it is, faddists, who have control of the Library rate, too often defraud the public of their rights by spending public money on their hobbies instead of directing it into more useful channels. If we are to raise funds for technical instruction, it will be as well to know exactly what we 'do raise, and to take care that there is no misapplication of the funds. In any case, there will be an outcry on the part of a section of ratepayers who have yet to learn that money spent upon education is after all the most economical of expenditure. Lord DERBY distributed the prizes in the evening, and made a I speech which was characterised by his usual fore- thought and good sense. He made it clear that he is not to be taken in by the Protectionists, and that their nostrum is no remedy for depression in trade. He said:—' _

---- - As to one part of your business—technical instruc- tion—there is now only a single opinion. We are harder pressed than ever we were before by the competition of foreign artisans and workmen, and even if we were to fall Wick on the lazy expedient of trying to protect our native industry by the old method of restrictive or prohibitory tariifs—which I don't think we are likely to do—(applause),—yet that would only help us where the home market is concerned. It would be useless as regards our ex- port trade.—(Hear, hear.) We are fighting for the markets of the world. We have held our own bith-

erto, but the struggle is sharper than ever, and we cannot afford to throw away any advantage which is possessed by other countries. This puts the issue very plainly, and it, is to be hoped Lord DEEBY'S remarks will be taken to heart by those who are disposed to resort to "lazy ex- pedients" in preference to sheer hard work and keen competition. His lordship apologised at the com- mencement of his address for being more familiar with the educational problems of twenty or thirty years ago than of those of to-day; but he showed that he has not lost interest in a question which formerly occupied so much of his attention, and that he is fully abreast of the times. It is satis- factory, too, to observe that he is not losing faith in the democracy. So far from crying out when the people go wrong, ho is more inclined to rejoice that they are so often right. This is a hopeful 'tone as coming from Lord DEBBY, for he is ,not a sanguine man; he does not believe in panaceas; and when he expresses his faith in the democracy, we may be quite sure that his faith is well- founded.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 12, 1887.

Professor Tyndall is still suffering from political rabies. He says :—" At present science is repre- sented in the House of Commons by that silly creature. Stuart, and by good-natured Roscoe, who knows nothing about the Irish question. Playf air hardly counts." The moral of this is—" Pay heed alone to the 'Professor, who understands every- thing about the Irish q4estion." But the country does not heed; it ha S had enough in matters political of sounding brass and tinkling Tyndall. •

Colonel Dopping threatens an action for libel against Professor Stuart and Mr. Gladstone on account of their statements as to his connection with the evictions at Gweedore. But he has caught a Tartar -in the Professor, who returns to his charge and adds to it. There is a story told of a noble lord who once complained to a friend that he had been described by an opponent as a scoun- drel. "Then why didn't you make him prove his words ? " said the friend. "Oh, there's the .mis- chief," was the reply; "that is exactly what I did." We commend this story to Colonel Dopping ; he may find that it has a moral.

The Government may think ' they have done a smart thing in putting Mr. O'Brien in prison. But they have not subdued him—he will not wear pri- son garb, or mix with felons. Still, he has suf- fered from the bread-and-water punishment, and has )lad to be removed to the gaol infirmary. There is a bitter feeling in the hearts of Irishmen at the way in which this leader whom they love is being treated; and it is likely to turn out that the Government will wish they had let Mr. O'Brien alone. It used to be a boast that Great Britain was the asylum of patriots; but now patriots, when they are Irish, are clapped into prison. And this is the Salisbury-Hartington idea of Govern- ment!

Volumes might be fillecl''on "Misunderstandings —their causes and effects;" and the subject even then would not be exhausted. The Rev. John Yonge has been under the necessity of explaining that there was no foundation for a curious rumour which had got abroad that he had been guilty of an attack upon the late Rev. R. Pilcher while lying ill. Those who know Mr. Yonge thoroughly know that he is incapable of such a thing. But it was necessary for those who know him only by repute that he should trace the evil story to its source. He has done so; he has not only scotched the snake, but killed it; and the community will be all the better for it.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
Yesterday Lord Egerton and other directors cut sods at Eastham, of the Nanchester Ship Canal. All the good things are promised" when the ship lands" and it will land, despite the pro- phets of evil.

The reception which has been accorded to Mr. J. L. Sullivan, the American pugilist, shows that our taste for the barbarous is not yet extinct. If we could only have sowebody butchered by Sullivan to make an English holiday, what a delighted crowd there would be!

The Salvationist who proposed marriage or murder to the lady of his love, seems to have talked about hell, and death, and damnation, un- til the horrible had become part of his nature. A month's training on the treadmill would perhaps sober him. There is such a thing as spiritual as well as spirituous intoxication.

It is very good of Alderman Davies to \ present, to the Warrington Police force, the large local picture in chalks, executed by his son, Mr. Percy Davies. Talent runs in the blood; but we will back the father against the son, when it comes to versifying. Mr. Percy Davies has described .his picture in verse, hut he is altogether too daring when he rhymes " often " with "common."

A boy of nine has been convicted, at Prescot, of stealing pears, to the value of twopence, from an orchard.. It is wrong, of course, to knock pears off a tree, and ppcket them; but how many boys of nine are there who look upon this as stealing P It would have been better for the lad if he had been made acquainted with a birch rod rather than the prisoner's dock. `

The Duke of Argyll knew what he was about in defending the sacred rights of property; he meant high rents and no interference. But the inter- ference has come in the shape of the Crofters' Commission. Rents are being reduced all round from twenty to sixty per cent. The average re- duction is statea to be about' 40 per cent. All things considered, the country can spare such an illiberal Liberia as the present Duke of Argyll.

The Liberal party has sustained a serious losEi in the death of Lord Wolverton. He had an open heart and an open hand, and a courage which was equal to his convictions. When it was seen that the classes were putting their purees together to overawe the masses, Lord Wolverton opened his purse to the other side, and spent a large sum in supporting the cause of Liberalism and Home Rule. He deserves to be kindly remembered by all friends of progress.

A "high ripper" at Runcorn, who assaulted a passer by, flourished a knife, and then assaulted two constables, has been bound over to keep the peace, and fined 20s. and costs for each assault on the constables. Whilst in the act of endeavouring to paint the town red, he said he was "not going home any more." It is a pity the magistrates were not in a position to make him as good as his word in this respect. There is a good deal to be said in favour of home without a high ripper.

Miss Edith Wrightson has been reading a paper before the members of the Padgate Wesleyan Mutual Improvement Society on "Social Life and its Duties." This is an innovation in the right direction; give the girls a chance, and we will wager a " pony" that they will attract the boys all the more. Why should the latter have it all to themselves in such societies 1' Let' the improve- ment really be mutual. Oh, woman! lovely woman! nature made thee, To temper man; we had been brutes without you.

The inquiry, at Paris, into what is known as the Caffarel scandals is a sorry business. Pudding and principle seem to go together with some people; when there is a lack of one, there is a lack of the other. The impecunious old General has, to say the least of it, made a fool of himself. Mr. Glad- stone once sarcastically referred to a distribution "of what the Turks called their honours." But what are honours worth that are bought as they have been in France? Honour, forsooth, when the whole transaction is dishonourable!

The Rev. Charles A. Bury has suddenly shot into the front rank of preachers by being invited to succeed the late Rev. Henry Ward Beecher. The high qualities which caused him to be appreciated in Wolverhampton seem to have been a great at- traction to the American congregation. The Rev. Dr. Parker has failed to suit their taste, because, while ;reaching simplicity, he is in practice elabor- ate to the highest degree. - He is too theatrical in style to gratify the highest taste. With him, as Emerson would have said, it is not so much the "What" as the "How."

It is satisfactory to see that something is being done with a view to local government reform. The clerk of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority reported that he had received a letter from the Clerk of the Peace for the county with re&rence to information as to boundaries, which was for the use of the Boundaries Commission. The way in which boundaries overlap is " a caution." There is a Warrington Alderman who cannot go home from business without being almost bewildered by the number of counties and townships he has to touch or cross.

It was also reported to the Runcorn Rural Sani- tary Authority that the ratepayers of Latchford, Grappenhall, and Thelwall are desirous of being again brought within the Runcorn Union. They want to be included with townships whose rates are low. Just so, and so say all of us. But it hap- pens that a large number of the residents of Latch- ford, Grappenhall, and Thelwall make their money in Warrington, and take all they can out of the town. It would therefore be "more german to the matter" if they were included in the borough of Warrington. If there is to be an !aeration of boundaries, let it be in this direction. Mr. Sutton, clerk to the Warrington Guardians, put the case strongly at the meeting on Wednesday.
