NEW POOR RATE FOR CRONTON.—OR Thursday the Widnes magistrates signed a poor rate of is. in the pound for the township of Cronton. The rate i s estimated to realise £245 2s. ed. The old rate had been collected with the exception of £3 ss. 9d. which was recoverable. , ENTERTAINMENT AT WIDNES. With the object of augmenting the fund for clearing St. Mary's Parish Church, a magic-lantern entertainment was given in the National School on Thursday evening. Mr. lon, of Liver- pool, had charge of the lantern, views of Brighton being shown. Mr. F. Neil presided. _ _ _

FALSE RUMOUR AT WIDNES.—We are glad to be able to give a denial to the rumour that Dr. McCambridge was dead. On Saturday last Dr. McDonnell had a long letter from his partner, who was then at Monte Video, South America, stating that he was enjoying the best of health. Dr. MeCambridge expects toe home in another month. VISITORS to BLACKPOOL ahOtlrd stay at the Station Temper- ance Hotel, right opposite Central Station. Central position. Commodious and accommodating. Terms easy.—Apply J. Boos AT LARGE AT WIDNES.—At Widftes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, the following persons were each fined 5s and costs, /s Bd, for allowing their dogs to be at large :--John Anderson, Victoria-road • Fenton Lawlor, Ann-street West; Charles Short, Widnes-road; Peter Coatsworth, Hale-road, Ditton ; and Charles Brassington, MoorBeld-road, Firnworth. THE MASTERSHIP OF RUNCORN BOARD Scnoot.—For the position of master to the Runcorn Board School there have been no less than 347 applications. The salary is fixed at £l2O per annum. A committee has carefully gone through the applications and testimonials and have selected six candidates to appear before the Board this (Saturday) afternoon, when a final selection will be made. RUNCORN CHURCH Issirritxx.—A. eonversazione in con- nection with this society took place in the boys' school- room, Church-street, on Tuesday evening. About ninety members were present, and a most enjoyable evening was spent. Besides vocal and instrumental music, there were microscopes, electric batteries, and a musical box for the amusement of the company, and refreshments were provided. WIDNES AMATEUR ELOCITTIONARY AND DRAMATIC SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of members was held on ' Monday. Mr. J. White presided. The statement of ac- counts, which showed a balance in hand of £37 3s Bd, was adopted. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., was elected presi- dent, and a considerable number of local gentlemen were appointed vice-presidents. Mr. R. Lewis was appointed hon. treasurer Mr. W. E. Oakden, hon. secretary; Mr. H. W. Cookson, acting manager; and Mr. E. M. Davies, stage manager. INDIGE-STION CURED by One box of Howell's Golden Herb _

ACCIDENT AT A WIDNES COPPER WORES.—A shocking accident occurred on Wednesday .at the Tharsis Copper Works to a youth named William Hancock, whose home is at 2, Charles-street, Simm's Cross. Hancock through some means at present unexplained fell from a "high level" to the ground, and alighting on a spade, a fearful gash was inflicted upon his head. He was at once con- veyed to the Accident Hospital, and received the atten- tion of Dr. McDonnell, but he is still in a very critical state, as the wound has bean rendered worse by the cop- per ore adhering to the flesh. Another person fell from the level at the same tirne{but luckily escaped with a shaking. The strange part of the affair is that the level is protected by rails on both sides. RUNCORN SECOND STAR-BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY. —The third annual meeting of the members of this society was held on Wednesday night in Bethesda School- room. Mr S. Pope occupied the chair and moved the adoption of the report and statement of meetings. In the report the directors stated that the Society was making steady progress. Mr Midwood seconded the motion which was carried. The retiring directors, Messrs J. MidwOod, T. D. Timmins, G. C. Beckitt and J. R. Firth were re-elected. The auditors, Messrs W. Pownell and Hugh Rowe, junior, were also re-elected. Subsequently an appropriation took place. Mr Frank Scott, agent to the goods department at Runcorn Station, was the lucky member, 'becoming entitled to £2OO free of interest for 14 years. PRESENTATION TO A RUNCORN ORGANIST—A gathering of a most interesting character took place a few evenings ago at the residence of Mr. R. Morris, in Duke's Field. Recently Mr. W. H. Grice, organist at St. Paul's Wes- leyan Chapel, was united in marriage to Miss Emily Matthis, daughter of Mr. H. Matthis, of Normacott, Staffordshire, and the choir and a few members of the congregation thought the opportunity a favourable one to show their esteem and regard for Mr. Grice, and to acknowledge his services. No difficulty was experienced in obtaining the necessary subscriptions, and a hand- some drawing-room timepiece was obtained. Inscribed upon the clock are the words "Presented to W. H. Grice, organist, by the choir and a few members of St. Paul's congregation on the occasion of his marriage, with their best wishes. Runcorn, 1887." With the ob- ject of making the presentation the choir assembled at the place, and Mr. and Mri. Morris gave an enjoyable social aspect to the ceremony by providing tea, the tables being set out with beautiful chrysanthemums. Subsequently, Mr. Morris appropriately performed the ceremony of presentation, remarking that Mr. Grice I had devoted much time and talent to the performance of his duties at the chapel, and it had afforded the sub- 'scribers great pleasure to be enabled to recognise his merits.—Mr. Clegg also made a few observations suit- able to the occasion. In acknowledging the gift, Mr. 'Grice disclaimed that his services deserved such hand- some recognition, and hepromised to continue to do all in his poiver for the choir and congregation of St. Paul's. During the evening songs were given by Miss Jones, Miss Simkin, and Miss Birkett ; and by the host and Mr. Clegg. Mr. Grice was the accompanist. • SMALL-PDX AT WIDNES.—A serious case of small-pox occurred at a house in Wellington-street during the past week. The patient is a man who has come from Sheffield, where the disease is very prevalent. The Sanitary 4uthority have had the case isolated. DEarir OF A WIDNES PEISONER.—WiIIiaM Priestley, a prisoter, died 'in the hospital of Birkdale Gaol early on Thursday morning. The deceased was com- mitted from Widnes on the 24th ultimo, on a 'charge of begging, and was sentenced to one calendar month's bard labour. The cause of death was intestinal obstruc- tion.

THEFT AT FATINWORTH.—Wore Mr. H. Graskell, jun., at Widnes Police Court, yesterday, Margaret E. Lally, a single woman, of Farnworth, waa charged with stealing three chemises, three pairs of drawers, three night dresses, several pinafores, and one feather, the property of Ann Edwardson a widow, of the same place. The prisoner, who admitted her guilt, was remanded until Monday. ROBBERY. FROM A WIDNES TRADESMEN.-011 Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, Anthony Welsh, 13 years of age, was charged with stealing a pair of boots, value lOs 9d, from the shop of William Williams, boot and shoe dealer, Waterloo-road. The prisoner attempted to pawn the boots at the shop of Mr. E. Imison, Church-street, Runcorn, by stating they were his rhother's. He was told to fetch his parent, but he did not return, and the boots were handed over to the police. The prosecutor identified the boots, which had not been missed until produced by the constable.—The prisoner, who said he was drunk when he committed the theft, was sentenced , to two months' hard labour. VIOLENT ASSAULT ON RUNCORN POLICE.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley, Peter O'Neil was charged with hav- ing, on Saturday night, the sth inst, committed a breach of the peace in High-street, and also assaulted Police Constables Sutherland and Jackson. Two independent ' witnesses, J. B. Dooley and Charles Ball, stated that the , prisoner was running about the street brandishing a knife in his hand, and threatening that he would "rip open" the first person that came near him, and the first constable that he met. A large crowd assembled, and the constables came upon the scene. Sutherland seized hold of the prisoner, who struck him on the face with his fist, and made his nose bleed. Jackson, who came to his aid, was cut iu four places upon the hand • but after a struggle the constables secured him and took him to the police station. On the first charge the prisoner was bound over to be of good behaviour for six mouths, and pay the costs 12s. 6d. He was also fined £1 and cost l 7s. for each assault. In all, the prisoner had to pay £3 6s. 4d., or go to gaol for two months. THErrs FROM WIDNES Scnoots.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mary Molyneux, 17 years of age, who resides at Liverpool-street, St. Helens, was charged with having, on the 2nd inst, stolen from Warrington- road Board School a shawl belonging to Joseph Harding, of 7, Lathom-street. Richard Grant, the caretaker of the schools, saw the prisoner in the cloak-room, and asked her business.. She replied that she had come to fetcji her sister in order that she might see her father, who had come from the Workhouse. On the girl's departure, the shawl could not be found, and the prisoner was sub- seqiiently apprehended with the article in her posses- sion. The prisoner was also charged with having, on the 31st August last, stolen from the same school a jacket be- longing to Kate Norris, of 90, Kent-street, a teacher at the school. It was proved that the prisoner had sold the jacket to Mrs. Duckworth, Of 79, Barter-street, St. Helens. The prisoner,who had been previously convicted, pleaded guilty to both charges, and she was sentenced to three months' hard labour.—Ferix Allander and James Allander, who have recently been whipped for commit- ting a felony, were charged with having, on the 7th inst, stolen from St. Bede's School, Appleton, two coats, one belonging to Isaac J. Arnold, and the other to Denis Murray, both scholars.--The boys pleaded guilty, and their father told the magistrates that he had done his best to keep the children under control, but he could do nothing with them.—On the first charge the Bench sen- tenced the prisoners to three weeks' imprisonment, after- wards to be confined in a reformatory school for five years. A sentence of one day's imprisonment was given on the second charge. • TER RIVAL BILLPOSTERS.—At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before his Honour Judge Thomp- son and 'a jury, the action brought by Joseph Smith, a billposter in the employlof Mr. W. G. Deacle advertis- ing contractor, St. Helens, \to recover £5O damages for wrongful imprisonment from Messrs. Abbott and Co., advertising contractors, was resumed. Smith was ar- rested on the sworn information of Nathaniel Edwards (Abbott and, Co.), on a charge of stealing boards, was kept in custody for twenty-four hours, and was then liberated on bait. The charge during remand was altered to one of receiving the boards knowing them to have been stolen, and Smith was acquitted. Mr. Swift, bar- rister, for Smith, contended that,, the proceedings had been taken maliciously, and haft arisen out of trade rivalry.—Mr. H. L. Riley urged that there was no evi- dence to prove malicious intent.—His Honour said the three points which the jury had to consider were—dirst, did defendants take reasonable care to informthemselves of the true state of the case; secondly, did they honestly believe the case which they had laid before the magis- trates • and thirdly, were defendants actuated by any indirect motive in preferring the charge P—After an absence of thirty-five minutes, the jury returned and answered the first question in the negative and the second and third questions in the affirmative .—His Hon- our said that was a verdict for the plaintiff .—The Fore- man: Yes.—His Honour: Then you have to consider the question of damages. You know the position de- fendant is in, and you know the character of the plain- tiff. The jury again retired, and on returning in a few minutes awarded the plaintiff £5 damages.—Mr. Swift asked for costs on the higher scale, saying the case had had to be taken to a higher court, from which it was re- mitted to that court—His Honour declined to allow costs on the higher scale.—Mr. Riley suggested that his Hon- our should stay execution to give defendants time to consider whether to apply for a new trial, but his Hon- our said this case in which the jury had been concerned was completed, and declined to accede to Mr. Riley's application. TEE TALK OF THE TOWN.—ROWCR'S Golden Herb Pills.—

div.p: Adrt.

Guy PAWICE'S DAY AT PENKETIL—OR Saturday the gunpowder plot day was celebrated with great interest at Penketh. Large bonfires were lighted here and there in the village. At Mr. E. Crossland's there was a very large one, and the usual guy was dressed and burned, to the great amusement of the young people. The rain marred to a great extent the sport. ASSOCIATION OF LOCAL BOARD CLERKS.—A meet- ing of the Association of Local Board clerks of Eng- land and Wales was held at the Mitre Hotel, Man- chester, on Saturday afternoon, when Mr. Hewitson (Swinton) presided. There was a large attendance of Local Board clerks, including Mr. R. H. Prescott, of Haydock, secretary of the Association. Mr. J. B. Goulburn (clerk to Turton and Little Lever Local Board), read a paper on " Local Government," in which he ably and intelligently reviewed the sub- ject from its earliest institution, its present posi- tion, and suggested several important amendments. His views were expounded in a masterly manner, and carried considerable weight. An interesting discussion followed, and cordial thanks were ten- dered to Mr. Goulburn. PENKETH WESLEYAN BAND OF IlopE.—On Fri- day the second of a series of meetings was held in the Wesleyan School, when the chair was taken by the Rev. J. J. Langham, Warrington, and the fol- lowing programme was gone through :—Recitation, "Boys' Right," W. Yearsley ; song, "Dear Father- land," choir; recitation, "Beyond the Garden Gate," Esther Tetlow ; song, "Autumn Winds," choir; reci- tation, "Two Drinkers," David Dobson; song, "As- sam Pekoe," choir; dialogue, "Band of Hope Spec- tacles," Misses Emma Hobson, Margaret Routledge, and Margaret E. Mainley ; song, "lip, hip, Harrah Miss Mabel Garnett and Co.; recitation, "The Golden Gate," Marion Ashton ; song. "Forest Voices," choir. There was a very good attendance, and the chairman's address was 'listened to with great pleasure tind heartily applauded. CLOSING OF MANCHESTER EXHIBITION. The Royal Jubilee Exhibition, which has been a source of gratification to nearly five millions of people, was finally closed on Thursday. No visitors were admitted after four o'clock in the afternoon, and by that time 24,420 persons had passed through the gateways, bringing up the total since the opening of the Exhibition in May last to 4,705,137. The chief feature of the day's proceedings was a musical entertainment in the Concert Hall. In the course of a short address Sir Joseph Lee, chairman of the Executive Committee, intimated that the enterprise had been a financial success. and that at aft early date the guarantors will be released from the liability they incurred in guaranteeing the sum of £140,000. The Exhibition was dosed and cleared of visitors shortly before seven o'clock, after which the members oi the Executive Committee, the Sectional Committees, and others dined together in the Palm Hodse. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Col. Ashton (in the chair), the Revs. T. W. N. Telmer and T. Whitley, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Hadfield, Lewis, Stokes, Lowe, Brandreth, Hall, Pickering, Hamilton; S. Taylor. CamPkin H. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk). ARMY RESERVE MEN AND PENSIONERS:A letter was read from the Local Government Board stating that they had been requested by the Secretary of State for War to ascertain the number of inmates in the Workhouse be- longing to the army reserve, or who may be pensioners, and also the number of army reserve men and pensioners who might be relieved by the Guardians.--It was stated that this information would be provided. THE NOMINATION OF GIJARDIANS.—A communication was read from the King's Lynn Board of Guardians ask- ing the Board to join,in a ,representation to the Local

Government Board, to the effect that it is desirable to make it imperative that before a person be nominated as a Guardian his assent should be obtained.—lt was decided, on the motion of Mr. Mclntyre, to agree to the above proposal. "LAW AND ORDER " IN IRELAND. - The following communication was received from the Bridgwater Board of Guardians, viz. :—" The above Board having received copy of resolutions passed by the Dewsbury- Guardians, under date 13th ult., expressing disapproval of the con- duct of the authorities in attempting to interfere with I the proceedings of the 'Limerick Board of Guardians. had considered same and passed resolutions thereupon as set out on the other side.' One of the resolutions referred to was as follows That the Board expresses its great satisfaction with the authorities in their determination to maintain law and order whether in the Board-room oi the Limerick Union, Mitchellstown London, Bridgewater, or elsewhere in the United Kingdom where exceptional' circumstances have rendered such unpleasant 'duties necessary." The other resolution was to the effect that the above resolution should be fonlarded to the Prime Minister, and a number of other important personages and some public bodies.—Mr HADFIELD said it was a pity that the ' Bridgewater and Dewsbury Guardians had not some- thing else to do than sending such bosh as that out. Put it in the waster paper basket. (Laughter).—The Chairman let it lie on the table.—The matter then dropped. THE ARREARS: APPOINTMENT OF COLLECTOR. - The Relief Supervision Committee recommended that £264 should be written off the list of arrears. There was not a single vise in which the late collector (Mr. Houghton) had received money and not accounted for it. It was explained that in the opinion of the committee there was £lBO 17s 4d out of the £284 that should not have been charged at all to relatives, as they had never been in a position to pay it. In the case of £B4 7s lid of the ar- rears promises had been made that it should be paid, so that in reality there had been very little real loss.—Ten applications for the vacant post of cellector had been re- ceived, and after consideration by the Board, Mr. Prod- sham, of Aston, was appointed. This was all the business.

div.head: OPENING OF A LIBERAL CLUB AT WIDNES.
div.p: OPENING OF A LIBERAL CLUB AT WIDNES.

The formal ceremony of opening the Widnes Liberal Club toOk place on Monday evening at the premises in Aldforde Chambers. The arrangents and objects of the club have been previously des- cribed. Amongst those present were E. K. Mus- pratt, J.l'., president of the Division Liberal Asso- ciation, Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., Dr. E. P. S. Counsel, Liberal candidate for Dublin University, Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, .1. L. 3luspratt, E. Carey, J. W. Ware- ing, F. Heyes, Alan Deacon, J. Morrison, H. B. Shores, J. J. Latham, J. W. Carlile, W. Colquitt, John Tallon, jun., Oeorge • Ogg, H. Fairclough, Thomas Crozier, J. E. Johnson, F. Cave (secre- tary), &c. 'Mr. Morrison gplve Mr. Muspratt a cordial welcome to Widnes Liberal Club, which had been formed for the pur- pose of providing a centre where the Liberal working- men of Widnes might meet for social recreation, and for the purpose of discussing and promoting objects inter- esting to the Liberal party. The club had been estab- lished on a very low basis as regarded the fee, which was I 4s. per annum, in order that every working man in the town might be enabled to join. The club had been established on thoroughly democratic principles. The management would be entirely in the hands of the com- mittee, and he believed that with care and attention the club would be made self-supporting. There were certain initial expenses connected with furniture, and they might have to ask the aid of friends to meet these charges. But afterwards the revenue, he believed, would equal the expenses. They had received letters of encouragement fm Mr T. S. Timmis, Mr F. H. Gos- sage, Mr Holbrook Gaskell, Mr F. Gaskell, Mr A Deacon, who all promised their cordial support to the club. (Ap- plause.) Mr. Muspratt said he declared the club open with great pleasure. The existence of a tlub. in Widnes was very much required. The constituency was of consider- able extent, and the member of Parliament was prac- tically returned by the working-men. It Was therefore desirable that the working-men should meet together socially, because after all every one wanted some recrea- tion; and it was also desirable that they should meet to- gether in a club like that; where Liberal questions could be discussed. It was by discussion one with another that the working-men would arrive at a much better in- sight of all political questions, and they would be able to judge more thoroughly and accurately than they other- wise would which candidate for Parliamentary honours properly represented their views. He was sure that the Liberal Working-men would join the club in sufficient numbers to make the club self-supporting, because an institution of that kind would not do the good it ought to do unless it was managed by working-men themselves —(applause) ; and it could not be managed by the work- ing-men themselves if they allowed their expenses to ex- ceed the income. (Hear, hear.) If they had to go to gentlemen who had long purses, and possibly not as good and sound political opinions as the members—if they had to go to those gentlemen and ask them for assistance, those gentlemen generally asked for some return. He did not think it was a wise position for working-men to be in. They had far better make the club self support- ing, and then they would be able to view the constitu- ency and say how they would be represented. (Ap- plause.) He had very much pleasure in declaring the club open. (Applause.) . Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P., whom the chairman introduced as the " Parnell of Wales," heartily congratulated them upon having a permanent home for the Liberals of Wid- nes. He thought their danger as Liberals was that their enthusiasm was like cataracts and waterfalls. Their enthusiasm came in very great force at election time or when then was a great public meeting; but during the ordinary times of registration and of canvassing, and the organising of districts, they had very little entgusiasm. He thought a club like theirs would do a great amount of good, and to show that he was not talking at random he would give them a little of the experience they had had in the Northwich Division. They won the election in 1885 by a great stream of Liberal enthusiasm, but in 1888 they failed disastrously, and he thought it was to a great extent due to the fact that there was no per- manent organisation anywhere in the division. After suffering defeat they looked to the machinery, and star- ted clubs in two of the chief towns, and in four of the contributory villages. They worked quietly and steadily during the winter, and when the time came for a con- test these little clubs gave a good account of themselves. He was sure such an example, small as it was, would be encouraging to them. (Hear, hear.) They had fought two excellent battles in Widnes' and he hoped when the time came for another political struggle they would show a different result. (Applause). Dr. Counsel also spoke and, said he believed Widnes had a great future before it. It was time they joined to- gether in establishing a club on Liberal Democratic prin- ciples, and he was quite certain when the next election came they would be successful in returning a Gladston- ian candidate to represent them. (Applause). • This concluded the proceedings, and those present ad- journed to the Liberal meeting.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of this Authority was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. Colonel Ashton presided. and there were also pre- sent the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Hadfield, Lewis Stokes, Lowe, Brandreth, Hall, Pickering. Hamilton;i II. Linaker (clerk), W. H. Linaker (assistant clerk), and Farrington (in- spector).

div.head: BOUNDkILIES.
div.p: THE BOUNDkILIES.

A letter was read from the office of the Clerk of the Peace asking for information as to the boundaries of the Rural Sanitary Authority's district, in order that it might be supplied to the Boundary Commissioners.—The Clerk said he had written to the Clerk of the Peace to say that there was no part of that Authority's district in any other county. It had occurred to him, however, that there was a piece of land about 57 or 60 acres in ex- tent which Might be transferred from the Northwich Union to the Runcorn.liThis piece of land had, by the works on the river Weaver, been divided from the town- ship of Acton, and was now really part of Dutton town- ship. It had no caxriage communication with Acton, and it was very inconvenient forfatepayers living upon it to attend meetings at Acton. He thought they might call the attention of the Local Government Board or the Commissioners to this matter, in order to see if they could have this piece of land added to Dutton.—The Assistant Clerk said that if the land had been severed by, the natural flow of the river it would have belonged to Dutton.—The Clerk said there was another alteration suggested—that the townships of Latchford, Grappen- , hall, and Thelwall should be taken from the Warrington Union and brought back to the Runcorn Union, to which they formerly belonged. The ratepayers of those town- ships were aesirous of being brought back.—Mr. Had- field: Arelthe rates lower here ?—The Clerk: I'es ; they are lower than in Warringtnn.—Mr. Hadfield: I suppose that is the reason they want to come back.—Mr. Mcln- tyre asked why the townships named were taken from the Runcorn Union ?—The Clerk said he did not know, as it was about two years before he came into that neighbourhood.—ln answer to a further question, the Clerk said that the townships of Latchford and Grappen- hall were in the highway district.—lt was agreed that the course suggested by the Clerk with regard to the piece of land referred to should be adopted. THE ROADWAY AT WESTON POINT.

Dr. Adam-s-, -medical officer, reported that in accor- dance si,ith instructions issued at the previous meeting of the authority he had inspectsd the roadway at Weston Point, mentioned in their instructions, and regretted that it was only in his power to repeat what he had often said in former reports on the subject, viz :—that the roadway was a disgrace to any civilised community, but that, unfortunately, it was not in his power to cer- tify that it was "a nuisance dangerous and injurious to health" within the meaning of the Acts relating to pub- lic health. It was a matter for serious regret to him that such was the case, for the granting of such a certi- ficate might do away with what was, in his opinion, a shocking state of roadway for even the most primitive township.—Mr. Hadfield : We have nothing to do with

it, then, as a question of nuisance ?—The Clerk: No, There is no way of forcing it to be done except by a cer- tain process, and that is around-about way.—Mr. Aaron: Let it lie.—Mr. Mclntyre: Then you must live in your primitive condition.—Mr. Aaron: Yes; it is a great hardship to the people.—lt was decided that the Clerk should, in reply to an inquiry read at the previous meet- ing, write to the Local Government Board to say that they had caused their medical officer,to report as to the road, and also to forward a copy of the medical officer's report.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.
div.p: MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. Adams reported the occurrence of scarlet fever at Norley. The disease at present was confined to one house, viz :—A small ,farm situated off the highway near toHatchmere. Five children had been attacked, of ages ranging from one to eleven years, but the cases were slight. A case of typhoid fever had also occurred at Kingsley. The case was an imported one as the patient had come home ill from Widnes. As other cases had occurred on the same premisesat Widnes, the Authority's nspector had wisely conununicated with the Widnes insrtctor. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. E. Carey, D. Wright, F. Heyes, S. Sadler, J. Taylor, R. Cook, J. Houghton, B. Brown, W. W. Gossage, T. Handley, J. T. Allen (clerk), W. Higginson (surveyor), I. Carr (engineer.)

THE VACANCY. The Chairman remarked that they were compelled by law to fill up the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. Husband within six weeks. He suggested, however, that the Board should ask the Local Government Board to allow them to keep the vacancy open until the elec- tion in March next, when Mr. Husband would have had to retire.—Mr. Taylor observed that if the Board appoin- ted a gentleman now and he lost his seat at the election, it would be very hard upon him.—Mr Wright moved and Mr Taylor seconded a resolution asking the Local Government Board for permission to keep the' vacancy open.—Carried.

r - SUGGESTED LICENSING SESSION FOR WIDNES. With regard to this matter which had been before a special meeting, the Clerk said he was informed that if the Board wished to do anything with regard to having a licensing session at Widnes, the correct course was to send a requisition to the Justices of Prescot Petty Sessional Division. Mr Carey: Is it possible for the justices to do it P—The Clerk: It is possible for the justices to adjourn the licensing sessions from place to place. They might adjourn the sessions to suit the Widnes portion of the Division.—Upon the motion of Mr Brown, seconded by Mr Wright, it was unanimously resolved to ask the justices to hold a general or an adjourned general licensing sessions at Widnes for the townships of Widnes, Ditton, Crouton and Bold.

THE FREE LECTURF.S. The Clerk read a letter, from the Local Government Board, who sanctioned the expenditure of a sum not ex- ceeding £l5 upon a course of free lectures on educational or scientific subjects.—The Chairman: I think that is very satisfactory.

MONEY NOT REQUIRED. The Local Government Board stated in a letter that they had received from the Public WorksrLoan Commis- sioners the sanction granted on the Bth September, 1880, to the borrowing by the Widnes Local Board of £38,800 for works of sewerage. The Board have cancelled the sanction as regards the sum of £14,960, which had not been raised thereunder.—The Clerk explained that the loan was obtained to make the main sewer from Sitaha,s Cross to the outlet at the river. The Board only spent £23,840 of the amount, and the Local Government Board had now cancelled the difference between the amounts.

GAS AND WATER CORMITTRE.-PRICE OF WATER REDUCED. The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee con- tained the report of the Engineer, who stated that the 650 yards of 3inch water main, at Barrow's Green, was well in hand, and the majority of the houses would have a supply of water by the end of the week. The mean rainfall for the month was 2.515 inches. The water in stock on the 26th October was 8,588,174 gallons. The illuminating power Of the gas averaged 17.24 candles. The committee examined the applications for the post of assistant gas and water manager, and at a subsequent date inteniewed five-of the applicants. It was recom- mended that T. Duxbury be•appointed at a salary of £lOO per annum. It was also recommended that the price of water be reduced one penny per 1,000 gallons on quantity consumed beyond 40 million gallons per annum' the reduction to date from the Ist October, 1887, and to be based upon the financial year's statement.— Mr Brown moved the confirmation of the minutes, and, referring to the proposed reduction in the price of water, stated that it was better that they should sell the water at a reduced price than have it thrown upon their hands.—Mr Wright seconded the motion, which was carried.

HIGHWAY MATTERS. The minutes of the Highway Committee tontained a letter from the Local Government Board, who sanctioned the`borrowing of £7,880 for sewers in Victoria-road, , Lugsdale-road, Ann-street, Milton-mad, • Widnes and Albert-roads, and Warrington-road. It was recommended that the following contracts be sealed :--Sayee and Ran- dle, £1,953 12s 6d for Warrington-road sewer; and S. Cowburn, £5,323 lOs for sewering Victoria-road, Lugsdale-road. Ann-street, Widnes and Albert-road, and Moss-bank. The plan and estimate for the paving, sewering, &c., of Ditton-road, from Victoria-road to the westerly bodndary of Todd Bros'. premises, were ex- amined and approved; and it was recommended that the usual notices be served upon the various owners to do the work.—Fri rate Streets The committee inspected the following streets: Viaduct-street from Church-street to Martley-street, Martley-street, Gerrard-street, Oak- land-street from Mersey-road to Irwell-street, John-street, Little John-street, White-street, Bridge-street, Terrace- road from Bank-street to John-street, Beamont-street, Bank-street from Mersey-road to Terrace-road, Davies- street, Hurst-st., West Bank-st., Pear-st., part of Ditton- road, and Alexandra-street. Recommended that the surveyor be instructed to prepare plans and estimates for the making, &c., of all the foregoing streets, with the exception of Bridge-street, Beamont-street, Bank-street, Davia4-street, West'liank-street, and Pear-street.—Mr. Carey moved the adoption of the minutes, and said it was the desire of the committee that the streets should be made as immediately as practicable without undue pressure or hardship upon any property owners, and without giving too much to the surveyor and his staff at a time. After the committee had done with the front streets they hoped to be permitted by the Board to at- tack the back passages. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Taylor seconded the motion.—Carried.

HEALTH CONMITTEE. The Medical Officer of Health reported to the Health Committee that during the month of October there were 102 births and 42 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 40.8 and 16.8 per 1,000. Zymotic diseases caused 7 deaths. The Inspector of Nuisances reported that there were 4 deaths from typhoid fever and enteric fever, and one each from dysentery diarrhoea and diptheria ; Dr. O'Keeffe accompanied the Inspector on an examination of the ashpits and closets in Newtown and West lank districts, which were found in a fair condition. The back passages, however, were in a very un.satisfactory state. The contractor's work throughout the township was in a very fair state.—ln moving the adoption of the minutes, Dr, O'Keeffe said the mortality in the township had almost come to its normal standard. In September the mortality was 23 per 1,000, and in August 37 per 1,000; and he was of opinion that this very high rate of mortality as to be attributed not to the non-removal or imperfect removal of nightsoil, but to the very high tem- perature that prevailed during several months during the summer.—Mr. W. W. Gossage seconded. The minutes were passed.

1 - FINANCE. The Finance Committee recommended that application be made to the Public Works Loan Commissioners for £7.880 for 30 years, repayable by equal half-yearly in- stalments of principal and interest. Accounts amount- ing to .£4,082 15s 9d were passed for payment. The minutes were passsed on the motion of :IHr., Handley.

- ----- - LORD MAYOVS BANQUET.—Lord Salisbury and a num- ber of the Cabinet Ministers were present at the Lord Mayor's banquet on Wednesday evening. In responding to the toast of " Her Majesty's Ministers," Lord Salis- bury remarked that though there had been nothing strik- ing during the year in foreign affairs, the Afghan Boun- dary, question had been settled. Ayoub Khan had sur- rendered to the Government of India. A settlement had also been arranged in respect to the Suez Canal and the New Hebrides. He saw no danger in any quarter, though the competition for larger armaments might cause uneasiness. He hoped that the difference with the United States would be settled. l'urning to domestic affairs, he said that those who thought there would bo no legislation until Home Rule were adopted, deceived themselves in supposing that the defenders of the integ- rity of ' the Empire would give way. The Government were unflinching in their determination to enforce law and order in Ireland, but their difficulties were great, especially in view of the attitude of the Opposition. Lawlessness, as they had seen in London, was contagious, and it must be checked.

Tsu Brompton Hospital for Consumptives, in Lon- don, reports that over fifty people out of every hundred consumptives are victims of constipated or inactive kidneys. Consumption is one of our national diseases, and the above report goes to prove what has often been said in our columns during the last few years, that kidney troubles are not only the cause of more than half of the cases of consumption but of ninety out of every hundred other common diseases. They who have taken this position, made their claims after elaborate in- vestigation, and their proof that they have discovered a specific for the terrible,and stealthy kidney diseases, which have become so prevalent among us, as wise and

convincing. We have recently received from them a fresh supply of their wonderful advertising. They have challenged the medical profession and science to investigate.. They have investigated, and those who are frank have ad- mitted the truth of their statements. They claim that ninety per cent. of diseases come originally from in- active kidneys; that ,these inactive kidneys allow the blood to become filled with uric acid poison; that this uric acid poison in the blood carries disease through every

organ. There is enough uric acid developed in the system within twenty-four hours to kill half-a-dozen men. This being a scientific fact, it requires only ordinary wisdom to see the effect inactive kidneys must have upon the system. If this poison is not removed, it ruins every organ. If the bowels, stomach, or liver become inactive, we know it at once, but other organs help them out. If the kid- neys become constipated and dormant, the warning comes later on, and often when it istoo late, because the effects are remote from the kidneys, and those organs are not suspected to be out of order. Or,ans„ that are weak and diseased are unable to re- sist the attacks of this poison, and the disease often takes the form of and is treated as a local affliction, when in reality the real cause of the trouble was inac- tive kidneys. Too many medical men of the present day hold what was a fact twenty years ago that kidney disease is in- curable, according td the medicines authorised by their code. Hence they ignore the original cause of disease it- self, and give their attention to useless treating of local

effects. They dose the patient with quinine, morphine, or with salts and other physics, hoping that thus nature may cure the disease; while the kidneys continue to waste away with inflammation, ulceration, and decay, and the victim eventually perishes. The same quantity of blood that passes through the heart passes through the kidneys. If the kidneys are diseased the blood soaks up this disease and takes it all through the system. Hence it is that the claim is made that Warner's SAFE Cure, the only known specific for kidney diseases,cures 90 per cent. of human ailments because it, and it alone, is able to maintain the natural activity of the kidneys, and to neutralise and remove the uric acid, or kidney poison, as fast as it is formed. If this acid is not removed, there is inactivity of the kidneys, and there will be produced in the system paralysis, apoplexy, dyspepsia, consumption, heart dis- ease, headaches, rheumatism, pneumonia and all the nameless diseases of delicate women. If the poisonous matter is separated from the blood, as fast as it is formed, these diseases, in a majority of cases, would not

exist. It only requiries a particle of small-pox virus to pro- duce that vile disease, and the poisonous matter from the kidneys, passing all through the system. and becoming lodgea at different weak points, is equally destructive, although more disguised. If it were possible for us to see into the kidneys, and haw quickly the blood passing through them goes to the heart and lungs and other parts of the system, carrying this deadly virus with it, all would believe without hesi- tation what has so often been stated in advertisements in these columns, that the kidneys are the most impor- tant organs in the body. They may regard this article as an advertisement and refuse to believe it, but that, is a matter over which we have no control. Careful investigation and science itself are proving beyond a doubt that this organ is, in fact, more important than any other in the system as a health regulator, and as such should be closely watched for the least sign of disordered action.—The Family Doctor, September 3.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), Al- dermen Davies and Harrison, and Councillors Fran- comb, Greening, and Pierpoint. THEFT FROM THE MARKET.—John Mullen, forge la- bourer, of 5, Buckley's-yard, Haydock-street, was charged with stealing an overcoat and three ve.sts, the property of a tailor and woollen draper named Gold- stein, of Manchester, who keeps a stall in the Warring- ton Market. He was sent to prison for four months,with hard labour. DRUNICENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for this offence :—Ellen Connor, in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday night, discharged Annie Daley, in But- termarket-street, sent to prison ;_ for a month; Margaret Fleming, in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday midnight, sent to prison for a month; MaiT Knockton, Irwood- street, on the 29th October, dismissed ; James Griffin, in Winwick-street, on the 29th October, fined 5s and costs; William Ford, at Market Gate, on Oa g9th October, fined 5s and costs; Henry Bridge, in Rose and Crown-street, fined 58 and costs; Thomas Hogan, in Horsemarket- street, on the 2nd inst, fined 55 and costs, e OADZELY cHARACTER.—James Miskell was fined 103 and costs for na7ing bcorl disorderly at the Work- house, on Saturday. Benoiwo.—John Joyce, who was charged with begging in Sankey-street, was dismissed.-IVlary Dyson was charged with begging in Buttermarket-strent, on Sunday evening. She was dismissed on promising to leave

rie town. OasratrertoN.—William Lomas and Joseph Blackmore were each fined 58. including costs, for causing an ob- struction with a pony and cart in Golborne-street. STONE Tuttowngo.—Thomas Rutter was fined 2s 6d for this offence. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Sutton and Mr. R. Garnett. DRUNEENNEB9.—John Jefferies, labourer, Foundry- street, was fined 5s and costs for having been drunk in Buttermarket-street, on the 28th ult. TRAVELLING wrruovr TlClEET.—Alexander Malcolm- son, Liverpool, was fined 103 and costs for having trav- elled on the London and North-Western Railway, from Liverpool to Warrington, on the previous day, without having paid his fare. WEDRESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough and Coun- cillor R. W. Franc,omb. DRUNKENNESS.—Austin Ca,rroll was fined 5s and costs for hp,ving been drunk in Butterrnarket-street, on the previous morning. TIITIR.SDAY.—Before Major Litton. DROSEENNE.99,—JOhn Grady, who was charged with having been drunk in Mill-street, was discharged with a caution. FRIT/AV.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gornall. Titarr ov S AND . —Thomas Armitage (11) and Joseph Glover (13) were summoned for having stolen a quan- tity of sand, value 61, the property of John Ireland Bla.ckburne, on the 3rd inst. The lads took the sand from a field near Longford-street. Mr. John White, who prosecuted, said that there was no desire to press the case, but it was wished that an intimation should be given that people could not take the sand with impunity. The mother of one of the boys said that she had no idea that he was doing wrong in taking the sand. The Bench fined the defendants is each, and cautioned them not to repeat the offence.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. WEDNIZDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. G-ossage. Richard Jones, 2, Duke-street, Runcorn, and John Shernan, 24, Victoria-street, were each fined 5g and costs for drunkenness.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TEMBSDAT.—Before Mr. T. S. Timmis and Mr. J. Brock. MisCELIANSOUS.—For being asleep on his cart at Bold, James Connolly was fined Ss and costs, 45 6d.—Edward Haynes, of -1, Charlotte-street, and Henry Penketh Mather, of no residence, were each fined for drunken- .

.‘ new. CHIMNEY ON FtgE.—ThoMaS Spruce was fined I.FI and costs for allowing the chimney of , his dwelling-house in Terrace-road to be on fire. THREATS.—Mary Catou, of Caroline-street, was sum- moned for using threatening language towards Emma Duke-street. The de Bromley, of 51, fendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months. WILFUL Dsusot.--,Sarah Hallet, a respectable-looking woman, who lives in Muspratt-street, was charged with unlawfully and wilfully breaking a pane of glass in the window of the house of William Jones, of Muspratt- street, doing damage to the extent of is 6d.—The defend- ant, who denied the allega,tion, said the action was brought out of malice, because her husband, whom she had left, lived with the complainant.—She was fined 2s 6d and costs, 8s Bd, and was also ordered to pay the damage.

-- RUNCORN PET'FY SESSIONS. MUNDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Mr. James Handley. CUIDINEYS o Fnm.—On the evidence of P.C. Kettle, and each de- fendant was ordered to pay 105 and costs, or go to gaol for It days.—For being drunk and disorderly in Fryer-

A BEGGAE.—On the evidence of P.C. Sutherland, ThoS. Brown was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging in Bridge-street. SLEEpwo OuT.—William Thomas Turner was charged with sleeping in the stables of Mr. Williams, at Top Locks. As this was the prisoner's first offence he was discharged with a caution.

Pexx.rra v. SMEDLEY HALL.—Playeci on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and after a pleasant and well- , contested game ended in a victory for Penketh by one goal, thrqv minors to nil. HALTON- V. FRODSHILM 2ND.—This matth was played at Frodsham, on Saturday, and after a very poor game resulted in favour of the visitors byl goal (disputed) and 3 minors, to 1 try (disputed) and 2 minors: FRODSAAM IST V. GRANGE, BIRKENHEAD.—The Frod- sham team journeyed to Birkenhead on Saturday to play , the above fixture. At half-time the score was--Frodsham 1 try and 4 minors to 1 minor. Result of the match : Frodsham, 2 tries, 8 minors, to 3 minors. The Frodsham club have placed seven matches this season, and have come off victors in each case. RUNCORN 2ND TEAM V. LITHERLAND.—The return match between the above teams was played at Runcorn on Saturday. The visitors won the toss, and lirazendale started from the centre for the home team. When half time was called, the score stood one try for Runcorn to Litherland nil. After a very even and well-contested game victory rested with the home team by one goal, one try, to Litherland one goal, one minor. Rtrscoeli FREE WANDERERS V. WIDNES FREE WAN- DERERS.—Thi3 match was played at Runcorn on Satur- day, nothing but minors being scored in the .first half. In the second Mercer obtained a try for the visitors, which was not improved upon. After the drop out, the home team following up, a scrimmage was formed, and, on the ball becoming loose, they dribbled over the line, and Walton secured a try, Robinson doing the needful. This brought the game to a close, and the victory rested with the home team by one goal, seven minors, to one try, two minors. WARRINOTO;i GRAM3fAR SCHOOL V. MANCHESTER GRATA- MAR SCHOOL.—This important Grammar School match was played at Arpley on Wednesday. Webster kicked off for the home team, and the forwards following up well, scored a minor. For about ten minutes play raged on the Manchester line', caused chiefly by the really splendid play of Haynes for the home team. By a bit of good play by Wilcox for the visitors, the ball was forced back, but Haynes gaining possession from a scrimmage, gained a grand try for the Warrington team. Webster kicked a splendid goal. After this play raged first in one quarter and then in another, the home team scoring a minor and Manchester a try. On change of ends the visitors pressed, but immediately afterwards the ball was taken into their 25 by a splendid bit of play by Webster. From passes by Haynes, Williamson gained the second and Hannah the rd try foi Warringtdn. Webster failed at goal, the positions being very difficult. At call of time Warrington Grammar School had won a good match by 1 goal, 2 tries, and 4 minors. to 1 try arid 1 minor. For the :homerot Webster and Haynes were the life and soul of the team, and for the visitors Booth, Wil- cox, and Evans played a good game. WIDNES V. BlRCH.—Played at Widnes on Saturday, when the home team won by two goals, two tries, and nine minors, to one try and one minor. Neither team was fully represented, the visitors playing thtee second team men whilst the two best Widnes forwards—Hughes and Smith—were playing in the county trial match, and , Fogg and Howard were unable to play. S. Morris, of Widnes, played for Birch, and was their best man. After a long spell of fine play, in which Widnes had a decided advantage, Parkinson obtained a try, but Plumpton failed at the place. This was followed by Plumpton 'dropping at goal, and missing by an ace, and crossing his opponent's line and appealing for a try, which was not allowed. Parkinson and Hardman subsequently had close shaves for dropped goals, after which Barker gained the second try for Widnes in fine style. The kick by Farrell was again a failure. A few minutes later, however, when Pennington secured another try, Farrell succeeded in guiding the hall over the cross-bar. A nar- row escape from scoring a dropped goal by Parkinson was followed by Eaves scoring a try for Birch. Morris contributing to it very effectively, and then Plumpton scored the last try in splendid style, Farrell doing the needful • and the game closed, aS above stahld, in Cbril- liant and well-earned victory for Widnes. Teams Widnes: S Bingham, hack; Plumpton (captain), Par- kinson and Barker, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Wilkinson, half backs; Kiddie, Hardman, Davenport, G. Bingham, T ''Pennington, Woods, Gondy, Barber, and Sampson, forwards. Birch: Case, back; T Higgmson, Eaves, and H Wheeler, threequarter backs; Broughton and E Higginbottom, half backs; Morris, Bainbridge, Escourt, A Wheeler. W Higginbottom, Hardman, Hay- ward, and Hasford, forwards. WARRINOTON Y. D,R9VOTITOIi BAN 00.9(" A "TEAms.)— ThC•se Ie:WU Met an the ground of the Warrington Foot- ball Club, Wilderspool Causeway, on Saturday, in fine weather, before 2,500 spectators. The hotrie team were considerably weakened owing to the unavoidable de- mands made upon them by the first team, but this did not prevent them from soaring another decided victory. The home captain won the toss, and Thomburn kicked off for the visitors at 3-30, Evans making a good return to Sadler, who mulled the ball. Jonas, Eyes, and Rand- ails dribbled to the Ranger's quarters, where Whittle passed to Appleton, this player putting in a nice kick. From a scrimmage on the line the Rangers managed to work the ball to centre. Whittle passed to Antrobu.s, and he to Evans, the latter player making a good kick. Whittle again passed to Antrobus, who got away with a nice run and passed to Evans, who transferred to Apple- ton. the last-named player making a splendid run in a- midst loud cheering. Isherwood took the place and sent the ball over the crossbar, but owing to Pole having touched the ball the goal could not be allowed. Moor- house dropped out, and no return being made play rested in mid-field. The visiting forwards, headed by Moor-. house, Wilson, and Squires, broke away with a dribble, but Appleton picked up and kicked to Sadler, this player being held by Bibby before he could return, and a good dribble by Randalls, Eyes, and Bate forced Thorburn to kick dead. Evans_ returned the drop-out, Williamson _ . .

making a short kick into touch. The home team now pressed their opponents on the goal line, Hodgson being allowed a free kick; but this did not afford relief, and from a scrimmage Whittle passed to Antrobus, who threw to Appleton, and this player picking up neatly made another brilliant run in, gaining his second try. Isherwood made a good attempt at goal. Thorburn re- started, the ball going into touch. Thorburn next passed to Pole, but he was brought down by Evans be- fore he could get far. Good play on the part of Squires and Pickard took play to the home quarters, Bibby sav- ing. Appleton removed the danger by a short run, and Antrobus passed to Evans, he putting in a dodgy run to centre, being brought down by Sadler. Good passing between Whittle, Evans, and Bibby resulted in the latter player taking operations to the visitors' goal line. Thorburn was here allowed a free kick for off-side tackling, but the kick was charged down and Thornley grounded the ball over the line. The point, however, was disallowed, a scrimmage being formed near the line, from which Antrobus got posses- sion and passed to Evans, who took a drop at goal, a minor point resulting. Wilson dropped out, and no return being made the hall was scrimmaged in centre. Whittle here passed to Antrobus, who put in a grand run to the line, being brought down by the full back. A short dribble by the Rangers to the quarter flag afforded temporary relief,laut good passing by Whittle, Antrobus, and Evans, resulted in Appleton dropping a goal. Thor- burn re-started, Bibby making a good return to Pole, this player putting in a dashing run, but he was pushed into touch by Appleton. Half time was now called, the score standing—Warrington 1 goal, 2 tries, and 2 minor points, to Broughton Rangers nothing. On change of ends Whittle re-started on behalf of the home team,plav resting near centre. Antrobus was next to the forewith a strong run, and Whittle passed to Evans, who made a short run and kick, Williamson being collared with the ball in his possession. A scrimmage was formed near the Rangers' goal line but the visitors' front rank managed to work the ball mit of danger, and Pole made a grand run to centre, Appleton stopping his progress. Antrobus next put in a strong run, but SIMS brought down by Thorburn, and from the scrimmage Whittle se- cured the ball and passed to Evans,who dropped at goal, Sadler returning into touch at the quarter flag. The home team now pressed their opponents, who had twice to save their lines by kicking the ball dead. The game was very evenly contested for a short time, until Whittle got hold from a scrimmage near centre and passed nicely to Evans, who ran through the thick of his opponents, gaining a grand try, Isherwood kicking a goal. Nothing further was scored up to the call of time, although Warrington continued to have,rather the best of the game, the final score being—Warrington, two goals, two tries, and four minor points, to Broughton Rangers nil. Teams: Warrington—Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Appleton, Evans, and Bibby; half backs Whittle (captain) and Antrobus; forwards, Eyes, Thornley, Jones, Randalls, Donohue, Isherwood, Lloyd, Holmes and Bate. Broughton Rangers—Vull hack, Wil- liamson; three-quarter backs Sadler, Hodgson, and Pole; half backs, Marsh and Thorburn (captain) ; for- wards, Moorhouse, Wilson, Broadfoot, Barrett, Halewood, Squires, Stanley, Cooper, and Pickard.

• RUNCORN V. ItiRKEAHEAD,PARK. This match, the first of the season'between the crack teams of Cheshire was played at the upper park before fully 4,000 spectators, several hundreds of whom came from Runcorn. The weather was fine, but the turf sbme- what sodden from recent rains. On W. Hughes starting te ball on behalf of Runcorn, Court returned into touch at tho half-way flag. Here some packs were formed, and following this Holden and Woods—the opposing full backs—indulged in some tall kicking. The result of this was that the former had the best of the exchange, and the Birkenhead forwards run the ,ball into the Runcop quarters. W. Hughes, however, relieved, and-after a good run passed to Wright, who grounded the ball over the Park line. Woods was called up for the place, and succeeded in piloting the ball over the bar. This reverse put the Park on theirmettle, and they pushed Runcorn into their own 25, but H. Hughes picking up smartly cleared his lines, and took play to the centre. Some capi- tal passing by Black, Tweedie, and Court here took the play to the Runcorn lines. After Woods had relieved Court and Tweedie each had an unsuccessful drop "at the Runcorn goal,but nothing accrued save a dead ball. Up to half-time this was all the scorinc, that was done. Cowen re-started the ball on behalf oeßirkenhead, but Woods got in his kick, and the ball was sent to the centre. Black here picked up,' and ran to the Runcorn quarter flag, where his progress was im- peded by Speakman. Court threaded his way through his opponents, and took play on the Runcorn line. Here Alexander picked up, and, amidst a round of tremen- dous cheering, grounded the ball behind the Runcorn posts. Holden took the place with success. Following this scrimmages were waged in the Park quarters, but this Was neutralised by capital passim"' on the part of the Birkenhead three-quarter backs. This resulted in play being taken to the Runcorn lines, and here Black i put n some good play, but Cawley cleared his lines in fine style, and then getting possession of the oval, and crossing the Park lines, a try was claimed, but not al- lowed, and only a minor resulted. The Runcornians then pressed for a short time during which the touching down process was again resorted to. Lunt then had a drop at -the Birkenhead goal, but this proved fruitless, and, as no further points were scored, the game remained drawn, with the score one goal each, Runcorn having an advantage in minors. Teams: Birkenhead Park—C. Holden, back ;D. Tweedie, J. A. Black, and G. Court. three-quarter backs; F. W. Spence and R. B. Ker, half- backs; D. Bingham, D. Williamson, J. Cowen A. G. Wood, P. H. Lockwood, T. Alexander, N. Allardice, R. P. Moodie, and C. Craig, forward. Runcorn—T. Woods, back; H. Cawley, H. P. Speakman, and E. Lunt, three- quarter backs; H. Hughes and H. G. Andrews, half backs; W. Hughes, W. Faulkner, W. Broady, W. Wright, J. Clarke, J. Lewis, G. Wainwright, J. Barnes, and J. Hoffland, forwards. Referee: Mr. W. H. W. Thorpe, president Cheshire County R.U. WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTpN RANGERS. _

• These two teams met on. Saturday at Broughton. Neither side was fully represented, as the visitors were without the services of Massey (who had not recovered from his accident received at 'Wigan on Monday), Fair Turner, and W. Dillon, who were assisting in the trial match of East v. West Lancashire at Whalley Range; whilst the Rangers suffered by the absence of Robertson and Tune, who were doing similar service also for their county. In Massey's absence a trial was given Daniels, a promising "A " three-quarter, 4ad he certainly did justice to his selection. The visitors having won the.toss decided to play with the wind at their backs, and at 3-30 Hoyle, as captain of the Rangers, started the leather, and a poor return being made the first scrimmage was formed in Waning,ton ter- ritory. The first to become prominent was Veale, who ' put in a couple of runs and seemed dangerous, but Daniels was equal to the occasion, and stopped his career ,by a smart piece of tackling. From a series of scrim- mages, in which the Warringtonians had a great advan- tage throughout, Frank Turner evaded the home for- wards, and for the first time invaded the Rangers' quar- ters, but this was neutralised by a good kick by Royle back to mid-field. Some loose play followed, and McGowan relieved the monotony by an excellent run to the Warrington line, being safely held by Jolley. Nevins stopped a rush of the Rangers' forwards, and Wood tried hard to score a legitimate point, but Warren checked him. The next item of interest was a huge kick by Barnes to Rodgers, who mulled the ball, and play was again taken on the Broughton line, but the home team gradually removed the ball to mid-field. 'Barnes made a series of kicks, and Squires relieved his side by a good kick to the Warrington line. Warren got away from a pack, and kicked to Boyle, collaring the latter before he could get in his return. Exchange kicking by Barnes, Jolley, and Rodgers aided the visiting team, and, from a ' scrimmage formed at the Rangers' quarter flag, Barnes essayed a drop at goal, a minor only accruing. Barnes returned the drop out, and neat passing by the home team backs settled play in neutral ground. Daniels next saved a rush of the home team forwards,and a pass from Wood to Royle was spoiled by smart tackling on the part of Craghan. Speakman passed to 'Daniels, who replied with a good run and kick to the half-way flag. Give and take play followed, and soon afterwards half-time was called with the score—Warrington one minor, to Broughton Rangers nil. Frank Turner re-commenced operations, play settling down at centre field. Davies and E. Dillon gained ground by smart dribbling to the Rangers' territory, but the home team rallied and threatened the visitors' citadel, Squires almost getting in. Nevins returned with interest a kick by McGowan. Jolley put in a strong run to the Rangers' lines, being smartly tackled by Moxon. A scrimmage being formed here, epeakman passed to Barnes, who made a good kick to Royle, that player failing to get the ball away, and shortly afterwards Boyle relieved the., pressure by a timely kick to half-way. Good passing between Warren Speakman, Barnes, and Jolley next looked like scoring. Daniels saved a rush of the home team in grand style, but the Rangers again invaded the Warrington territory. Warren was here applauded for tackling Wale, and Wood got away from apack at half-way, making a good run to the Warrington line. The visiting team worked desperately hard, and it was not until a good dribble was made by the Warringtonians, headed by Little Wood and Ashton, that relief was brought to their side. Nothing of much interest took place from now until the call of time, when after seventy minutes' uninteresting play the game remained drawn, the score being—Warrington one miner to Broughton Rangers nil. On the visiting side, Nevins never allowed his oppon- ents any opportunities, and his kicks saved disaster re- peatedly. Of the three-quarters, Daniels was particu- larly safe, Barnes andJolleyputtinginsome good work at times. The halves passed most unselfishly, but inaccur- ately. Of the eirwards, Littlewood, Davies, Frank Tur- ner, and Ashton were the pick. In the Rangers' ranks, Wood, McGowan, Moxon, Squires, and Royle were the most prominent. The following were the teams :—Warrington: Fall back, W. Nevins; three-quarters, J. Jollev, T. Barnes (captain), and W. Daniels; half-backs, W. Speakman and J. E. Warren; forwards, H. Ashton, Frank Turner, W. Fovey, R. Littlowood, T. Davies, E. Dillon, T. Crag- han, W. Hayes, and A. Molyneux. Broughton Rangers:. Full back, Rodgers'; three-quarters, R. R. Veale, A. Royle (captain), and J. McGowan; half-backs, J. W. Edge and W. Woods; forwards, T. Squires, B. Powell, F. Atkinson S. G. Harrison, J. Barlow, A. Idoxon, A. N. Jackson, G. Skidmore, and F. Fothergill. Um- pires, Messrs. Gilbert and Teggin. Referee, Mr. H. Lord.
