WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fertnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Robe-ts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, W. Houghton, Kilshall, Black- hurst, Jolley. Voisey. Heaton, Bonnell, Derbyshire, Isherwood, Harrison, Hubaphreys, Wright, Ribbert, Ratcliffe, J. Houghton, Clarke, Grange, . Strange, Brown, Jones, Balharry; J. C. Sutton - (clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and Ward (workhouse master). .
DAMAGE BY Tics GALE.—TME PADOATE SCHOOLS

COMMITTEE. This committee recommended that Messrs. Gibson and Son, builders, be requested to inspect roofs and repair damage done by the late gale.—Oa the motion of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were confirmed.

SCHOOL YEES. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 75 cases, 71 of which were old and 4 new cases.—On the Motion of Mr. BLACEMIRST, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minuted were adopted.

- • RDSIGNAT/ON OF MR GIBSON. A letter was read from Mr. Gibson, late of Thelwall, stating that as he had now left the neighbourhood be begged to tender his resignation as a member of the Board of Guardians and of various committees.--The CHAIRMAN said they were very sorry to lose Mr. Gibson, who had been a very useful member of the Board. He moved that the resignation be accepted.—Mr. DARBY- SHIRE seconded this proposal, and said that he wished to express the feeling that while a member representing Thelwall Mr. Gibson had performed his duties of a guar- dian conscientiously and efficierftly. (Hear, hear.) He was sorry for one that Mr. Gibson had removedifrom the neighbourhood, and he hoped that his succ ssor would be as good a man. (Hear' hear.)—Mr. GREENING said he was glad to endorse what Mr. Darbyshire had said. He was surd Mr. Gibson had been a very good member of ' that Board, and there was one thing he had always ad- mired about Mr. Gibson ; it was that he had opinions of his own, and expressed them freely. (Hear, hear.) They ' should not, perhaps, get a better man, but he hoped they might ,ret as good a one, (Hear, hear.)—The CHAIRMAH said there was no doubt that Mr. Gibson had a good deal of independence of character.—lt was, sug- gested by Mr. DARBYSH/RE that the feeling of the Board should be transmitted by the clerk to Mr. Gibson, and this was agreed to.—The CLERX said it was exceedingly desirable that Thelwall should be represented on the I Board under the circumstances they were now. in.—Mr. ,1 JOLLEY said it was desirable that Thelwall should be I represented, seeing that the 'Ship Canal would run right ' through the township.—The CLERK said there was not only that, but also the more important question of sewer- age, apd the still greater question of the boundaries. (Hear; hear.)—Mr. L Hortoirrox moved that the .Local Government Board bdasked to issue an order to enable Thelwall to elect another guardian, and this was agreed to. THE NOMINAION OF GUARDIANS. A letter was read from the Kings Lynn Beard of Guardians asking the Board to _petition the Local Gov- ernment, Board in favour of making it imperative that before a person was nominated to be a Guardian his written, assent should be obtained.— Mr. HARRISON moved that they petition as requested. He considered that what it was proposed to do was very desirable, as it would prevent frivolous nominations being made, con- trary to the desire of the person nominated.—Mr. JOLLEV seconded the proposal which was agreed to.

"LAW .4.ND ORDER" IN IRELAND. The following communication from the Bridgewater Board of Guardians was submitted, viz. :—" The above Board having received copy of resolutions passed by the Dewsbury Guardians, under date 13th ult., expressing disapproval of the conduct of the authorities in attempt- ing to interfere with ttle proceedings Of the Limerick Board of Guardians, Had considered same and passed resolutions thereto as set out on the other side." One of the resolutions on "the other side " was as follows: " That this Board expresses its great satisfaction , with the authorities in • their determination to maintain law and order whether in the Board-room of the Limerick Union, Mitcheistown, London, Bridgewater and elsewhere in the United King- dom where exceptional circumstances have rendered such unpleasant duties neces.4ary."—The CHAIRMAN; I think we had better not interfere with the 'natter let it lie on the table. (Hear, hear.)—This was agreed to.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

Warrington "A "team again scored a splendid victory on Saturday, notwithstanding that their ranks were weakened by some of their best players being called Upon to help the first team. Owing to the really good play that is to be witnessed, the "A " team matches are be- ginning to excite almost as much interest amongst spec- tators of the game as the encounters of the first team. The match of to-day with the Rochdale Hornets "A " team will, it is expected, be of a particularly interesting character,as the Hornets, like the home team, have never been beaten this season. The Hornets, we believe. claim to be the premier " A " team of Lancashire, and it may be confidently expected that VVhittle's followers will do their best to give this pretension its quietus. A correspondent who writes as an "unbiassed spectator "of the encounter at Frodsham, between Frodsham and Warrington Wanderers teams, complains of the inaccuracy of our report of the match. This report was 'sent in to us in the usual way and in these cases we have to rely uponthe accuracy and good faith of the writers. According to our Frodsham correspondent the result of the match was Frodsham two tries, three minors; Warrington Wanderers one try, three minors. Runcorn are still the champions of Cheshire. Twice last season the local team defeated the crack Birkenhead club rather heavily, and although the Park last Saturday did their utmost to regain their lost laurels, and were favoured in every possible way, they were doomed to disappointment. The draw was all in favour of Runcorn, whose score ought to have been increased by at least two tries • both Cawley and Wainwright crossed the line and planted the ball, and competent eye- witnesses declare that the points were gained in a fair and legitimate manner. The referee was, however, of a different opinion, and, in fact, he showed during the afternoon a strange consistency in deciding against the Runcorn club. The game was very stubbornly contested from start to finish. The wearers of the green have shown much better form on previous occasions. Their play lacked the combination which is usually a distinguishing feature. Especially was this noticeable amongst the forwards, and the brilliant individual play displayed at intervals did not counterbalance the defect. Of a good lot perhaps W. Hughes was the best. With the exception of Lunt, who did not justify his selection, the back division gave a capital aceouni of themselves, and quite ontshone their opponents. For the Park the forwards played a hard game, and Spence and Black were the best of the backs. To-day Runcorn meet Swinton at Irwell Lane. Al- though Runcorn have six men playing for the county. the result of the game is by no means the foregone con- clusion many would believe. Brazendale will be the back, Wainwright, Lunt and Riley, the three-quarters, and the forwards will fi-Ot be much weaker than usual. Having broken through their spell of ill-luck, Widnes are now going on from conquering to conquering. Birch were vanquished with the utmost ease, on Satur- day. Farrell was in grand form and Plumpton played a good gams. J. H. Smith, the captain, and T. Hughes

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER.

For the post of medical officer for No. 1 district and for Padgate Schools (vacant by the resignation of Dr. Jack) there were two applications, one from Dr. S. Can- nel' and the other from Dr. W. J. Peacock.—Mr. HARRI- SON proposed, and Mr. ISHERWOOD seconded, that Dr. Cannell be appointed; and Mr. GREENING proposed, and Mr. VOISEY seconded, that Dr. Peacock receive the ap- pointment. —After some conversation the proposals were put to the vote, when eight Guardians voted for Dr. , Cannel! and twelve for Dr. Peacock, the latter being ap- pointed.

div.head: ME. MINES' SALAEY.
div.p: ME. MINES' SALAEY.

Mr. JOLLEY moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded, that the decision come to at the previous meeting that the salary of Mr. Mines, superintendent of Padgate Schools, should be increased by £lO, be confirmed.—Mr. 'smart- WOOD moved that the board do not confirm the proposed increase. As a reason for this proposal he said that the incomes of both masters and workmen, as well as shop- keepers, had come down lately, and scarcely two-thirds of the ratepayers in Warrington knew how to meet their demands.—Mr. BLA.CICHITEST seconded Mr. Isherwood's proposal.—Mr. GREENING did not think tradesmen were in such a bad plight as had been stated, and, although it was true things were very bad, he did not think they were so bad as some people wished to represent them. The shopkeepers of the town were all going on, and they did not hear of anybody shutting up. Wages in the town were not dropping, and he did not know of any 1 manufactory in town where they were dropped. He did not think there was any town in Laneashire that was better off than Warrington. Further than that, he should just like to point out that the £lO did not apply to Warrington alone. It Was a Union charge, and ex- tended throughout the whole Union.—Mr. JOLLEY sup- ported the increase on the broad ground that Mr. Mines deserved it. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. HARRISON supported the proposed increase, and said the question they had to consider was whether Mr. Mines was adequately paid for what he did, and for gie responsibility he incurred. —Mr. BROWN, Mr. VOISEY, and Mr. DARBYSIIIRE also spoke in favour of the increa'se, which was ultimately granted by 14 votes to three.

div.head: BOUNDARIES QUESTION.-INTERESTING REPORT.
div.p: THE BOUNDARIES QUESTION.-INTERESTING REPORT.

The Clerk read a report which he had prepared to be submitted to the Commissioners appointed to in- quire as to local government boundaries. In the course of the report he stated that according to his reading of its provisions' the purpose of the Local Government (Boundaries) Act was to arrange to bring all Union areas into one county. If then the existing boundary of the Warrington Union was to be preserved that of the county of Lancaster would be so extended as to include the three Cheshire parishes. If a partial extension only be made, as of the substitution of the intended Ship Canal for the Mersey boundary, minor changes; of parish areas! by abolition of such portions thereof as otherwise would overlap the canal were involved. Annexation of the three parishes to Lancashire was practicable and would be an adjustment of boundaries free of material inconvenience to the inhabitants who would obtain by the divergence advantages equivalent to any they might be deprived of. To eliminate the three parishes from Warrington and to allocate them to another centre would inevitably be attended by many difficulties, local and general, and would be an: Act conducive to financial and administrative troubles without the security to the par- ishes of equally beneficial gains. The present compact- ness and connection of territory of districts, and the facilities of communication between them would be impaired, many orderly Conditions, the outcome of long practical experience, would be reversed and the general utility and parochial equality the present Guardians and their predecessors had ever sought to attain for the Union would be endangered by partition. Having referred to former change in the area of the Union whereby Kenyon and Golborne wdre detached from it, and Latchford, Grappenhall, and Thelwall added to it, Mr. Sutton pro- ceeded to say that it might be assumed that the Poor-law Commissioners at that time had substantial grounds for their procedure, and it might also be assumed that sub- sequent events had strengthened and in no way diminished the force of *these grounds. Warrington had been made the natural centre, and year by year the an- nexed district had more closely knitted itself to Warring- ton, so that by degrees the population had practically become one community, with one urban and one rural local authority, with a municipal area extending over the urban district, and a Parliamentary area including the whole urban and part of the rural district—united for the purpose of sewerage, water supply, and light- ing. Then Warrington was the market town, and was approachable by excellent services of train and omnibus at very low fares. The market days were the days of meeting of the Guardians. The -elected Cheshire g-uar- dians had invariably been persons engaged in agricul- ture, or had been connected with trade at Warrington. Notwithstanding the comparatively recent decease of four county magistrates, who were resident in the Che- shire district, six magistrates were qualified to act as members of the Rural Sanitary Authority (five of them being justices for Lancashire), and they wereeachresident either at Grappenhall Thelwalt. Not one was resident in any of the Laneashire townships, not even in the large town of Warrington. It would be thus seen that as Warrington needed room for extension, Grappenhall and Thelwall became the natural suburban points of ex- tension for residential ,purposes. Moreover, the land- owners and the resident gentry, &c., were almost exclu- sively persons who were now, or who had been in the past, directly intercksted in and connected with the manu- factories. the trades, and the. prof essions at Warrington, the poor inhabitants of which town included many who had been their employes or who were of the famililies of their

employes : and in other respects the several classes of people forming the population of the whole district were, or ought to be, in near touch with each other. The railway traffic of the district was largely dependent on Warrington. To transfer the rates levied in aid of the poor in respect of mansions, villa, lands, and railway profits from the needy of Warrington to the aid of those of a distant urban district between the inhabitants of which and the residents of Grappenhall and Thelwall there is nothing in common would be unjust. It must also be remembered that the poor were entitled to have consideration. The means of communication with a union centre might be wholly'immaterial to wealthy peo- ple; to the poor it was a matter of the first importance. If communication with another centre was formerly difficult it was now much more so. If that with War- rington was easy it was now much more so. It would thUs be seen that on every ground, except possibly that of sentiment, the extension of Lancashire so as to embrace the three Cheshire town- ships was the reasonable, and, indeed, the wily just con- clusion for the Commissioners to arrive at.—Mr. HARRI- SON moved that the report just read should be forwarded to the secretary of the Boundaries Commissioners. He remarked that the report suggested the best solution of the difficulty it referred to.—Mr. JOLLEY seconded this proposal. He thought that, if they. took into account all the circumstances of sewerage, gal, &c., it would be a grand mistake to sever the Cheshire towriships from ' the Unign.—Ml. DAREYSEIRB thought the report was a very excellent one and embraced all the points, or pretty ' nearly all the pfaints, but he should have, been glad if Mr. Sutton had, in the report, just referred to the finan- cial position of the Cheshire townships in relation to that Union as compared with , the Runcorn Union. Apart from that he thought the Grappenhall ratepayers when they read the report, would be satisfied that a change would not be beneficial to them in many- respects. He considered that the point of view with regard to the poor was a most important one to take. (Hear, hear.) It would be of great detriment to the poor of Thelwall if, in order to have a case heard, they had to go all the way to Dutton Work- house, a distance of eight or ten miles, without any rail- way or public means of conveyance, instead of coming to Warrington, a distance of 21 miles. (Hear, hear.)— The CLERK said they could afterwards go into the finan- cial question, but he happened to be rated both in the urban and rural portion of the Warrington Union, and also in the Runcorn Union, and, as far as his experience went, he fared better in 'Wellington than in Runcorn Union. He did not know, however, whether his remarks would apply altogether to the agricultural parishes, such as Grappenhall.—Mr. GREENING having also referred totheexcellent character of the report,Mr.Harrison's pro- posal was agreed to.—Mr. HARRISON said the drawing up of the report must have cost the Clerk a great deal of research and consideration, and he did not think an effort of that kind ought to be passed over in a formal manner. He therefore begged to move a vote of thanks to the clerk.—Mr. VOISEY seconded this proposal, which was agreed to unanimously, and the CLERK suitably acknow- ledged the compliment.

div.head: RECENT ILLNESS OF MR. BROWN.
div.p: THE RECENT ILLNESS OF MR. BROWN.

Mr. DAR-11-YS-RIRE—;RidIE:;-a to e-Zr-e.ss his plea- sure at seeing Mr. Brown amongst them again, .ancl so far restored to general health that he was tto come out. (Hear, hear.) He VMS pleased indeed to see him there, and that the Board would no doubt continue to have the advantag'es of his knowledge of poor-law matters. He hoped Mr. Brown.would go on progressing in health un- til restoration was complete. (Hear, ' hear.)—Mr. HAR- ROD'S was sure there was not a member of the Board who would not say " Amen" to so sweet a prayer as that of Mr. Darbyshire.—The CJIAIRMAN also expressed his plea- sure at seeing Mr. Brown again in attendance, and Mr. BROWN returned thanks for the kind wishes that had been expressed. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL

The first quarterly meeting of the Warrington Town Council was held at the Towif Hall, at noon, on Wednesday, for the purpose of electing a Mayor for the coming year, and for the transaction of other business. There were present Aldermen Pickmere, Holmes, Chandley, Burgess, Sutton, Harrison, Cros- field, Davies, and Webster; Councillors Greening, Jolley, Belton, Heaton, Wright, Tinsley, Fleming, W. herpoint, Platt, Blackhurst, Barker, Greenall, J. Taylor, Percival, Green, J. Pierpoint, H. Roberts, F. A. Roberts, Marsh, Francomb, Dixon, Ashton, Dakin, and J. V. Taylor; Messrs: Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Chorley (bor- ough treasurer), Gornall (medical officer), Longdin (borough surveyor), and Madeley (librarian).

div.head: gLEoTION OF MIYOR.
div.p: gLEoTION OF MIYOR.

Alderman Picaomul, the retiring Mayor, who had taken the chair, said the first business of the Council would be the election of his successor as Mayor of the borough. Councillor F. A. ROBERTS said it was, he was sure, the feeling of the Council that they regretted very much the necessity of having to provide a successor after the way in which Alderman Pickmere had conducted the business for so long. He was sure that all must feel the regret that by necessity Alderman Pickmere had to relinquish the position, and he only hoped that the time would soon corhe when Alderman Pickmere would be able to again wear the gown and chain He had very little to say to that Council as to the qualifications of the gentleman he was going to propose. Everyone in the Council had known him as a councillor and an alderman better than he had known him. He had known him for many years outside the Corporation, and he could testify that he considered, and he believed that Council considered, him a man eminently suitable for the post to which they should appoint him unanimously that day. The gentle- man that he wished to propose as mayor for the ensuing year was Mr. Thomas Hindmarsh Sutton. (Applause.) In moving that resolution he should like to refer to the feeling of the Liberal members of the Council in electing a Conservative as Mayor and supporting Alderman Sut- ton's nomination. There was a great desire on the part of many in that Council, and he hoped it would soon be the opinion of the majority, that polities should have no place at all within that chamber, even in the election of mayor, the election of aldermen, or in any form or shape whatever. (Hear, hear.) And if a Liberal, though an independent as regards municipal matters, should pro- pose a Conservative, he thought it did honour to the Conservative and honour to the Liberal who proposed him. (gear, hear.) He hoped they should soon find that not only a Liberal would propose a Conservative, but that a Conservative would propnse a Liberal. (Hear, hear, and applause). Alderman DAVIES said he had great pleasure in rising to second the motion made by Mr Councillor Roberts, that Alderman Thomas Sutton should be the next Mayor. He would also congratulate the Council on the fact that they were still getting nearer the millenium—(laughter, and hear, hear)—by casting out politics in anything that was done within that chamber in municipal matters. He thought it was a great progress that had been made. He had for many years considered that that was the proper course, and he was indeed pleased to follow a Liberal in proposing a Conservative Mayor—(hear, hear)—and he thought he could say for his Conservative friends around that table that when the time did approach when a Liberal should be deemed worthy of being the Mayor of that borough, the joint action of the Conservatives would be equally as readily given as in the case of the Liberals that day. As regarded Mr. Alderman Sutton, they all knew him well; the town knew him well enough without ren- dering' any more words from him necessary. They all hoped that his year of office would be as successful as Alderman Pickmere's. (Applause.) . .

Councillor PERCIVAL supported the proposal. From his own knowledge, he thought the appointment of Alderman Sutton would meet with the general approval of the inhabitants. (Hear, hear.) Alderman HOLMES thought they might congratulate Alderman Sutton on the fact that he was likely to be unanimously elected by the Council irrespective entirely of politics and party feeling. (Hear, hear.) Alderman CROSFIELD said he was delighted, as a mem- ber of that Council, that. Alderman Sutton had been pro- posed that day by an independent 'gentleman, who be- longed to the Liberal party. He had long, as they knew, desired that politics should be excluded from that Coun- cil Chamber, as he was very anxious that they should get into the Council Chamber the best men that could be got to represent the ratepayers, irrespective of politics. (Hear? hear.) He thought they had had long enough the experience of political fights in municipal matters to show them the neeessity of abolishing politics in regard ' to their . duties at that Council. . He did rejoice that day to think that Alderman Sutton would be elected by the unanimous vote ot the Council, and he hoped that in days to come, if it should happen that the most suit- able person to occupy the position of Mayor belonged to what was called the Liberal party, the Conservatives would unite with them as they had united with the Con- servatives. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Alderman HARRISON said the good old book, which every religious denomination regarded as inspired, told i them n effect that a man is not without honour save in his own coimtry, and among his own friends. He was of opinion that there never was a proverb, either sacred or profane, that did not admit to some extent of a quali, fled exception, and he thought that Mr. Alderman sut- ton would have the pleasure of realising for himself the truth of what he had said in that respect. He would in a few minutes be elected by his arm townsmen, and as a mere matter of observation, within 500 yards of the 'very spot where he was born, and would have conferred upon him the greatest distinction that it was in the power of his fellow-townsmen to confer upon a good and worthy citizen. (Hear, hear.) It could not be said that Mr. Alderman Stitton was obtaining his promotion either prematurely or undeservedly. (Hear, hear.) He had been a member of that Council for about 14 Years, and during that long period it might safely be said he had won the respect and esteem of all of them, and not only that, but the confidence of the public. He believed that Alder- man Sutton would pursue the even tenour of his way without undue ostentation; neither aspiring to be great, nor fearful of being too humble., (Applause.) The resolution was then put and carried unanimously by acclamation. The newly-elected Mayor thereup left the room, accompanied by the ex-Mapr, and soon after returned, wearing the robe and chain of office. The MAYOR then thanked the Council for the honour

they had done him in electing him unanimously to that position. It was a position of the greatept trust, and he should be altogether unworthy jof the confidence they reposed in him, if he failed to appreciate the compliment in a becoming and proper manner. The election to the office of Mayor was the highest honour that a municipal Corporation could confer upon any townsman—(hear, hear,)--and no one ought to accept that position unless he was prepared and willing to fulfil the-duties of the office to the best of his ability—(hear, hear,)—and to ,the satisfaction of the Council and the pub- lic generally. When he scanned over the names of the twenty-seven Mayors who had occu- pied that chair since the incorporation of the borough, and called to mind the very excellent qualifications which most of them possessed., a sense of his own in- feriority came upon him with double force. However, as they had thought fit to elect him the Mayor, he should, although not able to perform the duties of the office with the same dignity and ability as did the Mayors who had preceded him, he should at least do his best to fulfil those duties in such a manner as should be to his own credit, and to the satisfaction of the Council (Hear, hear.) They had very important work before them. Each successive year, he thought, brought more work and more responsibility than the past—(hear, hear) —but he thought that -if- they • put their shoulders to- gether they could meet all difficulties that might come. During the last ten or twelve years important work had been done. The Paving and Sewerage Committee, and the Sanitary Committee, had contributed to benefit the town in. a very great degree. When it was considered that during that time the death-rate had been reduced from 30 per 1,000 to less than 20 per 1,000, he thought it should be admitted that they had done something at all events. The sanitaty department had been a vexed question for some time passed, but he believed that when the Sanitary Committee presented a report of its proceedings, and of the financial position of the Longford scheme, everybody would be perfectly satisfied. He did not wish to open any question that might give offence to anyone but he must say that what had so far been done by the anyone, Committee had been done with the con- sent of the Council, and he as quite sure that if there were any complaints, or any g,rievance,s to remedy, every member of the committee would feel disposed, to the best of his ability, to remedy such grievances, whatever they might be. He was certain that if they would only work together, shoulder to shoulder, they would be a perfectly happy family, and whatever they did would be in the interests of the borough. (Hear, hear.)
APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY -MAYOR.
The MAYOR then appointed Alderman J. R. Pickmere to act as deputy-Mayor for the ensuing year.
IiFOIrNM:INT OF NUIaUeR _

The MAYOR said that with reference to the appointment of Mayor's chaplain, he should explain that he had been a member a St. Paul's Church almost all his life time, and he was now, and had been for many years, a war- den of that church. It was, therefore, only natural, perhaps, that he should desire to appoint the Rev. S. Wilkinson as his chaplain. He knew that it had been the custom to appoint the rector as chaplain, but in this case, considering the illness of the rector, who was per- fectly agreeable to the course he proposed to adopt, he should appoint the Rev. S. Wilkinson to act as Mayor's chaplain for the ensuing year.
THE QUARTERLY MEETINGS.
On the proposition of the MAyon, seconded by Alder- man PIC/1111E11B, it was resolved that quarterly meetings be held on the first Tuesdays in Februnry, May, and August of 1888. •
TAB STANDING _ORDERS.
The lkIATon proposed, and Alderman PICKMERE secon- ded, the adoption of the standing orders for the re- gulation of the proceedings of the Council and the com- mittees.

, Alderman CRANDLEY said he hid a slight alteration to suggest with reference to the order of debate, in order to prevent misunderstilndings. As thp matter was now when a persoWasked a question he forfeited his right to speak on certain subjects. .(" No"), He would instance the case of Councillor Bolton at 'a recent meeting. The MAYOR thought that arose entirely out of a mis- understanding. It was thought that there had been a reply to the questipn by the Chairman of the Committee, and if Councillor Bolton had not been so hasty all might have been explained. Councillor BOLTON disputed the statement that he had been hasty, and said he thought he had not been fairly dealt with.

The MAYOR: I'll make my first apology; lam sorry for making use of the word hasty. (Laughter). After a little further discussion the subject dropped, Alderman CUANDLEY remarking that if it was understood that it was admissable to ask a question that was sufficient for him. -

Alderman WEBSTBIST proposed and Alderman DAVIES seconded that the • following Members of the Council, viz ;—Aldermen Davies, Harrison, Sutton and Webster, and Councillfprs Holton Gieenall, Greening, Percival, F. A. Roberts and J. V. Taylor, and the following Non- Members of the Council, viz :—Messrs Wm. Beamont, Robert Davies, Wm. Fell, T. G. Rylands, Wm. Owen, James Paterson, Robert Pierpoint, J. E. Worsley and Linnveus Greening, constitute this committee for the ensuing year. Councillor H. ROBERTS proposed that the names of Mr. John Walker and Mr. Thomas Flood be added to those constituting this committee. He thought it would be a wise and advantageous thing to make this addition. The financial difficulty regarding this part of municipal matters at the present time would be better understood, . and those who werWadvocating a Free Lending Library would have a thorough knowledge of the finances, and would have considerable information imparted to , them. •
Counciller'Boxzmj : I shall expect my name taken off the Museum Committee if we are to be over-voted by non-members.

Councillor W. risiursotxT seconded the proposition. Both the gentlemen proposed, he said, were compara- tively young men, while a great many of the metabers of the committee were getting rather -dd. He thought that, under the circumstances of the case, it would be advisable to put them on the committee. Alderman DAVIES said that he thought the Council had been pretty well satisfied that the vexed question of the Library had been very satisfactorily disposed of. He was inclined to think that the inhabitants were thor- oughly satisfied as to to the condition of the Museum and Library. He hoped that, after reflection, Mr. Roberta would not press his motion. If the committee thought that the addition would tend to develop something more than had been done they should invite them to come; but he was quite satisfied that it would do no good whatever.

Councillor JOLLEY believed that it was for the interest of the town and the institution that things should goon as they were. Alderman WEBSTER did not think that there was the slightest ground for changing the constitution Of the committee. There were very serious objections to the addition of non-metn.bers of the Council; because they already nearly equalled the number of councillors on the committee. He was quite sure that the members of the Council should preponderate on such a committee. The Corporation itself was quite capable of managing the affairs of the institution, but the law allowed them to ask gentlemen, eminent in various ways in the borough, , to come to their assistance, and that had been done for a I number of years past. The gentlemen on the committee who were non-members of the Council were everyone of them specialists in some particular way, took charge of some especial department of the institution, and gave the benefit of their knowledge for the ratepayers dnd the in- stitution generally. He thought that it would not be to the interests of the institution to elect two persons who insisted on any particular line of action. Councillor PLATT said that he should support the orig- inal resolution, because he thought that the scheme brought forward by the committee should have a fair trial. The amendment might not be intended as such, but he looked upon it as a sort of vote of censure. (" No.") Well, it seemed to mean that the committee wanted further help in this matter, which he did not think was the case., He believed that the committee was quite capable of dealing with the question in a proper manner, and he was confident that they would do their best. . Councillor DIXON supported the amendment. Councillor H. Ron Ears disclaimed any intention of offering censure. He had moved his resolution from 'a desire to remove the impression that the financial posi tion of the institution was not thoroughly understood. He thought that if they could convince the gentlemen he had named as to what the actual position of the finances really was, the difficulties of the committee would be removed. The MAYOR then put the amendment, which was lost, those only voting for it who had spoken in its favour. Councillor H. ROBERTS said that he should like to ask in what respect were Mr. Owen and Mr. R. Pier- point specialists. There were other members' too; that he did not consider specialists, and hi failed to see the correctness ,of the assertion that all the members of the committee were specialists. Alderman DAVIES replied that he did not think it was necessary to say anythlng about Mr. Beamont. ,Mr. it. Davies was connected with botany ; Mr. Fell was a gnat authority on fishes; Mr. Itylands, it would be known, had special knowledge • Mr. W. Owen had given much time in connection with the buildings ; Mr. Paterson was a specialist in geology; Mr. R. Pierpoint had rendered useful service io the literary department; Mr. Worsley was a great arcineOlogist ; and Mr. L. Greening was a great naturalist. The original proposition was then confirmed. • APPOINTMENT OE OTHER COMMITTEES.

HER GREATEST HAPPINESS. ;
Vide " WE9TERN 31A1L," CARDIFF, Saturday, Oct. 15, 1887.
lIISS E. MELIRTISH, of 7, Clive-road, Canton, Cardiff, was suffering from a most severe form cf
Ilness. She had the advantage of the very best skill and care,
but all appeared -vain ; and he was at last recommended to
go to the Glamorgan and Monmouth Infirmary. Here she was
treated for several weeks for Bright's disease.
Milk diet,
vapour baths, and other prescriptions had no effect. On the
contrary, site became much worse, and her body commenced
to swell: At last, in March, she underwent an operation, and
some 16 or 18 quarts of water were removed from her side and
legs. She continued to get worse, and in May was discharged
'as incurable.
Her joarney to her home (then at Kings-
brompton, near Stlverton, in Somersetshire) was performed
with the greatest difficulty and suffering, and occupied several
days. Though a cure had teen pronounced hopeless, her father
Insisted on further professional advice, and again instru-
merits were applied, with the frightful result of withdraw-
lug 20 quarts of water from her each week. Again the medi- aet men pronounced the ease hopeless, and tihally they re-
linguiabed attendance on that ground. The unfortunate
victim was now hi despair. 1-ter sufferings were indeserih-
able, axid there' was no prospect except that of sink-
ing through slot's torture into an early grave.
"this time he berame acquainted with the details
of an extraordinary cure (the Well-known ease
of William Grayson) by Hop Bitters, and she resolved to try
them. Medical men. sanctioned the experiment, but warned
her that it could only be a, useless expense. However, Miss
'ilelhuish persisted, and in June she began to take the Bitters.
Her condition changed almost Immediately. The water
diminished, tft the surprise of the doctor, who had measured
her at intervals, and who declared that the change was noth-
bag short of miraculous. The improvement continued; she gained appetite,' and slept well. , For months previously she had been unable to retain food, or to enjoy continuous rest.
Within two months the water was practically checked. She eontinued to use the Hop Bitters, finding that they strength- ened her, in addition to relieving the disease, and within
three months of her commencing to take them she was able to

walk in the fields without help. This astonishing cure of one of the most awful diseases that affect humanity has made the deepest impression on both professional and lay inhabitants of the district. Miss Melhuish, the fortunate subject of what she

regards as almost a miracle, is now able to walk her seven or eight miles with ease: With a proper sense of grateful ap- preciation of the remedy, and with a laudable desire to help other sufferers by the diffusion of the precious information, she announces that her greatest homeless will be to show her, fellow creatures who may be suffering the tortures of this hideous disease how they may find relief. She will gladly Rive all information in her power to anyone who %%rites to her. We have recorded her address above.

"Dear Fred,—You will be surprised at receiving a letter from sue, but, Mink Ood, I am pleased to say I am getting better every day. I shall be so glad to I breathe the fresh air again. It has seemed a dreadful long time to be in bed. You know I was taken to thel hospital last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the kidneys. Well, on July 31 they tapped me, and took away 304 ounces of water. The same thing was done again on September 18, and 408 ounces of water obtained. On Oct. 9 I was discharged from the hos- I pital as incurable. In January this year (the 20t1.) was again tapped at home, and 360 ounces of water taken away. The St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the St. Bartholomew's Hospital, Chatham, also refused me, as being the worst case they had seen for years, and two local doctors gave me up as hopeless. When I came from the hospital it took three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an object of misery and despair. After the hospitals had reused me, and 11 doctiors given sne up: my wife persuaded me to try HOP BITTERS, and from the commencement have Improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks, and can now get downstairs and walk about without even a stick. With the aid of a few snore bottles of the Bitter; shall be well again. The water has left my lady and legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful medicine. I wish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with doctors' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the hospital I had no appetite whatever, but since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but must not mind that so long as lam getting well. Am cheerful now that recovery is 'near, for every one had given me up as a bad job.—With best wishes to
" Your affectionate brother,

" To the Hop Bitters Company (Limited), London.

," Gentlemen,—l enclose a letter from my brother- hi-law, William Grayson, Chatham. lie considers that he owes his life to your Hop Bitters, and feels he cannot say enough In Its praise. "Yours frilly,
"FRED. STAMMERS.
" 23, Curaitor-street, Chancery-lane, London.
"lint!, March 24.

Since I wrote you 10 days ago, I have improved wonderfully. To-day I walked to the barber's shop and got shaved, and back again by myself, without fatigue. This is the first time I have been out alone since last April-Lover 11 months. When I was dis- charged from the hospital, October 9, I weighed 21at. 41h.; now r weigh about 91t. (my usual weight).
'WILLIAM GRAYSON."

' HE SUPPOSED.—An American statesman got off at Falls View at Niagara. After exatuining it critically for a moment, he remarked to a bystander, " Huge affair, ain't it ? I suppose it runs all night too." An old German merchant in the City of London was informed that a lady had called to see him in his ab- sence. "A lady !" he mused aloud; "a lady !" Upon an accurate description being given, he suddenly brightened up, and added: "Oh, dot vas no lady! Dot was my wife.' A physician in New York city is said to have the fol- lowing inscription on his bill-heads :—" A patient's gratitude to his doctor is a part of his disease, and is most declared, when the fever is highest, cools off during convalescence, and entirely disappears with the complete return to health. N.B.—Office prescriptions and,atten- dance strictly cash." Dougald, who hails from Kingussie, and is on board the Clansman at Oban, this being the first time he has ever seen a steamer, watches with the utmost earnest- ness the volume of smoke escaping from the funnel; I then' running forward to the purser,he demands," Iss— , iss tis a poat ?" Purser: " Oh,yes ; this is a boat !" , Dougald, in astonished acdents : "Well, well, she's— ,1 she's stnokin' !" • I SHE SAVED HI/1.--," SO Miss Blank is married ?" he inquired. "Yes." "I beard that her father gave her a check for 510,000." "Yes, he did." "Was it good for anything ?" "Well, that's the point that puzzles every- body who was there. They were all crowding round to see if it was certified, when she held it aloft and ex- claimed,' Dear father, but these diamonds are enough!' She touched it to the gas, and away it went. I think it's a new rink, and one intended to save the old man." THEY HAD NOTICED THEM.—" We has been libben heah for two weeks," said a coloured man in Charleston, leaning over the fence and addressing his next-door neighbour, "but you hain't done take no notice of us. You don' seem to be awar' dat a fambily has moved in nex' do' to you." "Oh, yes, we has done tuk notice dat you moved in 1" " Huh ! Don' look like it. You nebber 'took no notice dat a 'spectable culled fambily hed be- come yo' neighbo'. Dat's a fac'." " Dat ain't de fac', sah. we done tuk notice dat you moved in, an' we hab locked up de chicken coop do' an' kep' de dog loose at night ebber since." Win= THE INFORMATION CAME Faom.—An English man of letters living at a certain village in Surrey had occasion to write to Dr. Munger, at Newhaven, in Con- necticut, and, thinking to please the latter, gave him some historical information about Newhaven which he had met with in his recent reading. Dr. Munger re- turned thanks warmly, and, not to be outdone in ,courtesy, enclosed a few facts about his correspondent's place a residence. A year afterwards the American came over, and happened to meet his English correspon- dent. The latter then reminded Dr. Munger of the full. and detailed' account he had sent him of his domicile, , adding, "I can't think' where you could have got so , much information about the place. You told me far more than I knew, though I had lived there for years." "On," said Dr. Munger, "that is very simple! I just tookelowuMurray'e Handbook, and,cppied out the par- ticulars." , Hz WANTED WATER.—One of those "English muffs, , ' ye kno' " went over into "the ntate,s " the other day from dnada,. He took lodgings at an inn in a border village, which shall be nameless. He had dinner; and among those who sat at the table with him was the 'waiting-maid, whom he designated as " servant "; but he received an indignant correction from the landlord. "We call our servants 'helps,' sir. They air not op- pressed; they air not Russian serfs." "All right," said the Englishman, "I shall remember." And he did; for in the morning he awoke the whole house by calling out at the top of his voice, which was like the tearing of a strong rag: "Help! help! Water! water !" In an instant every person equal to the task rushed into his room with a pail of water. "I am much obliged to you, I am sure," he said; "but I don't want so much water, ye kno'—l only want enough to shave with." "Shave with !" said the landlord; "what • did you mean by calling ' Help ! Water?' We thought the house was a-fire.' "You told me to call the servant' Help,' and I did. Did you think I would cry ' Water ! when I meant fire ?" The explanation, it would seem, was satisfactory. Dumas the elder often laughed at English stiffness and reserve. One of his stories was this—" One day Victor Hugo and I were invited to dine with the Duke of Decazes. Among the guests Were Lord and Lady Pal- merston—of course this happened before the February Revolution. • At mideight tea was handed round. Victor Hugo and I were sitting side by side, chatting merrily. Lord and Lady Palmerston had arrived very late and there had consequently been no opportunity to introduce us before dinner ; after dinner it seems it was forgotten. English custom consequently did not allow us to be addressed by the illustrious couple. All at once young Decazes came up and said, 'My dear Dumas, Lord Palmerston begs you will leave a chair free between you and Victor Hugo.' I hastened to do as he wished. We inoved away from each other, and placed a chair betweeil us. Thereupon Lord Palmerston entered, holding the hand of his wife, led her up to us, and in- vited her to sit down on the empty chair—all this with- out saying a word. 'My lady,' he said to his wife, 'what time have you?' She looeed at her watch and answered, 'Thirty-five past twelve." Well, then,' said the great minister, ' remember well that this day, at thirty-five minutes past twelve, you were sitting between Alexandre Dumas and Victor Hugo, an honour which you will probably never enjoy again in your life- time."Fhen he offered his arm again to his wife, and , took her back to her seat without saying a word to us— I because we had not been presented." Josies DOG.—A story is told of Josh Billings being i thrown on one occasion among a batch of students in a country town near New Haven. He was tramping along with a rusty yellow dog, and entered the bar- room of an hotel for some refreshments. A group of the Yale lads chanced to be there on a frolic, and iIIITD*- diately interviewed Billings, whom they evidently mis- took for a farmer. They inquired with affected in- terest after the health of his wife and children; and Josh, with counterfeited simplicity, gave them a graphic account of his family and farm. "Of course yen belong to the church?" asked one of the boys, "Yes, the Lord be praised, and my father and grandfather before me?' "Now I suppose you would not tell a lie," said one of the students. "Not for the world." "What will you take for that dog ?"—pointing to Josh's cur, which was crouching beneath his chair. "I won't take twenty dol- lars for that dog." "Twenty dollars! Why, he's not worth twenty cents l'' "I assure you I would not take twenty dollars for him." "Come, my friend," said the 1 student, who, with his companions, was bent on having Some fun with the old man—" now you say you won't tell a lie for the world. Let me see if you won't do it for twenty dollars. I'll give you twenty (dollars for your dog." "I'll not take it. , You will not? Here—let me see if this will not tempt you to lie," added the student, producing a small bag of half-dollars which he built up into small piles on the table, • Josh was sitting by the table with his hat in his hand, apparently uncon- cerned. "There," added the student—" there are twenty dollars, all in silver; I will give you that for the animal.' Josh quietly raised his hat to the edge of the table, and, as quick as thought, scraped all the money into it except one half-dollar; exclaiming, "I' won't take your twenty dollars. Nineteen and a halfis as much as that dog is worth; he is your property." A tremendous shout front his fellow-students clearly showed the would-be wag that-he was completely sold, and that ho , nee4 not look for sympathy from them; so he good- naturedly acknowledged himself beaten. ,

HELENS TOWN COUNCIL.

Sir,—l notice that during the past few months some interest has been excited by proposals made in the St. Helens Council Chamber to reduce the number of the members forming the different committees; to increase the number of councillors; to have a redistribution of "seats "—or wards—bill, and other similar measures. As a humble ratepayer, I would say by all means let us have each and eVeryone of these suggestions adopted. at any rate, they might be given a trial—more especially the two last mentioned. If a redistribution of the seats took place, and the number of members was increased, say to thirty-six, what a splendid Council we should possess. Why, with another dozen Kirk- hams, Johnsons (I need not say which), Browns, Fosters, &c., we should, at last, begin to ex- pect that the proper administration of the town would be assured; then we should be able to boast of a thor- ough and genuine representative chamber; and as to the increased numbers, why "The more the merrier." For instance, the proceedings on Wednesday last, judg- ing from what I have heard and read, were rendered more interesting and attractive to the outside public. Confessions—as per Mr. Kirkham—are good and whole- some reading, and the lessons they convey should be taken to heart by all.—Yours, Szc., A HUMBLE RATEPAYER. St. Helens, Nov. 10th, 1887.

div.head: GAMES AT RUNCORN FAIR.
div.p: THE GAMES AT RUNCORN FAIR.

Sir,—! do not altogether agree with your correspon- dent who, in the last issue of The Examiner," writing above the signature "A Parent," calls attention to the facilities afforded to youthful gambling at fairs. I do not coincide with all the opinions- that "A Parent" gives -expression to. Certainly there are sufficient temptations ito the rising generation n the shape of billiard rooms, 'cards, dice, &c., but, all the same, I think your corres- pondent is rather hard on "the unprincipled bipeds," who are allowed "to pursue their nefarious means of plunder with such impunity;" and thus cause children to be fleeced, "time after time, of their savings by these per- nicious games that are placed before the eyes of the in- experienced in so tempting a form." To be candid, sir, my sympathies rather incline to the side of the "un- principled bipeds," with whom I have had some few dealings. When a youth, I may explain, I attended a Sunday school, and in connection with that school there was a bazaar got up for some charitable purpose. This bazaar was an event in my life. I had a season ticket, sir. I had also two silver shillings to spend. Ah ! those sshillingS! They grew hot in the pocket of my knicker- bockertrousers, and their expenditure was a matter of pressing necessity. I disdained the bran pie, looked with disgust on the side shows, and finally invested my precious shekels in purchasing two lottery tickets, one giving me the chance of winning a magnificent tea-cosy, and 'the other of becoming the possessor of an extra nice 'fire-screen. As ill-luck would have 'RI became the pos- sessor of the fire-screen, and from that moment forward my juvenile soul was fired with ambition. How to earn a shilling at the expense of a penny was an engrossing thought, and in course of time I deveicped into a regu- lar little gambler, and thus it was I made the acquaint- ance of the" unprincipled biped" CIAM. Ido not wish to make this letter too much of a personal confessiag, but it is a fair question to ask how many of these incent little inexperienced ones who are from time to time fleeced of their savings have got a taste for that sort of thing from participating.in religious hussar lotteries? Any way, Sir, let us have fair play. "A Parent" seems to think that the law should be invoked in this matter. Then let the law also be invoked in regard to gambling under the cloak of religion, and let the parents take such cue of their children as to prevent their becoming the prey of "unprincipled bipeds," either religious or OTHERWISE. Warrington, November 10, 1887.

div.head: CALIFOTTIA AND BRITISH WOMEN.
div.p: CALIFOTTIA AND BRITISH WOMEN.

Sir,—My attention has been drawn to a letter signed Alice Westwood, San Francisco, California, which seems to discourage my desire to help needy gentlewomen of my own country to homes in California. I may state that San Francisco is 500 miles from Los Angeles and Pasadena, where I recommend them to go. The tone of morality and religion in the latter place, is higher than that of any town of its size at home. It has 10,000 in. habitants, and only one saloon, and efforts were being made when I was there to banish that one drink shop, meetings being held in the church for this purpose. it is a city of palace homes, where wealthy people from the east have retired to spend the rest of their days in an earthly paradise. They wonld gladly pay well and treat as one of themselves our educated women A committee of reception was formed at a meeting in the Baptist Church at my request, and I can assure all who go under my auspices that Christian ladies and gentlemen will meet them at the train on arrival, and care for them until they are located in the families of Christian tem- perance women, for it is the W.C.T.U. of California who receive these temperance women of our land. Miss Westwood sneaks of San Francisco as a nest of iniquity. I thiali I must say a word for it, although as

I said in my former letter, I do not advise ladies to go there, not that I think it a more wicked city than other large towns though, perhaps, vice is more apparent on the surface And there is less hypocrisy), but wages are lower, and it is a place where English, Irish, German, and Chinese congregate. It has more benevolent and philanthropic institutions than any place I have been in. A lady (Mrs Cooper) has a Bible class of more than 500 members of all denominations. It churches vie with each other in good works. They are not closed all the week like ours, but freely opened for all good objects. Most of them have free kinder-gartens and other good institutions connected with them. However it is not to San francisco I would direct attention, but to Los Angeres, Pasadena, and Roserville. There is one strange thing about Miss Westwood's letter, namely, that it appears in the Manchester " Examiner " Nov. 7th in reply to mine dated Oct. 7th of the same paper. I cannot see how one month could suffice to get a reply over a distance of 7,000 miles. In reference to the law against emigration, it does not ap- ply to those who pay their own passage and are prepared to be self-supporting on arrival. The needs of women in this country are great, and the needs of housekeepers are great in the places I have named. If we can bring questions of demands and supply together satisfactorily good will be done. I could easily refute Miss Westwood's statements on her own ground. I have letters from heads of families'in San Francisco, and also from the Secretary of the Girls' Union, urging me to try and induce our gentlewomen to go there,loo every week,but the crown of the mttty, viz., Pasadena, iseto be preferred. I have most grateful letters from those already there, who are rejoicing in the comfort and beauty around them. I Should like to say that I have no motive beyond thede- sire lo benlfit the women of my own country, and to serve the temperance women of California who will thus be set more at liberty to do the good work they so efficiently undertake. The W.C.T.U., of America, numbers up- wards of 200,000 of the best women of the land. My lecture on Cali fomia is now completed. I shall be glad to respond to calls to deliver it when those who wish to hear the truth about California may learn what I saw there.-Faithfully yours, MARGARET E. PARKER. The Home Lea, Penketh, Warrington, Nov. 11th, 18137.
DEATH OF _FATHER_ FENNELLEY,

OF RUNCORN. The Rev. William Fennelley, pastor of St. Edward's Roman Catholic Chapel, Runcorn, died at his residence, Irwell-lane, on Thursday afternoon. Although the sad event was not altogether unex- pected, the news of his demise was received with feelings of the deepest regret by his numerous parishioners, and by others who respected him for his personal worth. For the past ten months Father Fennelley had suffered so acutely from asthmatical bronchitis that he has been unable to perform his priestly duties, and Father Bosco. of bitten College, had officiated in his stead. 'A few weeks ago he formally intimated to the Bishop of the diocese his intention to relinquish the positioned ,parish priest, and his resignation, in the ordinary course of events, would have taken effect on Tuesday next. The de- ceased gentleman, who was of a family that has given more than one devoted son to the priedthood, , was a native of Ballingarry, county'lliippemrv, and was educated at Maynooth College. On completing , his education, he had charge of several 'missions in , England, St. Joseph's, Stockport, heing'the 'parish with which he was connected immediately •prior to coming to Runcorn about twelve years ago. Earnest in the performance of his religious duties, and in his attention to the welfare of his congregation, he also displayed a great and ac- tive interest in educational matters, and rthe day schools in connection with St Rdwartrs were highly successful. In 1877 he was elected a member of the School Board by the ratepayers. and he -retained that position up to the time of his death. 'ln the discussion of all questions he showed great business tact and ability, of which the members showed their appreciation two years ago by appointing him vice- chairman. Ms illness had, however, prevented him from attending the meetings for the last twelve months, but the proposed change in the constitu- tion of the new Board School brought him from the invalid's chamber. The effort was not repeated, and despite the medical skill of Dr. McDougall, Father Fennelley expired at the time stated. lie had ;it- tained the age of about '65 years. It is expected that his remains will be interred at Pantasaph on on Monday next.

div.head: REV. PETER MACKE-NZFE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: REV. PETER MACKE-NZFE AT RUNCORN.

The popular Wesleyan preacher, • the Rev. Peter MacKenzie paid a visit to Runcorn non Thursday. In the afternoon he held a special service in St. Paul's Chapel, and subsequently preadhed a characteristic sermon. There was a good congregation. In the evening the Public Hall was croWded with an audi- ence gathered to listen to Mr. MaCKenzie's lecture on the subject of •• Soloman ; his wealth, his wis- dom. and his power." The chair was occupied by Mr. Philia Speakman, who was -supported on the platform by the Revs. G. Wood. A. P. Watson, R. Hornabrook, E. Hall, and E. Williams; Messrs R. Norman, S. C Beckett, S. Pope, G. Bellamy. F. J. Norman, T. Boote, J. W. Woodland, J. Rawlinson, and E. Davies.

In his opening speech, the Chairman announced that the proceeds of the lecture would 'be devoted towards meeting the outlay of £9O upon a heating apparatus for Camden Sunday School. He knew of no institutiOn in Runcorn more worthy of their support. He had fre- quently likened the school to a 'bee hive, because from Sunday morning to Sunday evening the whole thing was working and it was well that the workers should be made comfortable. (Applause). The Lecturer, after a comprmientary reference to the chairman, dealt with his subject. He described Jerusalem now as cousin to Billingsgate on a Sunday morning, peopled with the ragged, the hungry and the starving; but said that in the days of Selomon it was a marvellous place. It was a land of corn and wine, and oil, favoured with God's peculiar smite, 'With every blessing blest. Its streets were the abode Of hucury, its markets were thronged with wares from every corner of creation; magnificent structures crowned the heights. and conspicuous above all the Temple glowed and glistened in all the glory of the rising, the meridian and the setting sun, and the smoke of incense ascended I morning and night into heaven. The magnificent structures erected by Solomon were mentioned and described, and his income was stated at £4795;000 a year. That was his stipend. Travelling preachers had not got up to that yet. They did not want to be bothered with it. (Laughter and applause.) Solomon-in his Lord Mayor's procession had 1,400 chariots going before him; 1,200 horsemen and every man amongst them had a horse nearly as good as Buffalo Bill. (Laughter.) Then there was a body guard of 500 stalwart men, with golden shields, and their heads were powdered, not with, the stuff we put on our flunkies, but powdered 'With gold dust. None of our stucco, none of your plaster of Paris there. (Laughter). The Lord Mayors'inlBB7 could not •come up to that. (Laughter.) Alluding to Solomon's wisdom, the Lecturer said he hada 'knowledge of the nature of birds and beasts, knew the virtue Of plants and the quality of precious stones, and he had also a marvellous power of foretelling things. Ile could cure all the ills that flesh was heir to. The wisdom of Solomon was seen in the fact that before ever he built a house for himself he Milt a temple for the Lord of Hosts that the people might worship the Supreme in the beauty of holiness. When God asked him what he would have, he asked for wisdom, knowledge. and understanding, for it was righteousness that exalted a nation, gave stability to a throne, and permanency to an empire. God was so pleased that Sdlomon did not ask for long life, or riches, or to be favoured with victory on the field of battle. that he granted his re- quest. Taking into account what he had written, and the fact that he had the cares of a kingdom, and.woo'd and won 700 wives, and had 300 concubines, Solomon was a marvellous and mysterious man. We had not got all that Solomon had written. He wrote 1,005 songs, and we had got a miserable one; we had 628 proverbs, and he wrote 3,000. In the song that he had given to usit required a spiritual mind to see its beauty, and it re- quired a spiritual mind to get the blessing out of it The wisdom of Solomon was seen in his proverbs, of which the lecturer gave some examples. As to Solomon's frilly, exclusiveness was the principle on which Judaism was built for a most Divine and proper reason. Now, Scfio- mon did not do wisely in this respect. He married foreign princesses. He woo'd. won, and married 700 wives, and if the Scripture said, "You are not be un- equally yoked together with unbelievers," what a state Solomon was in. He was not separate from the world ; but drank in the spirit of the world and became worldly. He was unrestrained in his pursuit of worldly pleasure. They might rest assured, however, that If we were to get happiness it must be by learning sobriety and temper- ance. In his old age King Solomon, with a multitude of wives, in the midst of strong passions of sensual in- dulgence, he was whirled away with the errors of demon worship; how his beauty was blighted, his strength prostrated, and his glory was covered in the dust. The lecturer urged the audience to Covet not the riches and vain pomp of this world, but to live so that they would have an inheritance that was incorruptible and that would never fade away. (Applause). On the motion of Mr. J. R. Frith, seconded by Mr. R. l'Corman, Mr. MacKenzie was cordially thanked for his lecture.
A vote of thanks was also accorded to the chairman, and the audience dispersed.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL THE WORKS COMMENCED. The directors of the Manchester Ship Canal ar- rived at Eastham, on Friday,, to formally witness 1 the operations in connection with the cutting of the Manchester Ship Canal at Eastham. The con- tractor had divided the canal works into. aine sec- tions of four and a half miles each, and on the Eastham section over 2,000 men will presently be fully employed. Taking this section as an illustra- tion, the canal wilt require for the next four years the services of 20,000 persons. Mr. Walker's contract for the canal is £6,000,000. The Suez Canal is 72 feet wide at the bottom, but the Manchester Ship Canal will have a minimum width of 120 ft. It will also be 26ft. deep. The Hooton Railway Station and the approaches to Benham were crowded on Friday with traction engines, steam. diggers, and machinery. Active operations will be commenced immediately. It will doubtless afford much pleasure to the shareholders to learn that so much progress has been made with the necessary preliminary work. In accordance with the idea of the original promo- ters, the lower portion of the Canal will be finished first, in order that it may be used for traffic whilst the upper reachestare being corapleted. Operations are, therefore, commencing at Eastham. and in a very short time a large body of men will be at work between that place and the mouth of the river Weaver, below Runcorn. Before long other por- tions of the canal will receive attention, and will absorb the labour of an army of men. Already the required land for a distance of fifteen mites—nearly half the entire length of the canal—has been se- cured, sad it is gratifying to be able to state that the landowners generally have metthe directors in a reasonable spirit. They evidently understand very plainly that in facilitating the labours of the directors and the completion of the canal at the earliest possible date they are also acting in a manner likely to secure their own ,individual in- terests. Hence the willingness with which most. of them have co-operated with the Board in taking the steps necessary before the land could be transferred to the Ship Canal Company. So far the amount that has been paid for land is Under the Parliamentary estimate, a fact avliieh proves that the promoters of the scheme did not endeavour to secure public sup- port by under-estimating the cost, but actually al- lowed more for the purchase of land than was necessary. Negotiations for the acquirement of the other land which is wanted are proceeding rapidly. and it is hoped with regard to this also that a like public spirit will be shown by the present owners. It would be an additional feather in the cap of the Me.nchester%hip 'Canal Company if its directors were able to say'that the amount paid by them to third parties,'ke., to arbitrators and their legal as- sistants, was the lowest on record in connection with a great public undertaking. LIBERAL MEETING AT WIDNES. A meeting 'held under the auspices of the Wid- nes Division Liberal Association, took place in the Baths Assembly Room on Monday evening for the purpose of protesting against the Irish policy of the Government. The building was crowded with an enthusiastic audience. Mr. E. K. Muspratt pre-, sided.'and lie was supported on the platform by Mr. T. E. -Ellis, M.P. for Merionethshire, Mr. D. Crilly. M.P. for North Mayo, Dr. Counsel, late candi- date for Dublin University. Dr. O'Keeffe, Dr. Mc- Donnell, Captain Brunner, Captain Wareing, Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, J. L. Muspratt. E. Carey, J. Fox. J. Morrison, H. B. Shores, &c. Mr. Muspratt said the registration work of the division' had just been completed. It had been very ' successful, and now that that was ended they pro- posed to hold a series of meetings inahe division to protest against the action of the Government under the Coercion Act. When that Act was being passed, the Government said it was only to be directed against crime, but since that, time it had been the endeavour of the Government to treat gentlemen like Mr. Dillon, M.P.—(cheers)—Mr. O'Brien, M.P. —(cheers)—and Mr. Sullivan, Lord Mayor of Dublin, as common gaol birds. (" Shame.' ) One of these gentlemen had been put in the common prison, and treated like a criminal, and he was glad to say that the result of this conduct was very different from that which the Government expected. As far as he could gather, the only effect hitherto had been that the names of Mr. O'Brien and these other gentlemen had been received with cheers—Uoud cheers)—by every. English audience, and that the Lord Mayor of Dublin had been invited to a banquet in his hon- our by the Liverpool Junior Reform Club This was a sign of the result which he held would fol- low the abominable and detestable action of the Government in treating their political epponents as common criminals. (Cheers). • Mr. H. B. Shores then read a letter from Mr. W. B. Bowrinz who, after expressing regret at his in- ability to attend the meeting and his sympathy with its objects, stated that it was. quite time the people of England awoke to the fact that the Present administrators of the law in Ireland were breakers of their own laws. (Applause.) Mr. Waring then moved the following resolution : " That this meeting desires to express its continued con- fidence in the Irish policy of M. W. E. Gladstone, and its strong disapproval of the arbitrary and illegal action of Her Majesty's Government in administering the Crimes Act in a manner contrary to the declarations made by the Ministers during the discussion of the measure in Parliament; and this meeting further con- demns the action of those members who now support the Government, contrary to the pledges given by them to th6r constituents at the last general election." (Cheers.) Mr. Waring condemned in the strongest terms the Coer- cion Act, and the manner in which it was administered, and went on to say that Coercion could only engender I one thing, and that was a spirit of bitter hostility in the minds of those against whom it was employed, and must inevitably bring about the total rout and destruction of those who employed it. (Cheers.) Under these circum- stances he asked-their undiminished and continued sup- port to Mr. Gladstone's Irish policy, which was a policy of Conciliation. (Cheers.) Mr. E. Carey seconded the resolution with the greatest Pleasure. He was glad to find that a meeting of Liberals in Widnes did not intend to introduce any subject of English, Scotch, or Welsh legislation which should inter- fere with the main object which the Liberal party now ' had in hand. (Cheers.) They must look neither to the ' right nor to the left until they had achieved this one ob- ject dear to their hearts, that was the setting of the Irish ; nation free to govern themselves in accordance with their own aspiration. (Cheers.) Dr. E. P. S. Counsel, late Home Rule candidate for the Dublin University. said it was impossible for any in- telligent man who had studied the career of Mr. Glad- , stone with an unprejudiced mind not to have confidence in Mr. Gladstone. All of them, he said, knew what had , happened recently in Ireland when Mr. O'Brien hadbeen sent to gaol in the most illegal manner after being wan- tonly assaulted by those who should have defended him from assault. They all knew that there had been lives , lost in Mitchelstown ; murders committed by men who, , he said, acted directly in the teethof thelaw .("Shame"). ' Who were now committing outrages? There had been statements made against the Irish leaders, and Mr. Gladstone in particular, that they had encouraged out- rages in Ireland. This was untrue. It was a gross per- version of the truth for Mr. Balfourto bring such a charge , against anyone, above all against one like Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) Mr. T. E. Ellis. M.P. for Merionethshire, in addressing the meeting, said that there was a large number of Radi- cals who complained very bitterly that Mr. Gladstone . put forward this great filth question In such a way as to break up the Liberal party. but'if they looked into and observed closely the events of to-day, they could not . but feel that whichever subject was taken up in 1885, ; it would have resulted inevitably in a partial break-up , of the Liberal party. There were four questions which , might have been taken up—the Irish question, the land question, disestablishment, and financiel reform. He ; maintained that whichever of these subjects had been taken no in earnest by the leader of the Liberal party, the Whigs and renegade Liberals would have broken away. The men who had left them had always been -drags, and it was well that they had left. , The Liberal party had renounced the policy of Coercion in Ireland, and, not content with renouncing the penal legislation of last century, they were renouncing equally ' the iniquitous system of governing Ireland by the despo- tism of Dublin Castle. In conclusion. Mr. Ellis said that now they could see that this system of landlordism was , doomed, and that 'Dublin Castle was going the way of all flesh. He hoped the electors of Widnes would do their duty in this struggle for giving Ireland a Native and National Parliament. (Cheers.) Mr. D. Crillv, M.P., supported the resolution. He said if the Tory Government thought that by their actions and unchristian policy they would force the Irish people to crime and outrage that party thought wrongly.. (Cheers.) In the old days the Irish people elected to tread the path of Passion.; to-day, haying confidence in the democracy and in the masses of England, the Irish leaders and the Irish people were determined to tread the path of patience. (Cheers.) The resolution was carried unanimously. The customary votes of thanks concluded the :proceed- ings. " Sapo-Liai," or Linseed Soap, cherishes-the cuticle. 6d. post free. COCKHEDGE MISSION MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The members of this class met on Mon- day stig'st to hear 'a paper read, upon" Success," by Mr. J. T. Blease. A very interesting discussion followed, in which Messrs. Hockenhull, Wright, Farrar, Atherton, Wadsworth, Oldham, and the president took part. The class is still increasing in numbers. HOLY TRINILY LYTERArtY SOCIETY.—At a meet- ing of this society on Monday evening, a paper on "Ancient and Modern Means and Methods of Con- veyance" was read before the members by Mr. F. W. Wood. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton occupiet the chair. In the course of the paper, Mr Wood dealt with the roads from those of the Romans until the present time, and then gave an interesting account of numerous vehicles that had been used in ancient and modern times. At the close of the paper a dis- cussion took place, and the essayist was awarded a cordial vote of thanks. WARRINGTON PEOPLE'S COLLEGE. -- Miss Sarah Sewards, Miss Annie H. Ashurst, and Miss Emily Brown who have recently completed their appren- ticeship as pupil teachers in this institution ,h sve each obtained Queen's scholarships of the first-class. standing respectively 107, 158, and 183 on the list. They will. enter the British and -Foreign School Society's Traininss College for School Mistresses, at Stockwell, in January next. 597 candidates for these scholarships were placed in the first-class, 1,240 in the second, and 333 in the third class, as the result of th e examinations held in July lees t hrough - out England. WYCLIFFE IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.. A very pleasant evening was spent on Tuesday in cennec- tion with this society, on the occasion of the Rev. J. Yonge giving a series of poetical readines. Selections were read by him from some of the well- known poets in a very accomplished -manner, and were attentively listened to by a large gathering of members and friends. Between the readings. selec- tions of music were given by Mrs. Pearson, Mr. Pearson, and Mr. W. H. Walling Son, accompanied on the piano by Mr. T. R. Ford, which considerably added to the pleasure of the evening. A Vote of thanks having been given to Mr. Yonge for his excellent entertainment, and to all who had helped, brought to a close a most enjoyable evening. DYSON S DIORAMA. AND G/PSY Each evening dining the week the noted diorama and gipsy choir of Mr. Joshua Dyson has formed the attraction at the Public Hall, which has, on the oc- casion of each performance, been crowded.. The en- tertainment provided by Mr. -Dyson is a combina- tion of pictorial representation and music, and is full of interest. Mr. Dyson is, indeed, a host in himself, and his little speeches explanatory of the scenes that-are represented are full of anecdote, and are an evidence of the store of knowledge that he possesses. The chair has each evening been taken by prominent local gentlemen. Independent of the interest attaching to the diorama itself, Mr. Dyson's gipsy choir give at intervals a very excellent musi- cal entertainment, the singing being of a very meri- torionworder. There was a complete change of pro- gramme each evening. The entertainment is to be repeatedthis (Saturday) evening. FENDERS. Fire Brasses, durbs. Tile Hearths, J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Earlestown.—Advt. A COMPLIMENT TO THE RETIRING MAYOR. '— At the Borough Court on Monday, Mr. T. Ridgway, solicitor, addressing Alderman Pickmere, who pre- sided on the bench as chief magistrate of the Borough, said he believed that that was the last day his Worship would sit is Mayor of the Borough .—Th e Mayor: For the presents—Mr. Ridgway said he wished to be allowed, on behalf of himself and the rest, ofthe members of the profession, to say how much they had been indebted to his Worship for the civility and csurteey whin he had always ren- dered the profession when disposing' of any cases that had been before him. Personally he was very much obliged to the Mayor for his kindness.—The Masyor, in reply, thanked Mr. Ridgway for his kind remarks. Since he had had the honour of being chief magistrate he had endeavoured to do his duty, and he should be very glad if his conduct had pleased not only the advocates, but the officers of the Court. and all conierned. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.— The members of this society met on Wednesday evening. when an able essay was given by Mr. But- ler on "The relations of science and religion." The chair was taken by Mr. S. B. Stringer. Referring to the immense strides made in every department dur- ing the present century. Mr. Butler stated there could be no conflict between science and religion, if he rightly understood the meaning of progress. which was from within, not without. He believed in progress because he believed in God. The fol- lowing reasons were advanced to explain why peo- ple think there is a conflict :-1. Putting too much trust in the traditional interpretation of Genesis. 2. With modern progress before theta (which has dealt so much with th , material) men have tended to materialism. 3. Professed unbeliever ei make a conflict whether there be one or not. The essayist proceeded to state that it was too early in the day, seeing that both science and religion were in a transitionary state, to say there is a conflict, and that eventually there could be none. Messrs. Storey, Barton,:llorton, Richardson, Hickman, Bennett, and the chairman Sook part in the debate.
