I THE ANCIENT GEOGILAPHY OF BRlTAlN.—Another of the series of lectures on "The ancient geography and geological history of Britain." was given in the Co-operative Hall, Warrington. on Monday even- ing, by 'Professor Boyd Dawkins. There was a large attendance In this lecture the leCturer dealt at some length, and in an instructive and interesting manner, with the geological and geographical con- ditions of the British ~Isles during the Old Red Sandstone' and Carboniferous periods. He remarked that during the Old Red Sandstone period there were certain chains of lakes in the British Isles.and in those liiites the old red'sandstenes were fOrrned and they were clearly proved to hare been isolated from one another and deposited in these lake basins by the way in which the shingle teaches lay in'rela- tion to the-older rocks. "They had ample proof of the sort of trees that flourished in that Old' Res Sandstone-time, the beautiful specimens of which have been so excellently described by Hugh Miller and others. The idea which they must form of the forestsin this country at.that period was that of the land covered with a dark sombre vegetation. There were also innunlerabls ferns, and some of the ferns which had been found in Ireland were amongst the-most beautiful of the fossil fernSfound in any part of-the world. They might ask him where was the sevatthat period. Well, the Devo- nian rocks were purely marine, and they stood un- mistakeably in the position-of the sea in the Old Red Sandstone time. The whole of ,the area of Devon. and nearly all, if not quite all, o 2 the area of Cornwall, was occupied by .the waters of the sea, and from the direction of Dev.mshire and West Somersetshiyethev could trace the sea right away under London. 'With regard to the animals, they found few instances of any vertebrate living on the land. Referring to the Carboniferous period—with whieh the greatness of Lancashire and Cheshire was inseparably associated—the lecturer remarked that if they stndied a piece of coal with the atten- tion it deserved they would find that it was .com- posed of two distinct elements. First of all they had the black element which milled their fingers, and secondly, they 'had the element which is bright and glittering and resinous, and -Which would not soil their fingers. Scattered in the piece of coal they would find little round bags, which were the snores of seeds of one of the plants of which the coal measures were formed. The 'blaring property of coal mainly depended upon the abundance of these little resinous bags, which, were almost iden- tical in shape to the resinous spores they would find on the club moss. Another kind of resin which was in coals was of exactly the same sort as that which exudes from the trunk of the pine tree. 'The black element in coal was formed simply by the decay of the rest of the plant. Professor Dawkins next ex- plained the manner in Which the coal beds were formed as they are now found. The lecture throughout was illustrated with maps and diagrams, and representations of fossil and other objects, RF:-OPENING. div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The state of affairs on the Stock Exchange this week has been the reverse of the preceeding one ; last week everything was buoyant, and brokers began to look upon. everything with quite a roseate view, prices were going up, the public were coming in the market, and a general and continued rise was to take place. The advent of this week belled the whole expectations. It began badly, grew worse, and has relapsed into even a worse state I than prevailed some three or four weeks ago. The Lon- don Mayor's show, combined with the shocking weather, prevented anything like even an apology for business possible. Added to this came the alarming rumours of the Emperor's and Crown Prince's health, which caused all the foreign Exchange to send down prices. Thursday the rumours became more vague, but more foreboding, with the result that a general collapse took place. Rus- sian 1873's fell 3, Egyptian, Hungarian and other inter- lAational stocks all show an appreciateddeeline. At the present moment investors would do well to hold their hands and touch nothing, as a rebound is certain to occur. •

Rio Tinto shares, which rose to 10i at the close of last week, have since declined, as was predicted in these columns, and those who have acted on the advice given here must have been able to clear a very good frofit. Home Rails, in sympathy with other stocks, show a decline' but there is no other reason for the fall. Several of these stocks are low, and offer a favourable opportunity for a purchase which is certain to prove profitable. American securities still, continue the see-saw move- ment which has characterised them for some time, and should with few exceptions to be left alone at the present time. '

The money market still remains quiet, and the demand for loans is on a very small scale. The directors of the Bank of England met on Thursday, but made no alteration in the bank rate, which remains at 4 per cent.
The company promoters still hold off. Every now and again there is a tentative sort of movement, but the general feeling is against anything like a boom in new in- vectments.

The announcement that the Empire Theatre is 'shortly coining out as a public company is premature, and we have authority for saying that in any event it will cer- tainly not be under the auspices of the people who brought out the Pavilion. _ _

The news which reached the City towards the closing hour of Thursday that the Imperial Bank of Germany had refused to advance loans on Russian stock caused quite a scare in Russian securities which fell at once 2}, having previously declined a half. Other international securities were affected, although in a much less degree. The advice tendered to investors in these columns has always been to get out of Russian and all international stocks which are from the nature of things subject to sudden panics. To a capital of £lOO,OOO in shares of £5 each the well-known match and vesta makers, Messrs R. Bell and Co., are inviting subscriptions, This is the oldest business in the trade and there is every reason to expect it will prove as profitable a business as Bryant and Mays. There is, in addition to the capital, £30,000 of five per cent debentures secured as a first charge upon the property and undertaking. The list closes on Tuesday for the country. ,

At Birdsall, near Mahon, on Thursday, Mrs. Parke, the wife of a farmer, died from poison administered to her by her nurse in mistake for medicine. 1 The throat of the Crown Prince of Germany was ex- amined at San Remo, on Wednesday, by the medical Men, and the result was very unfavourable. ANOTHER TRAGEDY IN LONDON.—Cries 9f " murder " were on Tuesday morning heard to proceed from No. 12, Euston-square, London, and on a policeman proceeding to the house, it was found that a terrible tragedy had been committed. The drawing-room floor of the house had been occupied for several months by a Frenchman, named Ernest Carter, aged 52, and Jeanne Hare, aged 22, a professional singer, who had been accompanied to this country by a man called Charles Kuss. On Monday night, all three went to the theatre, and returned home in the best of spirits, but early on Tuesday morning, Kuss, who slept in the apartment above the others, heard Carter calling for assistance, and on going down found Hure breathing her last. Carter observed that she had taken poison, and adding, "1 cannot live without her," at once pointed o,Vevolver at his breast, pulled the trigger, and fell dead, the bullet passing right through his body. Medical aid was immediately summoned, but without avail.
Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sustaining and nourishing beverage, Beware of imitations.— Advt.

The cause of death was a cold which he had caught on the Thursday, last week, and which rapidly developed in; o inflammation of the lungs. THEFT OF A HORSE AND COLLAR.—During Friday night last a horse and collar, the property of Mr. William Woods, of Stockton Heath, were stolen from the stable of Mrs. Potts, Lyrnm, whdre the animal, which was used to tow canal barges, had been put up for the night. Information was given to the police, and on Monday the horse was found alive at a" knacker's yard" in Man chester.

- - "THOMAS CARLYLE."-At the weekly meeting of the Lymm Mutual Improvement Society, held on Monday evening in the Wesleyan Schoolroom, a paper on "Thomas Carlyle" was read by Mr. John Brierley. After briefly noticing the various men of letters England had produced, from Chaucer to Shakespeare, followed by Milton, Dryden, Pope, Johnson, Byron, and Macaulay, Mr Brierley said they came in our own time to Thomas Carlyle, who might be regarded as the greatest literary light of thrzpast generation. Originally intended for the Church, he became a tutor, but neither as a minister nor a schoolmaster was Carlyle to do his life- work. Literature almost forced itself upon him, and his first efforts of any note were contributions to the Edinburgh Encyclopredia ;" but fame would probably be silent on these. His residence in Germany seems to have been the turning point in his career. There he formed the friendship of Goethe—a kindred soul. From this period might be dated that German influence, both in thought and phrase, which was the salient feature in most of Carlyle's works. His "Life of Schiller" was the first fruits of this element. He next translated Goethe's "Wilhelm Meister," His power of translation was, perhaps, one of the surest evidences of his literary ability, and in this field Carlyle had few rivals. At the conclusion of the paper a discussion ensued, the speakers 'being Messrs E. Brown, Gillanders, J. Dodds, W. Skilling, P.O. Moston, &c.

THE MURDER NEAR HEREFORD.—It is stated that Al- fred Seandrett, who was arrested at Worcester on Tues- day night, on a charge of being concerned in the murder of Mr. Ballard, at Tupsley, near Hereford, on the 19th ult., made a confession of his guilt yesterday morning, and also incriminated the man Jones, who was ar- rested a few days after the murder and is still in cus- tody.

THE GoVERNMENT AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION. - Sir Wm. Hart Dyke, who is paying-a political visit to Wor- cestershire, received at Worcester, on Tuesday, a depu- tation of gentlemen interested in educational matters, who urged various points in regard to the Government's Technical Education Bill. Sir William assured the depu- tation that the Government were thoroughly in earnAt in the matter, and hoped next session to carry measures dealing with this important question. He denied that the establishment of technical education in connection with elementary schools would entail additional burdens on the taxpayers, and he also dwelt on the importance of drawing as a foundation for technical education. SENTENCED TO DEATH FOR CHILD MURDER.-At the Notts and Lincoln Assizes, on Tuesday, at Nottingham. a domestic servant. named Mary Ann Warns, was tried for the wilful murder of her illegitimate child at Sutter- ton, Lincolnshire. On the 4th July the prisoner was delivered of a boy in Spilsby workhouse. After leaving she was seen at various places with the child, which was healthy, in her possession. A day or two after she left Sutterton the body of the child was dragged out of a hole in a field by dogs, and badly worried by them. When aamlited Warns said she had unintentionally given the baby an overdose of laudanum, but denied any viol- ence. A verdict of "Wilful murder," with a strong r,'- commendation to mercy, was returned. The prisoner was sentenced to death in the usual form. A Cabinet CO-tin-di was held at the Foreign Office on Friday which broke up after sitting nearly two hours. Dr. Bernard Finnegan, Roman Catholic Bishop of Kilmore, died on Friday morning at Collies ' House, Cavan. • The Hon. FL F. Cowper, formerly Liberal member for Herts, died at Panshanger on-Thursday night, after a lingering illnes.s. An epidemic of measles of a most alarming character is, prevalent at Tyldesley4 There are more than 200 cases under treatment. The fire at Mr. H. E. Randall's shoe manufactory at Northampton, which broke out on Thursday evening, raged until early on Friday morning. Two firemen were injured. _ The remains of the late Lord Wolverton were temporarily interred on Friday afternoon in the Parish Churchyard of Ham, near his lordship's seat at Combo. After attending the funeral Mr Gladstone caught the 5.30 express from Euston at Willesden and proceeded to Cheiter. Ax Ex-Somrsu SENTENCED TO DEATH.-At the Gloucester Assizes, on Friday, Enoch Wadley was sentenced to death for the murder of Elizabeth Hannah Evans at Kempley. Prisoner, who had been a soldier, criminally assaulted and stabbed the girl th death. The defence was insanity. A TRArALGAR-SQTYiRE MEETING.-MT William Saunders, formerly member of Parliament for East Hull, was arrested whilst making a speech in Trafalgar-square on Friday. It is understood that Mr Saunders, who had given the police notice of his intention, took this action, to test the right• of holding meetings in the square. • THE CAFFAREL SCANDALS. PARIS, Friday Afternoon.—M. Wilson was subjected to a judicial examination to-day. ' EXECUTION OF AMERICAN ANARCHISTS. - NEW YORK, Friday.—A telegram from Chicago states that the Anarchists Spies, Parsons, Fischer, and Engel have been duly executed. THE EMPRESS OF GERMANY PARALYSED. PARIS, Flamm—A telegram from Berlin to the " Matin ',' states that the Empress Augusta has had an attack of apoplexy, and that part of her body is para- lysed.
